title: What Buffalo Bills snap counts reveal about overtime escape against Rams
summary: Buffalo’s defense was forced to survive 82 snaps before one special-teams play changed everything. The Buffalo Bills’ 37-34 overtime win over the Los Angeles Rams had nearly everything: nine lead changes, 890 combined yards, 24 accepted penalties, a late collapse, an overtime fumble, a blocked field goal and, finally, a walk-off winner. The snap counts […]
full_text: Buffalo’s defense was forced to survive 82 snaps before one special-teams play changed everything. The Buffalo Bills’ 37-34 overtime win over the Los Angeles Rams had nearly everything: nine lead changes, 890 combined yards, 24 accepted penalties, a late collapse, an overtime fumble, a blocked field goal and, finally, a walk-off winner. The snap counts help explain why the game felt so exhausting. Buffalo played 64 offensive participation snaps compared with 82 for Los Angeles. The Bills’ defense spent nearly 38 minutes on the field and faced 54 Matthew Stafford pass attempts. Somehow, Buffalo survived it. The offense leaned on Josh Allen and James Cook, the defense bent until it could bend no further, and the special-teams unit supplied the plays that ultimately decided the game. Here is what the Bills’ Week 5 snap counts reveal. An injury forced Buffalo to change its offensive line Josh Allen, Dion Dawkins, Alec Anderson, Connor McGovern and O’Cyrus Torrence played all 64 offensive snaps. That left right tackle as the only position without complete continuity. Spencer Brown played 16 snaps before leaving with a back injury during the second quarter. Tylan Grable replaced him and played the remaining 48, giving him a 75% offensive share. Buffalo allowed only one official sack, which came on its opening possession, and the offensive line helped create 234 rushing yards at 6.3 yards per attempt. Grable stepped into a difficult assignment against a Rams front and helped the Bills continue running the ball effectively. His performance will become even more important if Brown is unable to play against the Las Vegas Raiders. James Cook’s workload returned, along with the ball-security concerns. After receiving only 12 carries against New England, Cook carried the ball 25 times in Los Angeles. He turned those opportunities into 111 yards and two touchdowns, playing 40 snaps, or 62% of Buffalo’s offense. Unfortunately, Cook also fumbled twice. Cook’s snap count and rushing production were encouraging. His ball security nearly made all of it irrelevant. Ty Johnson played only 14 offensive snaps, but his limited workload produced four receptions for 72 yards. Ray Davis received 10 snaps and added a 31-yard catch. Buffalo kept using its tight ends without getting much production. Dalton Kincaid and Dawson Knox each played 45 offensive snaps, a 70% share. Jackson Hawes received another 28 snaps, while Keleki Latu appeared on three offensive plays. The playing time did not translate into receiving production. Kincaid caught one pass for seven yards. Knox caught one for six. Together, they produced two receptions for 13 yards on five targets. Buffalo continues to devote substantial playing time to multiple-tight-end formations, but the passing-game return has disappeared over the past two weeks. The Bills dressed four tight ends and gave three of them meaningful offensive work, yet Allen received far more production from Johnson and Davis on a fraction of the snaps. A depleted receiver room created an unusual distribution. With DJ Moore and Joshua Palmer inactive, Keon Coleman led Buffalo’s wide receivers with 45 snaps. Khalil Shakir followed with 44, while Skyler Bell played 39 in his NFL debut. Shakir once again made his opportunities count. He caught all three of his targets for 80 yards, including a 57-yard reception in overtime. Buffalo did not ask Allen to throw often, but when it needed explosive plays through the air, Shakir and Johnson provided them. Eighty-two defensive snaps tell an uncomfortable story Cole Bishop played all 82 defensive snaps. C.J. Gardner-Johnson and Terrel Bernard each played 78, while Christian Benford logged 77 despite temporarily leaving with an injury. Davison Igbinosun played 69 snaps, Bradley Chubb received 67 and Greg Rousseau played 66. Those are enormous workloads, particularly for a defense missing Ed Oliver and Landon Jackson. They also reflect Buffalo’s inability to get off the field consistently. Los Angeles converted seven of 14 third downs and both of its fourth-down attempts. The Rams produced 33 first downs, scored touchdowns on all five red-zone possessions and held the ball for 37:57. Deone Walker played 63 snaps, followed by T.J. Sanders with 51, DeWayne Carter with 37, Michael Hoecht with 30 and Greg Gaines with 26. Phidarian Mathis received 15 snaps after being elevated for the game. Carter recorded Buffalo’s only sack. The Bills were credited with four quarterback hits, one each from Carter, Walker, Bernard and Rousseau. That was not nearly enough against Stafford, who completed 40 of 54 attempts for 383 yards and three touchdowns. Puka Nacua alone received 24 targets, catching 17 for 138 yards and a touchdown. Buffalo’s secondary tackled well after the catch, with Bishop recording 11 total tackles and Benford adding 10. The larger problem was how often the Bills were forced to tackle. Los Angeles kept extending possessions. Six special-teams snaps were enough for Rousseau Joe Andreessen and Sam Franklin led Buffalo with 23 special-teams snaps apiece. Trent Sherfield, Latu and Javon Solomon each played 17, while Hoecht, T. Parker, Jordan Kilgore and Keonta Elarms-Orr received 16. Rousseau played only six snaps on special teams. One was all he needed to make the biggest impact of the night. Special teams had influenced the game from the opening kick. Davis returned it 70 yards to the Los Angeles 26, immediately placing Buffalo in scoring range. He finished with 114 yards on three kickoff returns, while Greg Dortch added 105 yards on four returns. Together, Buffalo averaged 31.3 yards per kickoff return.
author: Sara Larson

title: Why NFL teams with late leads should be more aggressive on defense
summary: We’ve all seen it before. Many times. Too many times, in fact. A team has a lead late in the fourth quarter, and the defense seemingly operates not to lose, regularly sitting in conservative off-man or zone coverage. Blitzing is minimized. They try to keep everything in front. And all it does is allow the […]
full_text: We’ve all seen it before. Many times. Too many times, in fact. A team has a lead late in the fourth quarter, and the defense seemingly operates not to lose, regularly sitting in conservative off-man or zone coverage. Blitzing is minimized. They try to keep everything in front. And all it does is allow the opposing offense to do anything it wants as it matriculates the ball down the field to get the game-winning or game-tying score. Heck, we just saw it in the Buffalo Bills win over the Rams on Monday Night Football in Week 5. In a 27-27 game in the fourth quarter, Josh Allen led the Bills on a scoring drive, capped by a James Cook touchdown that, after the extra point, gave Buffalo a 34-27 lead with 1:39 remaining. Then the Bills defense played on back on its heels. No blitzes. Enormous cushion from the cornerbacks. Rams scored a touchdown on an eight-play drive that took 1:34 off the clock and didn’t even need to use a timeout. It was precisely the consensus defensive coordinator philosophy in these type of end-of-game scenarios. The idea for it first stems from a fear of allowing a deep pass over the top for a touchdown. Aligned with that fear is the thought that it’s harder for an offense to methodically move the ball down the field on a long drive without making a key mistake. A dropped pass that turns into an interception, the quarterback getting stripped while he’s sacked etc. So the defensive coordinators attempt to force the opposing offense into a long drive. And there’s credence to this line of thinking. But I think it’s wrong. Or, it’s probably more apt to write, it’s not the optimal way defenses should approach these late-game scenarios while holding a lead… and the reason isn’t solely based on the defense itself. And this dawned on me after studying the surge in end-of-half scoring a few weeks ago. Here’s my thesis statement on this topic: Defenses holding a lead late in games should deploy an aggressive strategy up front and in the secondary to make it as challenging as possible for the opposing offense to move the ball and all but completely eliminate any fear of allowing a quick touchdown BECAUSE allowing a quick score is not the worst possible outcome… allowing a slow one is. And the numbers back up this claim. I used the handy nflverse play-by-play data from 2001 to 2025 to check the outcomes for drives in the final 2:00 to 4:00 of the game when a team was trailing by between 4 to 8 points. In all of these scenarios, a touchdown was surrendered by the defense on 35.1% of those drives. So that’s the baseline. Of course I couldn’t view and assess if the defenses were “aggressive” or “conservative” in those scenarios. But the key to this study was the timing of the allowed touchdown and what transpired on the ensuing drive. How quickly did the defense allow the go-ahead or game-tying score? And how often did the originally leading team’s offense go on to retake the lead afterward? To find the differences here, I broke the initially allowed touchdown into two buckets — scoring drives of 90 seconds or less (quick TDs) and those that took more than 90 seconds (slow TDs). Here’s what I discovered: When a defense protecting a 4 to 8 point lead surrendered a touchdown on a possession beginning within 2:00 to 4:00 remaining in the game, the speed of the initially allowed score certainly mattered to the next offensive opportunity: After allowed touchdown drives that took 90 seconds or less, the original leading team scored (FG or TD) on the ensuing drive 33.7% of the time After allowed touchdown drives that took longer than 90 seconds, the original leading team scored (FG or TD) on the ensuing drive 19.4% of the time And that seams natural doesn’t it? More time on the clock, the stronger the likelihood of scoring. With how efficient offenses have gotten in late-game scenarios, it’s completely sensible for the defense with the lead to crank the aggression in search of a turnover even if that philosophy technically raises the chances of a quick-strike touchdown from the opponent. Because even in that scenario, giving your offense as much time as possible to counter is incredibly valuable.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Greg Rousseau earns AFC Special Teams Player of the Week after saving Bills in overtime
summary: Greg Rousseau is collecting NFL honors in more than one department. Less than two weeks after earning AFC defensive honors for the month of September, “Groot” adds another award for a game-saving block. The Buffalo Bills standout was named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week for Week 5 after blocking Harrison Mevis’ potential game-winning […]
full_text: Greg Rousseau is collecting NFL honors in more than one department. Less than two weeks after earning AFC defensive honors for the month of September, “Groot” adds another award for a game-saving block. The Buffalo Bills standout was named AFC Special Teams Player of the Week for Week 5 after blocking Harrison Mevis’ potential game-winning 48-yard field goal in overtime Monday night. The play gave Buffalo another possession, and Tyler Bass finished the job with a 45-yard kick to secure a 37-34 victory over the Los Angeles Rams. It is Rousseau’s first career AFC Special Teams Player of the Week award and Buffalo’s first in the category since Bass earned the honor in Week 9 of the 2024 season. According to the Bills PR, it was the NFL’s first blocked field goal in overtime since Pittsburgh’s T.J. Watt blocked an attempt against Cleveland on September 9, 2018. It was also the first overtime field-goal block that led to a victory since San Francisco’s Dontae Johnson blocked one against St. Louis on January 3, 2016, during the 2015 season. Buffalo’s previous field-goal block came at Atlanta on October 13, 2025. The player responsible? Rousseau. Joe Brady awarded Rousseau a game ball after Monday’s win, telling the locker room, “I’ll never get tired of giving him game balls.” With Rousseau finding new ways to change games, Brady may want to keep a few extras handy.
author: Sara Larson

title: Bills climb in Week 6 power rankings, but did the overtime escape convince everyone?
summary: Buffalo regains ground nationally as the Raiders slide ahead of Sunday’s matchup in Las Vegas. The Buffalo Bills needed a blocked field goal and one more Josh Allen rescue mission to leave Los Angeles with a win. The national power rankings rewarded them anyway. Buffalo improved to 4-1 with its 37-34 overtime victory over the […]
full_text: Buffalo regains ground nationally as the Raiders slide ahead of Sunday’s matchup in Las Vegas. The Buffalo Bills needed a blocked field goal and one more Josh Allen rescue mission to leave Los Angeles with a win. The national power rankings rewarded them anyway. Buffalo improved to 4-1 with its 37-34 overtime victory over the Rams, recovering some of the ground it lost after the Week 4 defeat against New England. Now the Bills head to Las Vegas to face a Raiders team whose encouraging start has given way to two consecutive losses. Once again, our comparison features ESPN, NFL.com, The Athletic, CBS Sports, USA Today, FOX Sports, Yahoo Sports and Pro Football Talk. Bills climb back into the consensus top three Buffalo rises from fifth to third in the eight-outlet consensus. Its average ranking improves from 5.38 to 4.25, placing the Bills behind only San Francisco and Kansas City in the combined standings. Seven of the eight outlets moved Buffalo up. Pro Football Talk held the Bills at fourth. ESPN, The Athletic, FOX Sports and Yahoo Sports now rank Buffalo third. USA Today remains the lowest of the group at seventh, with NFL.com placing the Bills sixth. That is an encouraging recovery, but Monday night did not suddenly erase Buffalo’s problems. Allen rushed for 121 yards, James Cook added 111 and the Bills finished with 234 rushing yards. The offensive line kept the ground game moving despite losing Spencer Brown during the second quarter. Greg Rousseau blocked the potential game-winning field goal in overtime, and Tyler Bass made the winning kick from 45 yards. Those are legitimate reasons to reward Buffalo. So are the issues that keep some outlets from moving the Bills higher: two turnovers, 13 penalties and a defense that allowed 454 yards and five touchdowns. FOX Sports’ Ralph Vacchiano moved Buffalo two spots to third while emphasizing Allen’s impact and the need to fix the defense. NFL.com’s Nick Shook similarly credited Buffalo’s resilience while identifying Cook’s ball security as a problem. The Bills proved they could find a way to win. They still have to prove they can make winning look less exhausting. Raiders slide after a difficult trip to New England Las Vegas began the season 3-0. Two games later, the Raiders are 3-2 and falling across every outlet in our comparison after a 45-17 loss to the Patriots. Their consensus position drops from 11th to 16th, while their average ranking falls from 11.50 to 16.25. CBS Sports delivered the largest drop, moving Las Vegas eight places to 18th. Yahoo Sports remains the most optimistic at 12th, while NFL.com has the Raiders 19th. New England produced 536 yards against Las Vegas, including 165 on the ground. The Raiders managed only 38 rushing yards themselves, leaving little balance to support Kirk Cousins and the passing game. The optimism surrounding the opening three wins has cooled considerably. Buffalo arrives with an opportunity to extend that slide. A rankings gap Buffalo needs to justify All eight outlets rank Buffalo ahead of Las Vegas. The difference between their average positions is 12 spots, compared with 6.13 entering Week 5. That does not make Sunday an automatic win. Buffalo’s defense just allowed Matthew Stafford to complete 40 passes and watched the Rams erase a seven-point deficit in 94 seconds. A struggling opponent does not eliminate those concerns, particularly when Brock Bowers remains capable of creating problems. He caught eight passes for 110 yards and a touchdown against New England despite the lopsided result. The Bills’ running game offers the clearest opportunity. Buffalo restored Cook’s workload in Los Angeles, and Allen’s legs repeatedly supplied the explosive plays the passing game lacked. Against a Raiders defense that struggled to stop New England on the ground, Buffalo has a chance to build on that production. The challenge is finishing drives, protecting the football and getting enough defensive stops to avoid another game that requires a last-second rescue. And where did the Rams land? Los Angeles falls from sixth to a tie for ninth in the same eight-outlet consensus, with its average ranking dropping from 7.63 to 9.63. The Athletic delivered the steepest decline, moving the Rams from fifth to 10th. NFL.com went the other direction, raising them from 13th to 12th despite the loss. At 2-3, the Rams still receive considerable respect, but another productive offensive performance ended with special-teams mistakes and a defeat. They remain the only team with a losing record in the consensus top 10. A win restored confidence, but a cleaner one would help keep it. The rankings reflect confidence in Buffalo’s ability to win even when the game becomes chaotic. Sunday offers a chance to show the Bills can also take control of a matchup and keep it. Allen and the special-teams unit have already shown they can rescue Buffalo. A less dramatic afternoon in Las Vegas would be a welcome change.
author: Sara Larson

title: Bills offense continues to deliver when defense falters
summary: The Buffalo Bills defeated the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night, thanks to a field goal in overtime to secure a 37-34 victory. Despite the shortcomings of the Bills defense, the offense once again stepped up behind the play of Josh Allen. As a fan, it often feels as if the offense steps up when […]
full_text: The Buffalo Bills defeated the Los Angeles Rams on Monday night, thanks to a field goal in overtime to secure a 37-34 victory. Despite the shortcomings of the Bills defense, the offense once again stepped up behind the play of Josh Allen. As a fan, it often feels as if the offense steps up when the Bills defense falters against some of the NFL’s top clubs. Sometimes I take these feelings with a grain of salt, as I can sometimes overreact when it comes to the defensive shortcomings of the team. But every once in awhile there is a statistic that shows I have not been overreacting, and that feeling in your gut has been warranted. That statistic comes courtesy of WTF Sports on X/Twitter, who shared that the Bills have won their last 8 games since allowing 31+ games per contest. The Bills have won each of their last 8 regular season games when allowing 31+ points. pic.twitter.com/LyNy8TVLuj — WTF Stats (@WTFstats) October 13, 2026 This streak goes back almost two years ago, and started with the Bills 48-42 victory over the Detroit Lions in December 2024. The fact that the Bills have given up 31+ points in a third of their past 24 regular season games is a conversation for another day. It should also be noted that the Bills have given up 31+ points in two other games this season – a 36-31 Week 1 win over the Houston Texans, and a 41-31 week two victory over the Lions. While the Bills lack of defense has certainly been frustrating, it has certainly led to some exciting football so far this season.
author: Anthony Marino

title: Who earned game balls after Bills escaped Week 5 with overtime win?
summary: One blocked field goal gave Buffalo life, and the Bills did not waste it. For most of Monday night, the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams seemed determined to see which team could deliver the final dramatic blow. Buffalo took a seven-point lead with 1:39 remaining. Los Angeles erased it in 94 seconds. The Bills […]
full_text: One blocked field goal gave Buffalo life, and the Bills did not waste it. For most of Monday night, the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Rams seemed determined to see which team could deliver the final dramatic blow. Buffalo took a seven-point lead with 1:39 remaining. Los Angeles erased it in 94 seconds. The Bills received the ball first in overtime, drove into Rams territory and then gave it away when James Cook fumbled. Los Angeles moved close enough to attempt a 48-yard field goal for the win. Greg Rousseau made sure it never had the chance. Rousseau blocked the kick, and Tyler Bass ended the game with a 45-yard field goal. Buffalo escaped SoFi Stadium with a 37-34 victory and improved to 4-1. Joe Brady recognized the three he felt deserved game balls. Game ball: Greg Rousseau “I’ll never get tired of giving him game balls,” Joe Brady said before recognizing Rousseau. Rousseau did not dominate the defensive box score. But none of that mattered when Buffalo needed one play to keep the game alive. Cook’s overtime fumble gave Los Angeles possession at its own 20-yard line. Matthew Stafford moved the Rams 50 yards in eight plays, setting up what should have been the game-winning attempt. Rousseau broke through the protection and got his hand on the kick. Instead of watching Los Angeles celebrate, Buffalo’s defense walked off the field having given Allen and the offense one final opportunity. Game ball: Tyler Bass Bass’ night was not perfect, but it ended perfectly. He made field goals from 49 and 23 yards during the first half before missing the extra point following Keon Coleman’s third-quarter touchdown. That miss briefly looked as though it might become a much larger part of the story. Bass answered when Buffalo needed him again. He made the extra point after Cook’s late touchdown and then converted from 45 yards in overtime, finishing the game with 11 total points. Game ball: Buffalo’s offensive line Buffalo entered the game with a depleted receiving corps and finished it without starting right tackle Spencer Brown, who left during the second quarter with a back injury. The offensive line still helped the Bills produce their best rushing performance of the season. Buffalo carried 37 times for 234 yards and three touchdowns, averaging 6.3 yards per attempt. Allen rushed for 121 yards, Cook added 111 more. Brown played only 16 offensive snaps before Tylan Grable replaced him for the remaining 48. Despite the adjustment, Buffalo allowed only one official sack and repeatedly created running lanes against a Rams defensive front featuring Aaron Donald. The Bills did not simply accumulate rushing yards on a handful of broken plays. They leaned on the ground game throughout the night, running 37 times compared with only 19 pass attempts. Honorable mention: Josh Allen Allen completed only 12 of 19 passes, finishing with 210 yards, one touchdown and one interception. Buffalo’s depleted receiving corps did not provide many easy answers, so Allen created his own. He carried the ball 10 times for 121 yards and a touchdown. Honorable mention: Ty Johnson Johnson played only 14 offensive snaps, but he made nearly every one of his opportunities count. He caught all four of his targets for 72 yards, including gains of 40 and 26. His four receptions accounted for one-third of Buffalo’s completions and more than one-third of its passing yards. That is a substantial contribution from a player who was on the field for only 22% of the offensive snaps. Honorable mention: James Cook Cook’s night requires two separate conversations. The first is about his production. After receiving only 12 carries against New England, he handled 25 against the Rams. The second conversation is about holding onto the football. Cook fumbled twice. Buffalo recovered the first, but the second came in overtime after the offense had already crossed midfield. That turnover gave the Rams a direct opportunity to win and required Rousseau to rescue the game. Cook may still deserve an honorary game ball after rushing for 111 yards and two touchdowns. But given how overtime went, and the 10 other lost fumbles since 2025; someone else should probably carry it to him and make sure the handoff is clean. The production was too important to ignore. So was the mistake. Both can be true.
author: Sara Larson

title: Carolina Panthers 2027 NFL Draft Prospect Profile: Jamari Sharpe
summary: The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the […]
full_text: BLOOMINGTON, IN - SEPTEMBER 19: Indiana Hoosiers DB Jamari Sharpe (22) warms up prior to a college football game between the Western Kentucky Hilltopppers and Indiana Hoosiers on September 19, 2026 at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, IN. (Photo by James Black/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2027 NFL Draft feels like forever away, and we’re all caught up in the start of the NFL season. Regardless, it’s never too early to look ahead to the Draft. This weekly series will take a closer look at some of the prospects the Carolina Panthers could select in the 2027 iteration of the Draft. In this series, we’ll only be looking at prospects the Panthers could seriously consider. This week our profile will focus on Indiana Hoosiers cornerback Jamari Sharpe Bio Sharpe (6’1”, 187 lbs.) was a speedster wide receiver and track star in Miami, FL before finally switching to corner his senior year of high school. The nephew of former NFL corner Glenn Sharpe, was only a three star recruit and signed with Indiana, redshirting his freshman season in 2022. As a redshirt freshman, he broke into the starting lineup for most games. The following season saw the Hoosiers hire Curt Cignetti, and Sharpe’s role on the defense dwindled. Despite the fewer snaps, there was a noticeable jump in Sharpe’s technique and understanding of the defensive concepts. Last season, Sharpe won the starting corner spot opposite D’Angelo Ponds (who was a second round pick in last year’s Draft). Including Indiana’s bowl games, Sharpe tallied 50 tackles, six for loss, six passes defended, a fumble recovery, and a National Championship sealing interception against Miami. He has continued to play well this season despite missing a game early in the year due to injury. Strengths/Weaknesses Sharpe’s biggest strength is his zone coverage. He does an excellent job of reading the quarterback’s eyes and driving on throws with his elite athleticism. His track star speed allows him to be more patient because he is confident in his recovery on downfield throws. His improved technique under Cignetti goes beyond just coverage, as his tackling has become a lot more consistent (only charged with four missed tackles in 2025). His size/speed combination is exactly what NFL defenses look for in an outside corner. Sharpe’s production has not matched his coverage ability, leading some scouts to be a bit wary. He only intercepted one pass through the entirety of Indiana’s championship run, and that one came at the very end of the Championship Game. While he has been able to force several fumbles, his run defense is average at best. He’s a willing run defender, but isn’t a game changer on the outside. Projection Jamari Sharpe is a rangy zone corner with the size and speed to be effective at the next level. His growth under Curt Cignetti demonstrates a coachability and desire to improve that defensive staffs will love. Starting all 16 games for a national championship team will be looked upon highly as well. While his man coverage skills lag behind his elite zone skills, he does well enough to stay on the field regardless of the coverage called. A team like the Panthers, who run a lot of off zone coverage, would be a perfect fit for Sharpe. Ejiro Evero’s defense (if he is still the DC next season) would allow Sharpe to use his eyes and speed to their fullest advantage. What do you think, Panthers fans? If Jamari Sharpe is available when the Panthers select in the 2027 NFL Draft, should they take him? Sound off in the comments!

title: Panthers get reinforcements out of the bye as they get ready for the Eagles
summary: An early bye week is normally not something NFL teams want. They’d rather it be towards the end of the season so the guys can get some R&R in preparation for the home stretch. It’s often wasted early in the season. But not for the Carolina Panthers this year. Training camp through the first four […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - SEPTEMBER 20: A Carolina Panthers football helmet on the turf prior to the start of the NFL game between the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons on September 20th, 2026 at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images An early bye week is normally not something NFL teams want. They’d rather it be towards the end of the season so the guys can get some R&R in preparation for the home stretch. It’s often wasted early in the season. But not for the Carolina Panthers this year. Training camp through the first four weeks of the season was rough on the roster, and guys were dropping like flies. But the week off has done some good. Players that had been out are back at practice, so it’s looking like we’ll get closer to what this roster is supposed to look like. Panthers Injury Report Monroe Freeling – DNP – Knee AJ Dillon – DNP – Ankle Damien Lewis – LP – Elbow Jaelan Phillips – LP – Hamstring Tommy Tremble – LP – Ribs Darren Waller – LP – Toe Taylor Moton – FP – Lungs Tershawn Wharton – FP – Neck Jalen Coker – FP – Quadriceps Bryce Young – FP – Knee Trevor Etienne – FP – Ankle Thomas Incoom – FP – Ribs The highlights here are in bold. Taylor Moton immediately jumped back into a full practice after a scary bout with a blood clot in his lungs that kept him out in training camp and the first few weeks of the season. The timing couldn’t be better, as rookie right tackle Monroe Freeling has been taking a beating while taking his lumps as a rookie, and he wasn’t at practice to start the week. On the other side of the ball, Tershawn Wharton is back after undergoing neck surgery in the offseason. He’s been plagued by injuries since signing with Carolina. Hopefully he’s fully healthy and able to build some momentum. It’s nice to see Damien Lewis and Jaelan Phillips back at practice, even in a limited fashion. It’s possible either could already be back this week, though I’d guess it’s more likely for Lewis than for Phillips given the nature of their respective injuries. Trevor Etienne and Thomas Incoom will also be making their returns from injured reserve, which gives the Panthers more depth and bodies for special teams. Etienne will probably get some carries as well if AJ Dillon is unable to give it a go. And Jalen Coker seems to be all good to go after getting banged up a couple times in the weeks leading up to the bye week. Eagles Injury Report Saquon Barkley – DNP – Hamstring Devonta Smith – DNP – Hamstring/toe Michael Carter II – DNP – Abdomen Will Shipley – DNP – Foot Drew Kendall – DNP – Knee Jalyx Hunt – DNP – Knee/ankle Jakorian Bennett – LP – Unspecified Marquise Brown – LP – Ankle Grant Calcaterra – LP – Back Landon Dickerson – LP – Knee AJ Espenesa – LP – Back Marcus Epps – LP – Groin Jonathan Greenard – LP – Ankle EJ Jenkins – LP – Toe Tyler Steen – LP – Shoulder Eli Stowers – LP – Quad Dontayvion Wicks – LP – Hamstring I left out the full practice participants because this list seemed plenty. It almost would have been shorter to list out the Eagles that are not on the injury report. Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni had expressed hope that their two offensive stars Saquon Barkley and Devonta Smith would be back this week, but the fact that neither practiced at all to start the week makes their status more questionable than he maybe let on. Starting center Drew Kendall is going to be out, which means starting left guard Willie Lampkin will move to center while Landon Dickerson will make his return from his knee injury to start at left guard on a suddenly depleted Eagles offensive line.

title: Panthers vs Eagles: Storylines to watch
summary: Hello CSR! We’re rocking and rolling into another game week as the 2-2 Panthers are coming off a bye and traveling to Philadelphia for a battle against the 2-3 Eagles. The Eagles started off 2-0 to begin the season but have since lost 3 straight games as they too have experienced the injury bug and […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - DECEMBER 08: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles runs the ball up the field in the fourth quarter of a game against the Carolina Panthers at Lincoln Financial Field on December 08, 2024 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Hello CSR! We’re rocking and rolling into another game week as the 2-2 Panthers are coming off a bye and traveling to Philadelphia for a battle against the 2-3 Eagles. The Eagles started off 2-0 to begin the season but have since lost 3 straight games as they too have experienced the injury bug and shuffling of their roster. OT Lane Johnson abruptly retired last week, they then traded C Cam Jurgens, and they’ve been dealing with multiple injuries at RB including Saquon Barkley, and were missing WR Devonta Smith last week. Those two specifically could be back this week, which might provide a boost to an offense that has struggled MIGHTILY this season. The Panthers have been dealing with several issues of their own, but could be getting back OT Taylor Moton, DT Turk Wharton, and RB Trevor Etienne this week from their own injury absences. We won’t know the status on any of these guys until much closer to the game, but we can still evaluate the storylines going into the game now. Offense: Dealing with the Eagles front, specifically Jalen Carter The Eagles could also be missing EDGE players Jalyx Hunt and Jonathan Greenard, but this is still a pretty strong unit that the Panthers beat up offensive line will be facing this week. They have LBs Zach Baun and Jihaad Campbell manning the front behind DL Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, and EDGE Nolan Smith Jr. Jalen Carter in particular could be a massive problem for this Panthers front, whether he lines up in the interior or on the outside. Carter can be extremely disruptive, causing 3 sacks and forcing 3 fumbles already this season, and for a Panthers unit that is playing well in the passing game but still allowing a ton of pressures on Bryce Young, Carter could very much be the X-Factor for this game plan. I don’t know how the Panthers will contain him, especially if both Taylor Moton and Monroe Freeling can’t play, and I didn’t necessarily like the matchup even if one of those two guys is playing. Brad Idzik could elect to again hammer the RPO plays to give Bryce Young some quick completions like they did against the Lions front seven, but the Eagles secondary is considerably better than the beat up unit that Detroit fielded. Defense: Contain Jalen Hurts The common denominator in both of the Panthers losses this season was facing a mobile quarterback. While week 1 was an all around bad defensive effort, the Panthers defense has done a relatively solid job in the other 3 games. However, when they faced the Browns, Deshaun Watson’s ability to extend plays and break contain was ultimately the downfall of the defense, who again weren’t “bad”, but those scrambles by Watson were back breaking when the defense was attempting to get off the field. Things won’t get any easier this week, as Hurts can definitely run and likely will since the rest of the offense for the Eagles has very much struggled to get much going. If there’s ever a game for the defense to clean up the issues with containing the quarterback and preventing scrambles, its this one. Having Devin Lloyd back will certainly help, but he can’t do it all and he very much needs the edge defenders to do their job. Bonus storyline: The plan at cornerback While the Panthers walked away with a win against a very productive Detroit offense in week 4, their cornerbacks got targeted quite a bit, specifically Akayleb Evans. Now, nobody expected both Mike Jackson and Jaycee Horn to go down in the same game the week prior, but the Panthers didn’t really change the formula too much during their bye week. Will Lee, Evans, and Chau Smith-Wade still are the only cornerbacks on the active roster, and they did some churning on the practice squad and have 5 guys eligible to be promoted to the game day roster there. The Eagles have some speedy options between the always reliable Devonta Smith, Makai Lemon, and some of their other depth. The passing offense for them hasn’t been great for several weeks, but Nick Sirianni may choose to let Jalen Hurts put some air yards out there to try and get their offense back on some sort of schedule. Ejiro Evero will need a plan to limit the big plays, and obviously their safety room will play into the equation as well. What are you watching for this week, Panthers fans?

title: Bears offense searching for consistency
summary: After a brutal loss to the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, the Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson emphasized one issue the offense continues to face: a lack of consistency. With Caleb Williams sidelined, Johnson noted the unit’s struggles have varied from week to week, ranging from red-zone issues to three-and-outs and turnovers. “As a […]
full_text: CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 04: Head coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears looks on during the second quarter of the game against the New York Jets at Soldier Field on October 04, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Jessie Alcheh/Getty Images) | Getty Images After a brutal loss to the Green Bay Packers on Sunday, the Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson emphasized one issue the offense continues to face: a lack of consistency. With Caleb Williams sidelined, Johnson noted the unit’s struggles have varied from week to week, ranging from red-zone issues to three-and-outs and turnovers. “As a whole, it’s just consistency. Our play style needs to show up on a regular basis,” Johnson said. “It’s getting back to what we did all through camp and how we started the first week of the season. I don’t know that we’ve done that at a consistent level since then.” After scoring 59 points on 552 total yards of offense, including 291 rushing yards and eight touchdowns Week 1, the Bears followed it up in Week 2 with just 297 total yards and a single field goal. One could point to the weather or the eight penalties the Bears committed in Week 2 as reasons for the drop-off, but a similar pattern emerged between Weeks 4 and 5. In Week 4, the Bears ran 89 plays, recorded 492 total yards, didn’t punt once, and had a time of possession of 42:45. A totally dominant performance from the offense. The following week, however, the Bears managed just 246 total yards and seven points. Of course, having backup quarterback Tyson Bagent standing in for Caleb Williams plays a significant role in the offense’s struggles. Still, Johnson expects more from this unit despite the circumstances. Johnson acknowledged that the offense struggled to find a rhythm on Sunday and took responsibility for his role in getting the group going. “Certainly, as a playcaller, I got to help get these guys in a better rhythm to move the ball down the field,” Johnson said. The Bears conducted a walk-through on Wednesday instead of a full practice. Johnson explained that this was the plan going into the season, allowing the team to take a big-picture look at the first five weeks before their bye in Week 10. The goal was to focus on the fundamentals by simplifying things offensively as the team looks to reset and regain consistency. “It’s a little bit more back to the basics for us as a unit,” Johnson said. “Taking the volume down in terms of the plays going into the game plan here for a base day a little bit, and just make sure we get really good at the little things. I think sometimes when things go haywire, that’s usually the best reaction, is to make sure that we’re going back to what we believe in and what we’re about.” Can the Bears find the consistency they need heading into Week 6?

full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Caleb Williams #18 of the Chicago Bears warms up prior to the game against the Green Bay Packers at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Daniel Bartel/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. Welp, the Chicago Bears were without Caleb Williams again, and they fell to the Green Bay Packers in Lambeau Field on Sunday. In the three games Caleb missed, the Bears went 2-1, and if you consider the dark place fans’ minds went when Caleb was carted off the field in Week 2, a 2-1 record is pretty, pretty, pretty good. I tried looking up team records for when a backup quarterback was forced into the starting role, but those aren’t readily available. But many NFL coaches would be happy to come away at .500 if QB1 was sidelined. Most fans would tell you the same if their starting quarterback was injured. So why are so many fans so angsty over the Bears’ situation? Long-time NFL coach Tom Moore, owner of 4 Super Bowl rings and best known for his time as the offensive coordinator with the Indianapolis Colts with Peyton Manning (1998-2010), had the perfect line about playing games with the backup quarterback. Jon Gruden, who was an analyst at the time, asked Moore why he wasn’t giving the backups any practice time behind Manning, and Moore said something that would feel right at home in Chicago in 2026: ‘Fellas, if 18 (Manning) goes down we’re f****d, and we don’t practice f****d.’ Chicago’s 18 (Williams) has missed games for the first time in his career, and Case Keenum and Tyson Bagent helped them to a couple of wins. While there’s been no official announcement, it appears Caleb will be back on Sunday against the Atlanta Falcons. Do you think he can shake off the rust and get the Bears’ offense back on track? The Bears sit at 3-2 with two disappointing losses to NFC North rivals (it’s like déjà vu), but there’s a lot of football left to be played. title: Chicago Bears Pass Protection Analysis on the Sacks Allowed vs Packers
summary: In hindsight, the Chicago Bears probably should have started the 38-year-old veteran quarterback in a divisional road game instead of a player making just his sixth career start. Chances are it wouldn’t have mattered, because the Green Bay Packers’ offense was locked in, but Case Keenum has been there, done that, having played plenty of […]
full_text: Oct 11, 2026; Green Bay, Wisconsin, USA; Chicago Bears quarterback Tyson Bagent (17) is sacked by Green Bay Packers cornerback Brandon Cisse (2) during their football game at Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin. Mandatory Credit: Dan Powers USAToday Network via IMAGN images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect In hindsight, the Chicago Bears probably should have started the 38-year-old veteran quarterback in a divisional road game instead of a player making just his sixth career start. Chances are it wouldn’t have mattered, because the Green Bay Packers’ offense was locked in, but Case Keenum has been there, done that, having played plenty of divisional road games. Tyson Bagent was fine in Soldier Field against the New York Jets, but playing the Packers in Lambeau is a different atmosphere, and Bagent was off his game. I don’t fault Ben Johnson for rolling with Bagent, because you don’t know how a player will react in those moments until they get a chance. He had his chance, and hopefully Bagent learns from his experience in Green Bay, and hopefully we never have to see him play a meaningful snap for the Bears again. That’s not a knock on Bagent; I just want Caleb Williams to stay healthy. Let’s get into the Sackwatch! Sack 8: 1st Quarter: 2-9-CHI 44 (13:28) (Shotgun) T.Bagent sacked at CHI 33 for -11 yards (D.Wyatt) Bagent takes the shotgun snap, gathers, and works through a couple of progressions before he feels pressure. He escapes it, then slips trying to plant. Not sure if he was trying to cut up to scramble or if he was setting to throw deep to Kalif Raymond, who broke free downfield. Slipping on the field feels like an unfortunate sacks happen moment, but… Garrett Bradbury, what are you doing? He sets up in a great position to protect the right A-gap; right guard Jonah Jackson passes his guy (Devonte Wyatt, #95) off to the center, Bradbury, who then overextends and loses balance. Who knows if Bagent keeps his feet; maybe he does something to avoid the sack, but I can’t let Bradbury off the hook here, so half the blame to him and half to sacks happen. Sack 9: 2nd Quarter: 2-4-CHI 16 (1:00) (No Huddle, Shotgun) T.Bagent sacked at CHI 10 for -6 yards (B.Cisse) The Packers blitzed to Bagent’s right, and he appeared to see it and be aware of the possibility pre-snap because running back D’Andre Swift went left. Meaning: a free blitzer from the right would be Bagent’s responsibility. So with him looking into the blitz and wideout Luther Burden III on the quick in route, why not throw with anticipation and hit Burden coming out of his break? Swift was planning to chip Lukas Van Ness’ (#90) outside shoulder, but tight end Colston Loveland gave the edge up way too quickly on the left side, and that pressure got home. But that ball should have been out. This one is on Bagent. Sack 10: 4th Quarter: 1-10-GB 39 (4:20) (Shotgun) C.Keenum sacked at GB 47 for -8 yards (D.Wyatt). FUMBLES (D.Wyatt) [D.Wyatt], RECOVERED by GB-D.Dennis-Sutton at GB 41 The Bears were in an empty set, and the Packers only rushed 4. Case Keenum started to pull the trigger to Rome Odunze, who settled between two zone defenders, but Green Bay’s hash defender didn’t widen out enough. The Packers did a good job all afternoon taking away the intermediate middle of the field stuff, probably knowing that Bagent (or Keenum) wouldn’t look to push the ball downfield as much. Sometimes you got to tip your hat at a good game plan by the defense. Burden, who went over the top of Rome, appears to be the second read, and it was there if Keenum wasn’t forced to move. And why was he forced to move? Bradbury set up and wasn’t in a good position to accept the pass off from Jackson here. He offered little resistance to Waytt, who got the strip-sack and threw Keenum to the ground. Can I split this one again? Yes, I can, so half to Bradbury and half to Green Bay’s nice coverage (sacks happen). Sack 11: 4th Quarter: 2-10-CHI 32 (1:47) (Shotgun) C.Keenum sacked at CHI 21 for -11 yards (D.Dennis-Sutton) At this point in the game, the Bears are looking for points, so Keenum is looking downfield at the three deep receivers. When (if) he decided to look for Loveland as the checkdown over the middle, EDGE Dani Dennis-Sutton (#51) was already in his face. Left tackle Theo Benedet didn’t seem to expect a quick move to the inside gap, and Dennis-Sutton shot through for the sack. This one is on Benedet… although I will say his pass protection has looked better this year compared to last season. Here’s the individual Sackwatch tally after five games: Sacks happen – 3 Garrett Bradbury – 2 Theo Benedet – 1.5 Jonah Jackson – 1 Colston Loveland – 1 Tyson Bagent – 1 Darnell Wright – 1 Caleb Williams – .5 And here are the total Bears’ sacks allowed through 5 games in the Sackwatch era: 2010 – 21 Martz 2011 – 18 Martz 2012 – 14 Tice 2013 – 9 Trestman 2014 – 12 Trestman 2015 – 11 Gase 2016 – 11 Loggains 2017 – 9 Loggains 2018 – 12 Nagy 2019 – 13 Nagy 2020 – 11 Nagy 2021 – 18 Nagy 2022 – 18 Getsy 2023 – 20 Getsy 2024 – 17 Waldron 2025 – 10 Johnson 2026 – 11 Johnson

title: Chicago Bears Midweek Musings: Hello Darkness, My Old Friend
summary: Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: Have you ever watched a movie, hated it, then found yourself watching it again and again? Maybe it’s a popular movie that was always on when you […]
full_text: GREEN BAY, WISCONSIN - OCTOBER 11: Christian Watson #9 of the Green Bay Packers catches a touchdown pass against Dillon Thieneman #31 of the Chicago Bears during the third quarter at Lambeau Field on October 11, 2026 in Green Bay, Wisconsin. (Photo by Daniel Bartel/Getty Images) | Getty Images Some random thoughts about the Chicago Bears and other things, mostly football-related as we count down the hours until we get to watch this team play football again: Have you ever watched a movie, hated it, then found yourself watching it again and again? Maybe it’s a popular movie that was always on when you were growing up that didn’t hit you right or something your spouse loves to put on regularly that just isn’t in your genre. You find yourself watching a few minutes before you think – “I’ve seen this movie before… I hate this movie, I need to get out of here”? That’s watching the Bears go to Lambeau for the vast majority of my life. Same movie with a rotating cast of characters, like endless additions to the Night of the Living Dead franchise where no one escapes, and the zombies always win. It’s boring, and I’m ready for a new series to start for real when our protagonist gets back healthy. For those that may have never spent time in Wisconsin, my experience is that the default side next to a burger or sandwich is cheese curds instead of fries. Might be the only time fries would be considered the healthier side option. I mentioned last week that I thought Tyson Bagent’s film against the Jets was a little better than I expected it to be on second watch. Unfortunately, and this might be hard to believe, I think the Packers tape was worse than I thought it would be. I’m not sure if he lost confidence after the first pick and things unraveled from there, but it was truly awful tape. I’ve seen some criticism of Ben Johnson’s gameplay, and I’d just invite anyone with that opinion to make sure they watch the tape before settling into that as their final answer. Johnson was far from perfect, but he did more than enough schematically for Bagent to succeed. The biggest criticism you could have of Johnson was his decision to start Bagent over Keenum in the first place, which may be fair. Bagent’s workout of the burpee broad jump mile made some waves a couple years ago, which is easily the most insane workout I’ve ever heard of and I can’t get over it. I was asked recently if I wanted to do a Hyrox race, which features a burpee broad jump station as part of the experience. For 80 meters. Still too far for me, I think. The Bears will likely get Caleb Williams back this week against the Atlanta Falcons. That’s great news as Atlanta has a lot of firepower in their skill players and the Bears may need to win a shootout. They’re dealing with some quarterback injury issues as well and it would be a huge win if Chicago sees Tua Tagovailoa instead of Michael Penix. The fall between those two isn’t as big as Williams to Bagent, but it’s significant. I watched that Atlanta – Baltimore game and it will be a good challenge for the Bears defense to try and limit Bijan Robinson in this one. Best defense against Bijan will likely be a Caleb Williams offense that runs out to an early lead and forces Atlanta into a negative game script. Forcing a banged-up Penix or a fully functioning Tua into throwing 35+ times will lead to turnover opportunities, something this Bears defense desperately needs. This time last year I was in New Zealand. One of those once-in-a-lifetime trips. I always try to eat local fare wherever I travel and of course, I had my share of kiwifruit. I’ve kept that going back stateside but I’m a much bigger fan of the gold kiwifruit. Pro tip: cut the kiwifruit in half and scoop with a spoon. I’m officially panicking about Jaylon Johnson. Problem is, the Bears don’t really have anywhere to go on that one. Kyler Gordon’s return only goes so far. We’re officially on Khalil Mack watch, and I, for one, couldn’t be happier. He’s playing some good football on a bad Chargers squad and one would like to believe that Chicago would be the one place he’d be happy to go back to a place with familiarity and where he’s beloved. It’s a position of need for Chicago, and everything is lining up perfectly. I also personally love the idea of Mack returning so I can dig out that throwback jersey and wear it again. You got any musings? Hit the comments and let me know what’s up.

title: Boye Mafe has been a fantastic NFL free agency signing for the Bengals
summary: On the first day of free agency in March, the Bengals made two splashes with signing edge rusher Boye Mafe and safety Bryan Cook. Both won Super Bowls with their previous teams, and both players are entering the prime of their careers. In particular, Mafe has given the Bengals exactly what they paid for… and […]
full_text: On the first day of free agency in March, the Bengals made two splashes with signing edge rusher Boye Mafe and safety Bryan Cook. Both won Super Bowls with their previous teams, and both players are entering the prime of their careers. In particular, Mafe has given the Bengals exactly what they paid for … and more. “Right now, it’s a mindset to go out there and show who I can be as a player,” Mafe said after Sunday’s win over Miami. “With the coaches trusting me to be that player, it’s up to me to uphold that in my end of the bargain.” Mafe signed a three-year, $60 million deal with the Bengals in free agency. Through five games, Mafe has three sacks, five tackles for loss, four quarterback hits, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery, and one pass defensed. Sunday in Miami, Mafe had a sack, a tackle for loss, two quarterback hits, and a pass defensed. Mafe also pressured Malik Willis and forced a wobbly pass that Jordan Battle intercepted. “He has a lot of juice, man,” defensive tackle BJ Hill said. “He can get after the quarterback. He can do it all. He’s the guy you want on your team. I knew we had something special when he got here. He’s a different cat,” Hill said. “He’s just different. That’s all I can say. You’ll have to ask him. He’s different. You love to have that energy. You love having guys like that.” It’s also the stats you don’t see on Mafe that stand out. Mafe’s PFF grade Sunday was 88.0, the highest of his career. His second-highest was in Week 1 this season at 86.5. In addition, Mafe’s 77.1 pass-rushing grade is tied for 13th among 103 edge players who’ve played in at least 20% of their team’s defensive snaps. Among all NFL players, his 25 pressures rank sixth. Mafe is 27 years old, which is the same age Trey Hendrickson was when the Bengals signed him in free agency in 2021. But Mafe brings far more versatility than Hendrickson. He can defend the run, pressure the quarterback, and cause turnovers. Look no further than his strip-sack of Baker Mayfield in the fourth quarter of Week 1. “He’s willing to do anything,” Zac Taylor said about Mafe. “Stop the run. Drop. Rush. Rush inside … That didn’t surprise me. That’s what we were banking on, that he’d give you that type of effort. He’s completely bought in.” Finishing has been an issue for the Bengals’ defense in recent seasons. Who’s their closer? It’s a question we asked a lot in those recent seasons, but Mafe could be that for this team. “He has come in and been extremely competitive from Day 1,” said left tackle Orlando Brown Jr., who faced Mafe in 2023 when Mafe was with the Seahawks and played against him throughout training camp this summer. “He’s just a really good and smart football player who knows when to show up. What’s most impressive is some of the clean wins that he has. He figures out a way to finish. That’s a sign of a great defensive end. It’s crazy. I feel like he has gotten better even since he got here.” While Dexter Lawrence grabbed a lot of the headlines this offseason in the Bengals’ signings and trades, Mafe may turn out to be their most important signing. So far, the Bengals are getting a great return on investment with him.

full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals found themselves back in the win column after a hot one in Miami against the Dolphins. Some were worried this could be a trap game for the Bengals, but the team controlled the game from start to finish. One interesting storyline that came to light this past weekend was the running back situation between Chase Brown and Samaje Perine. Brown has been good for the Bengals since being drafted but has struggled to find his groove through five games so far in 2026. The run game has really struggled in general this season, but Perine has added a much-needed spark each time he enters the game. That consistent spark has given Perine more snaps, and he officially surpassed Brown in carries against the Dolphins. Perine finished the day with 14 carries for 68 yards while Brown tallied 39 yards on 13 carries. Brown also coughed up the football inside the red zone while Perine found the end zone on a touchdown pass from Joe Burrow. A big part of why Perine played more appeared to be due to Brown’s fumble in the first half. Prior to that, Brown had more than double the number of snaps that Perine had. But after the fumble, Perine ended up getting five more snaps the rest of the game than Brown did. Chase Brown fumbled near the goal line with 7:03 remaining in the 2nd quarter of Week 5. title: AFC North Standings: Ravens on top entering Week 6
summary: An overtime victory over a much-improved Atlanta Falcons team left the Baltimore Ravens in first place in the AFC North after the fifth week of the season. Meanwhile, wins by Cincinnati and Pittsburgh, coupled with a loss by the Cleveland Browns, created a logjam for the runner-up spot. Let’s take a look at the AFC […]
full_text: An overtime victory over a much-improved Atlanta Falcons team left the Baltimore Ravens in first place in the AFC North after the fifth week of the season. Meanwhile, wins by Cincinnati and Pittsburgh, coupled with a loss by the Cleveland Browns, created a logjam for the runner-up spot. Let’s take a look at the AFC North heading into Week 6. Bengals look ready for bye in win over Miami Joe Burrow threw four touchdown passes, including a spectacular 45-yard scoring strike to Ja’Marr Chase, as Cincinnati snapped a two-game losing streak with a 31-24 victory over Miami. Burrow completed 23 of 32 passes for 190 yards, spreading the ball among nine receivers. Chase, who missed practice time during the week because of a concussion, finished with six catches for 77 yards. Mike Gesicki, Tanner Hudson and Samaje Perine also caught touchdown passes as the Bengals improved to 3-2. Cincinnati’s defense also played a major role in the victory. Safety Jordan Battle intercepted Miami quarterback Malik Willis twice in the second quarter, helping the Bengals build a 21-7 halftime advantage. An 81-yard opening kickoff return by Dohnte Meyers set up Cincinnati’s first touchdown. The Dolphins rallied late, cutting the deficit to seven points in the final minute, but a missed extra point and unsuccessful onside kick ended their comeback attempt. Thankfully, the Bengals are getting a bye this week that will hopefully help them clean things up with a massive Week 7 game at Baltimore looming. Jets slow Cleveland’s roll Cleveland’s three-game winning streak came to an end in a rain-soaked 17-12 loss to the New York Jets. The Browns struggled to protect quarterback Deshaun Watson, who was sacked eight times and completed just 15 of 33 passes for 155 yards. Watson connected with rookie Denzel Boston on a 29-yard touchdown pass midway through the fourth quarter, briefly giving Cleveland a 12-10 lead. Andre Szmyt missed the extra point, however, leaving the Browns vulnerable to a late comeback. The decisive mistake came on special teams after Cleveland’s defense had forced a New York punt. A high snap sailed past punter Corey Bojorquez, allowing the Jets to recover deep in Browns territory. Three plays later, Braelon Allen scored on a 22-yard run to put New York ahead with just over three minutes remaining. Cleveland had one final opportunity, but Watson was strip-sacked on fourth down, sealing the loss. The Browns fell to 3-2 after a game in which their defense kept them competitive but offensive struggles and costly mistakes proved decisive. Warren does it all for Steelers Jaylen Warren delivered one of the most impressive performances of his career, accounting for 188 yards from scrimmage and two touchdowns as Pittsburgh defeated Indianapolis 34-22. Warren scored on an 80-yard reception in the first quarter and broke loose for a 50-yard touchdown run in the third, providing the offensive spark the Steelers needed after their previous week’s loss to Cleveland. With Rico Dowdle sidelined by a toe injury, Warren has emerged as Pittsburgh’s primary offensive weapon. The victory improved the Steelers’ record to 3-2. Quarterback Aaron Rodgers completed 22 of 31 passes for 235 yards and three touchdowns, including two scoring throws to tight end Pat Freiermuth. Pittsburgh repeatedly answered Indianapolis scoring drives, preventing the Colts from taking control despite several opportunities. The Steelers also benefited from Indianapolis’ inability to finish drives, as the Colts settled for five field goals. Ravens overcome Falcons Backup quarterback Tyler Huntley rallied Baltimore from an eight-point deficit in the final minute of regulation before scoring the winning touchdown in overtime as the Ravens defeated Atlanta 30-23. Filling in for the injured Lamar Jackson, Huntley completed 24 of 32 passes for 201 yards and two touchdowns. His 7-yard scoring pass to Devontez Walker with 40 seconds remaining brought Baltimore within two points, and Derrick Henry converted the ensuing two-point attempt to force overtime. Huntley then scored on a 1-yard quarterback sneak to give the Ravens the lead. Baltimore’s defense finished the job when safety Kyle Hamilton intercepted Atlanta’s backup quarterback, Tua Tagovailoa. Henry rushed for 102 yards against a Falcons defense that entered the game ranked first against the run, while the Ravens overcame several stalled drives and three first-half field goals. The victory improved Baltimore’s record to 4-1 and gave the Ravens sole possession of first place in the AFC North. AFC North Standings Week 6 Because the Bengals are the only team with a loss and no wins in division play, they sit in last place in the AFC North heading into Week 6. A win at Baltimore in Week 7 would go along way in their race for the division lead, but a loss could put them in a deep hole if the Ravens also win this week vs. the Browns.

title: Dexter Lawrence leads the way in Cincinnati’s newly dangerous defensive line
summary: The 2025 Cincinnati Bengals had one of the weirdest defenses you’ll ever see. According to FTN’s data, Cincinnati’s Defensive DVOA of 30.1% in Weeks 1-9 was the worst in the history of the metric, which currently goes back to 1977. But from Week 10 through the end of the regular season, the Bengals improved their […]
full_text: by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2025 Cincinnati Bengals had one of the weirdest defenses you’ll ever see. According to FTN’s data , Cincinnati’s Defensive DVOA of 30.1% in Weeks 1-9 was the worst in the history of the metric, which currently goes back to 1977. But from Week 10 through the end of the regular season, the Bengals improved their Defensive DVOA to -2.2% (Defensive DVOA is better when it’s negative), up from 32nd to 13th. That didn’t quite erase the sins of the early season — the Bengals finished 30th in Defensive DVOA ahead of only the Dallas Cowboys and the New York Jets — but there was enough on the bone for management to spend in both draft capital and actual dollars to improve things on that side of the ball. So, uncharacteristically, they did. They traded the No. 10 overall pick in the 2026 draft to the New York Giants for Dexter Lawrence, the 6’4”, 342-pound one-of-one defensive tackle, and then signed Lawrence to a one-year, $28 million contract with $10 million guaranteed. They also signed former Washington and Minnesota Vikings defensive tackle Jonathan Allen to a two-year, $25 million deal with $10.5 million guaranteed. They also signed former Seattle Seahawks edge-rusher Boye Mafe to a three-year, $60 million contract with $19 million guaranteed, and they selected Texas A&M edge-rusher Cashius Howell with the 41st overall pick in the second round of the 2026 draft. A radical makeover, to be sure. How’s it all working out? Well, the Bengals currently rank 14th in Defensive DVOA, and fifth in the NFL in Total DVOA, behind only the San Francisco 49ers, Jacksonville Jaguars, Buffalo Bills, and the Kansas City Chiefs. And the newly minted defensive line has made all the difference. Per SumerSports: The Bengals are pressuring opposing quarterbacks 41.6% of the time this season, as opposed to 36.5% in 2025. The defense is averaging 16.4 pressures per game this season, as opposed to 13.1 in 2025. The sack rate has risen from 5.8% in 2025 to 8.6% in 2026, and through five games, the Bengals have nearly half the sacks (17) as they did in the entire 2025 season (35). All the new guys acquired via trade or free agency have been balling out. Lawrence has 3.0 sacks and 14 pressures. Allen has 3.0 sacks and 16 pressures. Mafe has 3.0 sacks and 21 pressures. But with Lawrence, you have to put metrics aside, because it all starts with him. Very few players in football history have presented opposing offenses with Lawrence’s combination of size, strength, speed, agility, and technique. This season, Lawrence has been double-teamed on 94 of his 234 snaps, and while that’s absolutely what you have to do with Sexy Dexy, it doesn’t always go as planned. Double-teaming Dexter Lawrence is not an option — it is a necessity. Doesn't mean it's going to work, though. pic.twitter.com/OGWQcNaRAq — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 14, 2026 Pretty insane stuff for a guy who spends as much time as Lawrence does either straight over the center, or shaded to one side. Per Sports Info Solutions, Lawrence leads the NFL with two sacks and 11 total pressures from the 0-tech (head over) and 1-tech (shaded) alignments. Nobody else in the NFL has more than six pressures from those alignments. Of course, Lawrence isn’t just there to disrupt on his own; part of his value is how he opens things up for his linemates. That’s where Jonathan Allen comes in. All three of Allen’s sacks this season have come when he’s on the interior of the line along with Lawrence. Level 1 of that particular kung fu is simply having Allen and Lawrence in gap concepts designed to maximize their specific attributes. Level 2 of the kung fu happens when Allen and Lawrence start stunting. That is not a pleasant experience for any offensive line. Jonathan Allen and Dexter Lawrence in the same interior defensive line. Pack a lunch. It's going to be a long day. pic.twitter.com/fm2tvW4hgt — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 14, 2026 Then, there’s Mafe, who is a prominent player in his own right — but he’s also feasting on the fact that when Lawrence and Allen are doing their things… well, Mafe has been doubled just 10 times this season, and for good reason. Boye Mafe: The third axis of evil in the @Bengals ' new defensive front. pic.twitter.com/3G6iUK9VWm — Doug Farrar ✍ (@NFL_DougFarrar) October 14, 2026 Defensive coordinator Al Golden, and defensive line coach/run game coordinator Jerry Montgomery have done a nice job of rotating the defensive linemen — six different guys have more than 80 snaps this season — and when you combine that with the talent up top, this has become one of the toughest fronts to deal with in the NFL. “This is by far the fewest amount of snaps I’ve played in a long time, but it was really good,” Allen said after the Bengals’ 33-27 Week 1 win over the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. Allen had a sack in that game. “The rotation was awesome. In the third quarter [when Allen got his sack] and fourth quarter, we were fresh and just rolling.” Lawrence played just 35 snaps in that game, but he announced himself with three pressures. “It shows up because of the production a lot of guys around him get oftentimes,” head coach Zac Taylor said of Lawrence and the overall idea. “He still was in there and made his presence felt, and Baker [Mayfield] had to try to get away from him a couple times. [Lawrence] had some runs he really affected as well. But as much as anything, you just see the production that comes to other people because of the attention he draws.” So yes, Dexter Lawrence is the star of this show, but he’s got all kinds of stars around him, and there’s enough talent to keep everybody fresh. That should make this Bengals defense problematic for every opponent they face this season… and their season may last well beyond Week 18 at this rate.

full_text: The Cincinnati Bengals are 3-2 heading into their Week 6 bye, and while there’s been plenty to get excited about, there’s also been plenty of cause for concern. Despite their winning record, the Bengals are a far cry from the team we envisioned after their Week 2 victory in Houston. There have been some outstanding individual performances, but there have also been some glaring disappointments. With five games in the books, it’s time to take stock of who’s exceeding expectations and who’s falling short. Here are the Bengals’ winners and losers through the first five weeks of the season, starting with the good. WINNERS Evan McPherson McPherson has absolutely earned the nickname “Money Mac” so far this season. He’s been perfect through five games, connecting on all 10 of his field-goal attempts, including a season-long 58-yarder. Incredibly, five of those 10 attempts have come from beyond 50 yards. What’s even more impressive, though, is that McPherson hasn’t missed a field goal since Week 11 of the 2025 season. He’s now made 22 consecutive field goals, setting a new franchise record previously held by Shayne Graham. Hopefully, he’ll continue adding to that total and establish a record that takes a generation to break. Amarius Mims Mims has been outstanding at right tackle for the Bengals this season. He’s currently ranked as PFF’s 10th-best offensive tackle with a pass-blocking grade of 78.8, having allowed just four total pressures and one sack. His run-blocking grade leaves a little to be desired, but let’s face it: The Bengals’ offense is going to run through Joe Burrow and the passing game more often than not. Mims’ ability to protect Burrow’s right side has been nothing short of fantastic, and he’s quickly establishing himself as one of the most important pieces of Cincinnati’s offensive line. Boye Mafe The Bengals appear to have struck gold in free agency at the edge rusher position once again. Coming off a Super Bowl championship season with the Seattle Seahawks, Mafe signed a three-year deal with Cincinnati and has wasted no time making his presence felt. He’s currently tied with Byron Young for the second-most quarterback hurries in the NFL with 20, just one behind league leader Aidan Hutchinson. Mafe has also been solid against the run, earning a respectable 75.1 run-defense grade from PFF. Like Trey Hendrickson before him, Mafe has hit the ground running in Cincinnati. If he keeps playing at this level, his signing could go down as one of the Bengals’ best offseason moves. Mike Gesicki Gesicki caught four touchdown passes over his first two seasons with the Bengals. Through five games in 2026, he’s already matched that total. It’s clear opposing defenses are doing everything they can to prevent Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins from beating them. That’s created opportunities for Gesicki, who has flourished in his role as a tight end/slot receiver hybrid specializing in finding open space. With Burrow, Chase, Higgins, and Gesicki all under contract through the 2027 season, the Bengals have the makings of an offensive core that could do some serious damage in the postseason. Of course, they have to get there first. Dexter Lawrence Lawrence has been worth every bit of the No. 10 overall pick the Bengals traded to acquire him. It’s hard to imagine anyone Cincinnati could have selected with that pick making the kind of immediate impact Lawrence has had on this defense. He’s currently PFF’s third-ranked interior defensive lineman with an overall defensive grade of 82.5. The two players ranked ahead of him have played only about two-thirds as many snaps as Lawrence. He also has the third-most quarterback hurries among defensive tackles and is tied for fifth in sacks at the position. Lawrence is massive, disruptive, and capable of changing an opposing offense’s game plan simply by lining up across from it. He’s been everything the Bengals could have hoped for when they shipped a top-10 pick to the Giants. Jonathan Allen Allen was somewhat overlooked among the Bengals’ offseason acquisitions, largely because his arrival was overshadowed by the blockbuster trade for Lawrence. However, he’s been nearly as impressive, particularly as a pass rusher. Through five games, Allen has recorded 10 quarterback hurries, four hits and two sacks from the interior of the defensive line, complementing Lawrence’s three sacks. In a conference featuring Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen, and a division with Lamar Jackson and Aaron Rodgers, the Bengals need all the pass rushers they can get. Allen and Lawrence have given Cincinnati an interior pass rush that opposing offenses simply can’t afford to ignore. Dalton Risner Risner appears to have been the final piece of the puzzle for the Bengals’ offensive line. He’s currently PFF’s eighth-ranked guard with an overall offensive grade of 81.7, including an 80.7 run-blocking grade and a 73.7 pass-blocking grade. For an offense as pass-happy as Cincinnati’s, having an offensive line that can be trusted is enormous. This is also the first season of Burrow’s career in which he’s had the same five starting offensive linemen in consecutive seasons. That continuity, combined with Risner’s strong play, has helped give the Bengals some much-needed stability up front. Risner is scheduled to become a free agent after this season, and if he finishes the year the way he’s started it, he’s going to earn himself a nice new contract. Hopefully, the Bengals are the ones who give it to him. Tee Higgins Chase is the Bengals’ No. 1 receiver and, in my opinion, the best wide receiver in the NFL. That shouldn’t take anything away from how fantastic Higgins has been this season. He’s currently PFF’s 10th-ranked wide receiver with an outstanding overall offensive grade of 90.0, and he’s on pace for more than 90 receptions and 1,400 receiving yards. He only has one touchdown through five games, but he’s been Mr. Reliable whenever opposing defenses devote extra attention to keeping Chase away from Burrow. Higgins would be the unquestioned No. 1 receiver on plenty of NFL teams. The Bengals are fortunate enough to have him as their No. 2. LOSERS Orlando Brown Jr. While everything seems to be going right at right tackle, the same can’t be said for the other side of Cincinnati’s offensive line. Brown has struggled mightily to start the season. Among offensive tackles who have played at least 80% of their team’s snaps, Brown ranks as the seventh-worst pass blocker, according to PFF, with a grade of 62.2. He’s also surrendered three sacks and 12 total pressures. Speed rushers, in particular, have given him fits. At times, he almost looks like he’s trying to get a head start before the snap just to avoid getting beaten around the edge, putting himself at risk of drawing false-start penalties. Hopefully, the bye week gives Brown an opportunity to regroup and come back looking a little less stiff. If his play doesn’t improve, though, finding Burrow a new blindside protector may need to become one of Cincinnati’s top priorities this offseason. Darrin Simmons Simmons has been the Bengals’ special teams coordinator since 2003 and their assistant head coach since 2020. Usually, that’s a good thing. When special teams are doing their job, we rarely have much reason to talk about them. Unfortunately, that’s not been the case this season. Outside of McPherson’s outstanding kicking, Cincinnati’s special teams units have been unreliable, undisciplined and, at times, downright costly. Against the Steelers, the Bengals committed a roughing-the-kicker penalty and muffed a punt, mistakes that ultimately resulted in 10 points for Pittsburgh. The problems continued against Miami. Lawrence was flagged for roughing the snapper, turning what would have been a Dolphins field goal into a touchdown. Erick All committed a 15-yard penalty that pushed McPherson out of field-goal range, and Dohnte Meyers fielded a kickoff near the four-yard line before allowing his momentum to carry him…
