title: The clock is ticking for Kellen Moore and the Saints
summary: The New Orleans Saints are running out of excuses. Last week, the Saints’ embarrassing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons raised serious questions about Kellen Moore’s tenure in New Orleans. After another disappointing performance, those questions are only getting louder. The Saints fell 23-13 to the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, dropping to 1-4 and losing […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 11: Kellen Moore head coach of the New Orleans Saints looks on during the second half of a game against the Minnesota Vikings at Caesars Superdome on October 11, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints are running out of excuses. Last week, the Saints’ embarrassing 45-24 loss to the Atlanta Falcons raised serious questions about Kellen Moore’s tenure in New Orleans. After another disappointing performance, those questions are only getting louder. The Saints fell 23-13 to the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, dropping to 1-4 and losing their third consecutive home game. What was already a frustrating start to the season has quickly become a concerning trend under Moore, who is now 7-15 through his first 22 games as the Saints’ head coach. And the numbers paint an ugly picture of where this team stands. New Orleans is 3-8 at home under Moore and has struggled to establish any kind of consistency offensively. The Saints have yet to score more than seven points in the first quarter during his tenure, have held just one first-quarter lead and have led at halftime only four times in 22 games. This goes beyond a few slow starts. It points to a team that consistently puts itself in a hole before halftime. The Saints have scored just 35 first-quarter points under Moore, the fewest in the NFL over that span. They have also recorded 29 first-quarter three-and-outs, the most in the league, making it difficult to build momentum or put opposing defenses under pressure early. Sunday’s loss to Minnesota was another example of those struggles. The offensive struggles reached another level. The Saints finished with just 142 total yards, their fewest in a game since recording 128 in a 26-7 loss to Carolina in Week 2 of the 2021 season. It was also the third-fewest total yards New Orleans has recorded in a game since 2000, adding to Moore’s growing list of concerns. The defensive numbers have not helped matters, either. The Saints have a minus-10 turnover differential under Moore, the third-worst mark in the league. It’s hard to win in the NFL when you struggle to start games and consistently lose the turnover battle. Last week, the question was how much longer the organization would wait for Moore to turn his team’s preparation and execution issues into results. One week later, there is even less reason to believe the answers are coming quickly and given Gayle Benson’s comments yesterday , the clock is running out. Firing a head coach midway into his second season is a significant decision, and the Saints still have time to change the direction of their season. However, patience becomes harder to justify when the same problems continue to surface. At 1-4, New Orleans needs more than another promise to make adjustments. They need to show tangible improvement, particularly to open the game, where the struggles have become a defining characteristic of Moore’s tenure. If the Saints can’t find a way to change that pattern soon, the conversation surrounding Moore’s future will only get louder.

full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - OCTOBER 11: Kellen Moore head coach of the New Orleans Saints talks with Tyler Shough #6 during the first half of a game against the Minnesota Vikings at Caesars Superdome on October 11, 2026, in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Derick Hingle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New Orleans Saints have plunged, rather quickly, from a promising 1-1 to a severely deflating 1-4 record for the 2026 regular season. Their Week 6 trip to the Big Apple to play the New York Giants is as pivotal as any, and here’s what either outcome could mean for the black and gold. If the Saints win: Call it coping, call it ridiculous, call it whatever you wish in the comments. The Saints remain in a relatively easy stretch of schedule, and Sunday could turn out to be the first step back to reclaiming a .500 record by mid-November. The Giants haven’t won, or in fact played against, a team that currently possesses a winning record. They were beaten handily by the Rams and squeezed by a bad Titans team. They pose no tougher a challenge than the black and gold have faced during their three-week winless home stretch. New York’s running game has been poor, an area that has hurt the Saints in recent games. The defense imposing a continuation of that Giants trend could bode well if a New Orleans offense, which is still showing sporadic displays of explosive potential, can kick into gear on the other side of the ball. Victory would stop the bleeding, bring a sigh of relief, and keep the door on the playoffs open for now. If the Saints lose: A fourth consecutive defeat would spell a borderline crisis. At some point, even with consideration for the injury concerns, something has to give. Either New Orleans finds a way to win football games, or changes will be made. What that might look like remains to be seen, but coaches tend to be the easiest target in these circumstances. At 1-5, it would be tough to envision a route to a division title for this team. title: Saints’ owner Gayle Benson calls 1-4 start ‘Unacceptable’
summary: New Orleans Saints owner Gayle Benson made headlines Tuesday after delivering a candid message about the team’s disappointing 1-4 start to the season. After beginning her day at the Saints’ Day of Service at Second Harvest Food Bank, Benson attended the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club’s monthly luncheon, where she delivered an eight-minute speech that […]
full_text: New Orleans Saints owner Gayle Benson made headlines Tuesday after delivering a candid message about the team’s disappointing 1-4 start to the season. After beginning her day at the Saints’ Day of Service at Second Harvest Food Bank, Benson attended the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club’s monthly luncheon, where she delivered an eight-minute speech that quickly drew not only local but national attention. “Before I reflect on our 60th season, I want to address where we stand. We are 1–4. That is not acceptable to me, and it falls short of what our fans truly deserve. I hear the frustration directed toward our team and our organization. It is not lost on me. Our fans invest their time and their hearts in the Saints. They are right to expect more than we have delivered. As owner, the responsibility does start with me. I will not make excuses, and I will not accept this level of performance as our standard. I am committed to making the decisions necessary to improve this team. Everyone in this organization understands the urgency. We must prepare better, execute consistently and correct the mistakes that are costing us the games. Words will not restore our fans’ confidence. Our performance must do that. Our 60th season reminds us why that responsibility matters. Generations of families have built their Sundays around the Saints. Their loyalty has sustained this franchise through extraordinary victories and difficult years. We must never take it for granted. 20 years ago, the Saints returned to the Superdome after Hurricane Katrina. We all remember Steve Gleason’s blocked punt, the roar of the crowd and what it meant to see our city come together once again. Losing this year’s anniversary game to Atlanta, truly disappointing. Hearing our fans’ memories of that homecoming reinforced how deeply this team is woven into their lives. This season, we also honored Drew Brees at his Pro Football Hall of Fame induction and, this past Sunday, with his place in the Ring of Honor. Watching Drew receive his gold jacket at Tom Benson Hall of Fame Stadium was especially meaningful to me. His legacy includes a championship, extraordinary records and a lasting commitment to New Orleans. It also includes a standard of preparation, discipline and accountability. The best way to honor that legacy is to uphold those standards today. Kellen Moore and his coaches are responsible for preparing our players to perform. Mickey Loomis and our football staff are responsible for building a roster capable of sustained success. Our players are responsible for their preparation and execution, and I am responsible for this organization. There is a great deal of football ahead. Our response must show up on the field. On October 25, as you all know, we face the Pittsburgh Steelers in Paris, with a trip to the Giants this Sunday. Our priority is to prepare to win. Through the NFL’s Global Markets Program, teams build relationships with fans internationally. I chose France because of its deep historical and cultural ties to Louisiana. This game is part of our participation in the league’s international schedule, and we intend to make that commitment count. Our business staff is working closely with economic development leaders across Louisiana to attract international business and investment to our city, state and region. Those relationships can create opportunities here at home long after the game ends. I’m also working to bring the Super Bowl back to New Orleans in 2031. However, there are no promises from the league to date, but hopefully we will hear something in March. Our city’s hospitality, culture and people make us an exceptional host, and we are determined to earn that opportunity. These efforts matter to our community. Our obligation to deliver better football remains clear. To the coaches here today: You know what leadership requires when a team struggles. You confront the problems, make corrections and hold yourself to the same standard you demand of others. That is what I expect throughout our organization. To our fans: I hear you. I understand your disappointment, and I share your determination to see this team succeed. Your support deserves a response you can see on the field. We cannot change the results of our first five games. We are responsible for what we do next. I expect better. Our fans deserve better and I am determined to see that we deliver it. Thank you all for your attention and may God bless you.“ Benson’s remarks sent a clear message that the Saints’ struggles have not gone unnoticed by ownership. While acknowledging the growing frustration surrounding the team’s disappointing start, she made it clear that the organization must be held accountable for its performance on the field. For a franchise celebrating its 60th season, expectations remain high, and Benson understands the passion and loyalty of a fan base that has stood by the team through both the highs and lows. Her willingness to publicly address the team’s struggles was a significant moment, particularly because it is not something she does often. Much of the responsibility for turning things around now falls on second-year head coach Kellen Moore, who faces the challenge of getting his team back on track after a disappointing start. While Moore continues to build his vision for the franchise, patience can wear thin when results fail to meet expectations. Finding consistency, correcting mistakes and getting the most out of his players will be critical as the Saints look to turn their season around. With plenty of football still to be played, the Saints have an opportunity to change the narrative, but that will require much more than words. Benson’s message was one of accountability, urgency and a commitment to giving Saints fans the product they deserve. Now, it is up to Moore, his coaching staff and the players to respond on the field and show that the organization is moving in the right direction.

title: Saints, Ochsner Health and Entergy team up for Day of Service to benefit New Orleans seniors

More than 40 volunteers from the Saints, Ochsner Health and Entergy participated in the event, including members of the Saints Cheer Krewe, former Saints kicker Garrett Hartley, […]
full_text: On Tuesday, October 13, the New Orleans Saints, Ochsner Health and Entergy joined forces for a Day of Service at Second Harvest Food Bank to support local seniors. More than 40 volunteers from the Saints, Ochsner Health and Entergy participated in the event, including members of the Saints Cheer Krewe, former Saints kicker Garrett Hartley, wide receiver Devery Henderson and running back Deuce McAllister. According to Lindsey Hendrix, chief impact officer at Second Harvest Food Bank, volunteers packed 1,120 meal boxes to be distributed later that day to senior residents at HANO’s Guste High Rise in New Orleans. In addition to providing meals, the event offered residents access to free health screenings, including blood pressure and glucose checks. Residents also had the opportunity to receive energy efficiency assessments and information about Entergy’s Energy Smart program, which helps households identify ways to reduce energy consumption and lower utility costs. The collaborative effort brought together community partners to address food insecurity, promote health and wellness, and provide valuable resources to seniors throughout the New Orleans area. .

summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to for the Giants as hey prepare for the New Orleans Saints. full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to for the Giants as hey prepare for the New Orleans Saints. First-place Giants are a distant third in betting odds to win the NFC East | Pro Football Talk It’s not hard to understand why the bettors aren’t sold on the Giants: Despite managing to win three games, they haven’t looked particularly good while doing so, on either offense or defense. (Their special teams are playing well.) Starting quarterback Jaxson Dart is out for the season and there are doubts about how long they can keep winning with Jameis Winston. And their schedule has been easy; all five teams they’ve played currently have losing records. The schedule stays easy this week, with a home game against the 1-4 Saints. The Giants are 1.5-point underdogs, which underscores how little faith the bettors have in them. If the Giants manage to win on Sunday, their odds to win the division may improve a little. But it won’t be until November 8, when they travel to Philadelphia to take on the Eagles, when the Giants can make a statement that they really are the best team in the NFC East. Unless the Giants keep winning through that game, they’re going to stay long shots to win the division. Team culture on display “Let’s stay a family, man. Please. Stay a family. Family on three: one, two, three…” Let’s go, #BigBlue pic.twitter.com/pdOC0DH9PL — NYGfaninCLT (@clt_ny) October 13, 2026 NFL spread, straight-up picks: Rams, Chiefs, Colts top Week 6 confidence rankings | The Athletic The Giants are developing an identity — a never-say-die outfit that raises its level of play when it matters the most. Jameis Winston was atrocious in the first half, but came out throwing lasers in the second half and overtime, Malik Nabers and Isaiah Likely were ballers and the defense made big stops. The Saints are almost certain to be a popular pick. They’ve lost three straight and the Giants aren’t that good. But a bounceback is coming. And I believe the Giants defense — keyed by surging pass-rusher Abdul Carter and top draft-pick Arvell Reese — will spinebuster the game for Tyler Shough. The Saints’ inability to run the football will be their undoing. Why John Harbaugh’s track record may separate the Giants from the rest of the NFC East | New York Post John Harbaugh was on the phone with his wife after the Giants did not win and did not lose last Sunday against the Commanders. Ingrid Harbaugh was tuned in to various NFL games on what turned into a wild and wacky Sunday of action. It can be Crazy Town around the NFL and especially in the NFC East. The Giants want to live in Sane City and have the head coach to keep the crazy out. Dru Phillips: Giants’ defensive stands stem from preseason practice | USAToday.com Cornerback Dru Phillips said the results trace back to repetition in practice rather than any sudden change in personnel or scheme. “I definitely feel like, especially in the preseason, we went through these situations so many times in practice where we get into the game, and we all trust each other — it’s not like you got to be Superman and make a play,” Phillips said. “It’s more just do your job and I believe everybody can — we can get off the field if everyone just does their job…Dennard has a way of cooking things up, but it’s definitely not I would say a consistent thing. It’s a week-by-week thing off of, I guess what we’re seeing and how we feel. So, you just go out there and if they send me I’m going to try my best to go get there and everything but the percentage is just it goes off the flow of the game.” Jameis on his time in the Big Easy Jameis Winston speaks highly of his time in New Orleans ahead of their matchup against the Saints this week: pic.twitter.com/xuV5qrvIn1 — SNY Giants (@SNYGiants) October 14, 2026 How Giants embrace ‘Jameis Winston Experience’ for what it truly means | The Record Many within the NFL have been consumed by the caricature created by Jameis Winston with his charisma, persona and flat-out quirkiness continuing to command attention. What other player could get Giants coach John Harbaugh, answering a question during Monday’s video call about his quarterback’s seemingly unwavering optimism, to go from speaking on Jameis Winston to Winston Churchill without batting an eye, and somehow making that transition seamlessly? J.J. McCarthy’s Giants debut offered a glimpse: What’s next? | NJ.com Still, don’t be surprised if Harbaugh gives McCarthy another shot Sunday in a similar package to what Nagy used in Washington. After all, Harbaugh said he liked the look of the plan Nagy and Co. had for McCarthy. “I do, and I think we’ll grow,” Harbaugh said. “We just have to see. It just all depends. We’re in a situation now where it’s by any means necessary. So we’re all on board for whoever, however. Sometimes, it’s going to work. Sometimes, it’s not. We had a chance in a couple of those to make big plays.” You weekly “Did you see that play the rookie made?” highlight Watch Arvell Reese take the block with one hand and tackle the ball carrier with the other 😮 @arvxll | @Giants | @OhioStateFB pic.twitter.com/70gR1Gi23X — NFL (@NFL) October 14, 2026 2026 NFL offensive line rankings: Lions move into top spot | PFF 17. New York Giants (up 3). The Giants benched John Michael Schmitz Jr. ahead of Week 4, with Bryan Hudson replacing him in the starting lineup. The move has paid off so far, with Hudson notching PFF grades above 70.0 in both starts. Hudson has allowed just one pressure from 102 pass-blocking snaps, producing a 96.8% PFF pass-block win rate across those two starts. As Nabers continues to recover from the ACL injury he suffered last season, he might accrue more volume. But Likely is ahead right now and has proved to be a key part of this new Giants offense. title: Saints’ owner turns up the pressure before game vs. NY Giants
summary: The New York Giants’ opponent this week, the New Orleans Saints, are under pressure from ownership after a disappointing 1-4 start to the 2026 NFL season. Owner Gayle Benson ratcheted up the heat on Tuesday. “I will not make excuses, and I will not accept this level of performance as our standard,” Benson said Tuesday […]
full_text: Gayle Benson | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants’ opponent this week, the New Orleans Saints, are under pressure from ownership after a disappointing 1-4 start to the 2026 NFL season. Owner Gayle Benson ratcheted up the heat on Tuesday. “I will not make excuses, and I will not accept this level of performance as our standard,” Benson said Tuesday at the Greater New Orleans Quarterback Club. “I am committed to making the decisions necessary to improve this team. Everyone in this organization understands the urgency. We must prepare better, execute consistently and correct the mistakes that are costing us the games. “Words will not restore our fans’ confidence. Our performance must do better.” The Saints have lost three games to the Las Vegas Raiders, Atlanta Falcons, and Minnesota Vikings. New Orleans’ five opponents this season have a combined 17-8 record, a .680 winning percentage. They lost to the Vikings on Sunday, 23-13. Kellen Moore is in his second season as the Saints’ head coach. Mickey Loomis has been general manager since 2002. Benson name-dropped both during her rant. “Kellen Moore and his coaches are responsible for preparing our players to perform,” she said. “Mickey Loomis and our football staff are responsible for building a roster capable of sustained success. Our players are responsible for their preparation and execution. I am responsible for holding this organization accountable.” The Saints, thus, come to MetLife Stadium on Sunday knowing that if things don’t change on the field their owner will take matters into her own hands. “There’s a great deal of football ahead of us, but our response must show up on the field,” Benson said.

title: NY Giants sign a guard to bolster their offensive line depth
summary: The New York Giants are signing guard Josh Gesky to their practice squad, per multiple reports. ESPN’s Jordan Raanan was the first to report the signing, followed by Aaron Wilson. Gesky, 23, originally signed with the Green Bay Packers as an undrafted rookie out of Illinois and will reunite with former Illini teammate JC Davis […]
full_text: Offensive guard Josh Gesky rides a bicycle to practice. | Getty Images The New York Giants are signing guard Josh Gesky to their practice squad, per multiple reports. ESPN’s Jordan Raanan was the first to report the signing, followed by Aaron Wilson. Gesky, 23, originally signed with the Green Bay Packers as an undrafted rookie out of Illinois and will reunite with former Illini teammate JC Davis as a Giant. Gesky appeared in 48 games over the course of his college career and started 34 games for Illinois, with 32 of his starts coming at left guard. He has adequate size for a guard at 6-foot-5, and roughly 310 pounds and solid athleticism for the position. He was regarded as a better pass protector than run blocker coming out of college, though that seems to be due to questions regarding leverage more than play strength in the run game. Still, Gesky was a relatively sought-after rookie free agent, with the Packers guaranteeing $200,000 of his rookie salary to entice him to Green Bay. He was ultimately waived in the Packers’ final cut-downs and re-signed to their practice squad. The Packers released him earlier this week as they reshuffled their practice squad. The corresponding roster move was the release of defensive tackle C.J. Ravenall.

title: Are the 2026 New York Giants a good team?
summary: In The Feed this week I saw someone complain that in the ESPN Power Rankings after Week 5, the New York Giants were ranked only No. 19 in the NFL despite their 3-1-1 record and first place standing the NFC EastDivision…and that is down two places from their No. 17 ranking the week before. BBV’s […]
full_text: Jameis Winston | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect In The Feed this week I saw someone complain that in the ESPN Power Rankings after Week 5, the New York Giants were ranked only No. 19 in the NFL despite their 3-1-1 record and first place standing the NFC EastDivision…and that is down two places from their No. 17 ranking the week before. BBV’s Nick Falato has the Giants ranked only 18th. It gets worse. The Athletic’s Josh Kendall and Chad Graff also have the Giants at No. 19 in their power rankings this week, but their statistical model guy, Austin Mock, did his own power ranking analysis with his model, and the model rates the Giants as…No. 31: Don’t let the chaotic NFC East make you believe the Giants are a good football team. They are not — at least not so far. The Giants’ offense ranks in the bottom 10 in just about every important offensive metric, and the defense isn’t much better, especially against the run. They rank in the bottom five in rush EPA and explosive run rate. If you can’t stop the run, life is going to be easy for opposing quarterbacks, especially with star outside linebacker Brian Burns out for the season. What’s going on? Are the Giants worse than their fans think? Certainly the hiring of John Harbaugh as head coach has had a major positive effect on how Giants fans view the team (notwithstanding Kyle Hamilton’s veiled knock on Harbaugh after last Sunday’s Ravens game). It seems to have had a positive effect on Giants players themselves (the ones he has not released or benched, anyway). And you have to give them credit for recovering from the dual shock of losing Jaxson Dart and being drubbed by the Rams to go 2-0-1 after that. To what extent is this a mirage, though? Let’s look at a variety of metrics of team and opponent performance to get a feel for where this team stands relative to other teams and what that might portend for the rest of the season. The bad news: I am going to show you metrics from Pro Football Focus , whose individual player grades I report on every week and that many of you hate. The good news: The stats I’m going to show are not based on the PFF grades that are the subject of your ire, but rather on by now standard metrics such as expected points added (EPA), which is calculated from outcomes of plays and their effect on eventual scoring by an offense. (For the record, though, PFF’s traditional grading system based on film review has the Giants ranked 23rd in the NFL overall, 25th on offense, 14th on defense, and 4th on special teams.) First, a plot of defensive vs. offensive EPA. These are adjusted for opponent quality and recent results are weighted more heavily in an attempt to make them more predictive of the future: The shading indicates teams of similar quality, though with different degrees of offensive and defensive strength depending on where they fall along the diagonal. This paints an even more bleak picture of the present state of the Giants than the subjective analyst power rankings I mentioned earlier and is more in line with Mock’s computer model. According to this diagram, the Giants are one of the absolute worst teams in the NFL. They have gotten their wins against almost equally bad teams (Tennessee, Arizona) and a tie with a team only a little better than they are (Washington). Only their defeat of Dallas was any kind of accomplishment given the Cowboys’ elite offense, but it was facilitated by their league-worst defense. Of comfort is that their one loss was to the Rams, one of the top five teams in the NFL on this chart (which notably does not include special teams). Also note that they are right next to this Sunday’s opponent, New Orleans. So that seems to support the naysayers. But there’s some good news. Even though PFF weighs recents results more to give them more predictive value, past performance may not be indicative of future results, as they say. First, let’s look at rushing and passing separately: As has been evident recently, the Giants are one of the worst rushing teams in the NFL (as Mock noted in his comment about their lack of explosive rushing plays). Maybe their running backs aren’t great. Maybe their offensive line is poor at run blocking. Maybe their run philosophy and run-pass mix leave something to be desired, as Chris Pflum discussed . Their passing game isn’t bad, though, considering they’re on their second quarterback of the season. The Giants are slightly lower than middle of the pack in passing. Given that they’ve played in the rain (and sometimes wind) three weeks in a row, that’s all right. The question is that this 3-1-1 record has been compiled against what most see as a soft schedule, and future opponents look to be more formidable (e.g., San Francisco, Seattle, Jacksonville). Here’s a 30,000-foot view of that: Good news and bad news: Thus far the Giants have faced offenses that are slightly better than average on the whole and they’ve held up at least adequately and sometimes better than that. On the other hand they’ve faced some of the league’s worst defenses so far. In the future? Actually, it doesn’t look all that much worse based on play thus far. The defensive strength of their future opponents overall is somewhat but not much better than what they’ve already seen, and the offenses are if anything a bit worse. Thus, it’s not outlandish to imagine that their strong 3-1-1 start might be sustainable going forward. The team you don’t want to be is the Los Angeles Chargers. They’re 0-5 already and according to the right panel they overall have the toughest future schedule in the NFL. Interested in something the Giants are almost best in the NFL at? Fourth down on both sides of the ball: The Giants and the Cincinnati Bengals lead the league in combined EPA gained on fourth down on offense and defense. The defense has been especially “clutch,” trailing only Cincinnati. I would like to see that diagram before and after Dennard Wilson decided to start blitzing a lot. Finally, since John Harbaugh’s training was as a special teams coach and no one ever looks at special teams, here are two special team ranking figures: The Giants are the NFL’s best in expected points added on punts and in the top 10 in expected points added on kickoffs. They’re slightly negative in EPA on field goals (I bet that diagram looked a lot different before Dominic Zvada’s bad outing in Washington). The bottom line Yes, there’s some validity to the opinions of those analysts who discount the Giants’ 3-1-1 record and place them in the bottom half of the NFL. There are some good things to build on, though. The Giants’ future schedule may not be as tough overall as it looked when the season began, even though there are a few individual games that will be difficult for them to win. To capitalize on that, though, they absolutely have to become a better rushing team. They have been a good fourth down team and they will have to continue that. Their special teams play will help if last Sunday’s field goal meltdown is an isolated occurrence. What will bear watching is how good a passing team they can be. If Jameis Winston can limit turnovers and give them a dangerous downfield attack (and if Matt Nagy leans into the passing game more than he has so far), the Giants have a chance to do some business this year.

title: Film review: NY Giants’ Marcus Mbow against the Commanders in Week 5
summary: The New York Giants had an improbable comeback that resulted in a wacky Week 5 tie against the Washington Commanders. New York was down 14 points in the fourth quarter, and the Giants’ offense scored three touchdowns to send the game into overtime. Starting right tackle Jermaine Eleumunor was injured midway through the third quarter […]
full_text: Marcus Mbow | Julian Leshay Guadalupe/NorthJersey.com / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The New York Giants had an improbable comeback that resulted in a wacky Week 5 tie against the Washington Commanders. New York was down 14 points in the fourth quarter, and the Giants’ offense scored three touchdowns to send the game into overtime. Starting right tackle Jermaine Eleumunor was injured midway through the third quarter when the score of the game was 19-6, Washington. Marcus Mbow took over the right tackle responsibilities and played well for the Giants. He surrendered two pressures in 45 snaps (37 pass-blocking snaps), with Washington pinning their ears back in obvious pass-rushing situations. The second-year fifth-round draft pick out of Purdue wasn’t flawless, but he executed his assignments well and allowed the Giants to function well without Eleumunor. Let’s get into his tape. ( Marcus Mbow is No. 71 ) Pass protection via GIPHY Mbow’s first snap was this third-and-8 at the Washington 47-yard line. The Giants helped Mbow with a Theo Johnson (84) chip and release, but Washington attacked the right side of the Giants’ line of scrimmage; Dan Quinn sent an E/T twist to Mbow and rookie Francis Mauigoa (65). Odafe Oweh (98) was the hammer with Frankie Luvu (4) looping to Mbow’s side. It’s an effortless pass-off by Mbow to the rookie guard. Mbow does a solid job recentering his gravity, dropping his hips and attacking Luvu on the twist. He does lean a bit into the contact and gets his chest parallel to the deck, but his feet follow Luvu up the arc, and his inside hand placement on the lower back of Luvu allows Mbow to steer the pass-rusher. It’s an impressive bend from Mbow, who succeeded, despite less-than-desirable technique. via GIPHY A few plays later, the Giants are on second-and-5, and Mbow shows a crisp, smooth vertical set against Dorance Armstrong (92). Mbow is square to his target, moves quickly to match Armstrong, and lands both hands inside the chest while cutting off the angle for the edge rusher. via GIPHY K’Lavon Chaisson (45) rushed from a wide angle, and Mbow adjusted his set mid-set; a flat step to start turned vertical to match Chaisson’s pass-rushing path. Mbow maintained a low profile with hands ready to attack, as his feet situated his positioning. Once Chaisson committed to power through the outside shoulder, Mbow sank himself low and absorbed the contact. Chaisson pushed Mbow back slightly, but the second-year offensive lineman got his feet underneath him and sat back on his hips. via GIPHY Here’s another quality vertical set by Mbow, matching the rush and stalling the edge rusher at the top of the arc. Luckily for the Giants, the officials called back the now-infamous pass interference call. via GIPHY Mbow does a good job restricting space after Chaisson attempted to separate and get width; Mbow kept everything tight and stayed grasped on Chaisson for a very good rep on the deep dig route to Malik Nabers (1). Below we see Mbow exercise patience with his inside hand punch, which appears to have quality force into contact that allows him to steer. His feet/hands combination combines quickness with adequate overall pop. via GIPHY via GIPHY This isn’t a crisp rep against defensive lineman Daron Payne (94), who challenged Mbow with his power. Mbow, though, held up and forced Payne wide, allowing Jameis Winston to rush for 15 yards with an excellent — elite — pump-fake 12 yards downfield. via GIPHY Mbow had some anchor issues as a rookie. While his anchor wasn’t perfect in Week 5, he seemed sturdier, doing a better job getting his feet under him while keeping his hips low. Chaisson’s initial power pushed Mbow back a bit, but the second-year tackle absorbed the contact well and kept the pocket intact. Could improve Mbow has foot quickness, but he was beaten around the edge a couple of times, resulting in pressure: via GIPHY via GIPHY Mbow is patient, and sometimes too patient, with how he chooses to engage these rushers; again, it’s not a lack of foot-quickness, but overall framing and confidence. Also, reps can help all of this with timing. Credit to Mbow, though, for flipping his hips and getting his arms out without fully compromising the pocket. via GIPHY Mbow loses inside on a shifty rush that was combined with a violent cross-chop that timed up Mbow’s punch perfectly. The B-Gap was penetrated, and Winston was forced off the spot for a short run. This was one of Mbow’s worst reps in a passing situation. Run game The Giants did not run the football much after Mbow entered the game, but the important third-and-3 crack toss to Cam Skattebo that went for 19 yards was run toward Mbow’s side, and he looked good operating in space: via GIPHY Mbow gets out around the blocks of Malachi Fields (88) and Darnell Mooney (17) to locate the contain defender and allow Skattebo to cut inside and find the most explosive run of the day in overtime for the Giants. via GIPHY Mbow gets a free release up to Sonny Styles (52), but the linebacker does a good job staying tight to the line of scrimmage and restricting space. Mbow doesn’t make clean contact and gets into the block sloppily, but he positions himself between Styles and the running back’s path, though he doesn’t create much space. via GIPHY Mbow gets discarded by Daron Payne, which resulted in the Cam Skattebo fumble — it was Payne who helped punch the ball out. Mbow’s run blocking wasn’t tested much in Week 5, but it was a rough rep against one of the league’s better defensive linemen. Final thoughts Mbow played well filling in for Eleumunor. He helped protect Winston during the Giants’ comeback effort. Was it perfect? No, but it was effective. Although the above play against Payne may not suggest success, it’s an interesting idea to consider trying Mbow, or even J.C. Davis, as cross-training on the inside, which was a popular talking point throughout the offseason. The Giants should try and get their best five out there on Sunday; Mbow is good, but the jury remains out on him playing inside.

title: 5 NY Giants-Saints storylines: Optimism in the midst of ‘crazy town’
summary: “A pessimist sees the difficulty in every opportunity; an optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.” New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh is a Winston Churchill admirer. In trying to make a point during his Monday call with New York media, Harbaugh was reaching to recall that Churchill quote as the coach was describing […]
full_text: Sir Winston Churchill “A pessimist sees the difficulty in every opportunity; an optimist sees the opportunity in every difficulty.” New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh is a Winston Churchill admirer. In trying to make a point during his Monday call with New York media, Harbaugh was reaching to recall that Churchill quote as the coach was describing the positive attitude of quarterback Jameis Winston. Here is the full quote from Harbaugh about Winston: “It’s awesome. I mean, it’s how important is it for a person? I mean, it’s the best thing to be around, and it’s genuine. I mean, he’s a very strong faith person. He’s a very strong Christian. He is a very good guy. He works extremely hard. He’s very motivated. He’s an unbelievable competitor. He’s tough as can be. He’s a fighter, and he just doesn’t let adversity get him down. He understands. It’s like (former NBA player) Michael Jordan or (16 th President of the United States) Abraham Lincoln or all the different stories you’ve heard. It’s not how many times you get knocked down, it’s how many times you get back up. You need to be plus-one in the get up category. And that’s exactly what he does every single day of his life, I would say. “And that’s why people like him are always successful. I mean, most successful people are optimists. Didn’t (former Prime Minister of the United Kingdom Winston) Churchill say that he knew a lot of successful people in his life. He knew a lot of pessimists in his life. And none of the successful people were the pessimists. Are you aware of that quote? It’s along those lines.” Why do I bring this up? Because Harbaugh, Winston and the Giants are trying each week to be the optimists in a difficult situation. They have lost their quarterback, Jaxson Dart, for the season. Yet, they have gone 2-0-1 since. They have lost their defensive leader, Brian Burns, for the season. Yet, players like Abdul Carter, Arvell Reese, Jevon Holland and Tae Banks have stepped up to help the Giants go without a loss in their last three games. Some want to belittle the NFC East, throwing around the ‘NFC Least’ moniker with the long-downtrodden Giants leading the division while the Philadelphia Eagles and Dallas Cowboys lose winnable games, and the Washington Commanders embarrass themselves. The Giants, though, are trying to play the role of the optimistic opportunist in the midst of the NFC East chaos. The Giants have commissioned ‘1-0’ t-shirts you often see Harbaugh and the players wearing. The idea, of course, is to just focus on going 1-0 every week despite the chaos of the division, the players who aren’t and won’t be there to help, and even the daily disruption of the construction at the Giants’ facility that has players lockering, showering, and lifting in temporary quarters in a parking lot once reserved for staff and media. In the middle of ‘crazy-town’ Even Sunday against the Commanders, the pessimist would say the Giants should have won the game. And, certainly there is an argument to be made for that. The optimist would say despite everything that happened in overtime they were down 14 points with eight minutes to play and did not lose. And they gained ground in the division despite the game ending in a tie. “The whole NFL is like crazy-town right now.” — John Harbaugh “We just got to really just do the best we can. Because you just can’t predict what’s going to happen,” Harbaugh said. “And you’ve got to keep chasing all those things all the time, every week. You got to keep rolling through. You can’t practice them all in one week. So, you got to keep rolling through them as much as you can. Don’t get complacent. Look for new things. If you see something, if you see a hole in what you’re doing, try to plug it up before it comes up. But man, it’s a crazy league. My wife, she was visiting my daughter and so I was talking to her after the game. And she’s watching games on TV. And she says, the whole NFL is like crazy-town right now. It’s crazy-town. It’s like, there’s so much crazy going on in this league right now. That’s what makes it so exciting, I guess. “And we were right in the middle of it. And we would like to do a lot of things better, we’d like to play. And we’re so proud of the good things and things we did well. And there’s so many things that we know we can do better. And we’re going to chase, we’re going to chase with everything we’ve got. Because we’ve got next week to try to be a better football team. And our guys are very, very optimistic. They’re very optimistic about that. Very optimistic that they can improve and get better and get ready for the next challenge.” The Rodney Dangerfield of the NFL This one goes along with the ‘NFC Least’ theme. The Giants are in sole possession first place in the NFC East five games into the season. The New Orleans Saints, the Giants’ Week 6 opponent, are 1-4. The game will be at MetLife Stadium, where the Giants are 3-0 this season. Despite that, FanDuel Sportsbook has installed the Saints as 1.5-point favorites. I get that the combined record of New Orleans’ opponents is 17-8 (.680 winning percentage), while Giants’ opponents are 6-18-1 (.260 winning percentage). Yes, the Saints are likely better than their record and may still make a run at a title in the less-than-spectacular NFC South. Still, the Giants being the home underdog in this situation feels disrespectful. Running the ball The Giants are built to be a running team. They are 29th in the NFL in their usage of ‘11’ personnel, a more wide open offensive set with one running back, one tight end, and three wide receivers. They are first in the league in their usage of ‘22’ personnel, which is two running backs, two tight ends, one wide receiver. Patrick Ricard has played 116 snaps, more than any other fullback in the league. The Giants want to play power football with Ricard, blocking tight end Chris Manhertz, and straight-ahead pile-pushing backs Cam Skattebo and Najee Harris. Unfortunately, the complement to all of that — Jaxson Dart’s ability to create chunk plays in the quarterback run game — is gone for the remainder of the season. The Giants tried on Sunday against the Commanders to reinsert the threat of that quarterback run game by using J.J. McCarthy for a few plays. It didn’t work, but Harbaugh won’t give up on it after just one try. The Giants know they have to do something. The numbers are not pretty: They still do not have a 20-yard run from a running back this season — Skattebo’s overtime 19-yarder in Week 5 is their longest. Only eight teams have fewer than the Giants’ 10 runs of at least 10 yards. The Giants’ EPA per rush is -0.15, 26th in the league. The Giants average 3.7 yards per running play, 24th overall. Their rushing success tate of 38.8% is 21st. The Giants have -65 rushing yards over expected, meaning NextGen Stats believes their rushers have left at least 65 yards on the table. That’s 29th. The Giants are 26th in the league in yards before contact (0.86). Defenses are nullifying the Giants’ run game without stacking the box with extra defenders. The Giants have faced a stacked box just 19% of the time, 24th in the NFL. “We definitely need more explosives in the run game,” Harbaugh said on Monday. “That’s definitely something that we’ll be chasing and looking for. Every play has got its own story that is told. We look back at it and study it. I think everybody in the offense will tell you this play, that play, whatever. There’s always something that can be done better. A lot of times it’s the difference in the play. It’s really our execution mostly, usually. Sometimes you’re overwhelmed with numbers or something like that. But there’s definitely been plays where we can get more yards on. “We’ve got all the players we need to win all the games, to win every single game. All the players we need to win every single game. But we’re always looking too, to get better. The first way to get better is that the players, you have get better. That’s really…

title: NY Giants fill open roster spot with veteran linebacker
summary: The New York Giants on Tuesday added veteran linebacker Malik Harrison to their 53-man roster, filling the spot opened on Saturday when defensive lineman Chauncey Golston was placed on injured reserve. Harrison, 28, is in his seventh NFL season. He spent the first five seasons of his career with the Baltimore Ravens after being a […]
full_text: Malik Harrison | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants on Tuesday added veteran linebacker Malik Harrison to their 53-man roster, filling the spot opened on Saturday when defensive lineman Chauncey Golston was placed on injured reserve. Harrison, 28, is in his seventh NFL season. He spent the first five seasons of his career with the Baltimore Ravens after being a third-round pick by the Ravens in the 2020 NFL Draft. Harrison spent the 2025 season with the Pittsburgh Steelers. In 90 regular-season games, he has made 43 starts. Harrison has signficant experience playing both inside and outside linebacker, so he provides the Giants depth at that level of their defense. He has also been a valuable special teams contributor throughout his career. Harrison was elevated from the practice squad for the first three games this season, the maximum allowed by NFL rules. He played 56 snaps, all on special teams, with two solo tackles. To take Harrison’s spot on the practice squad, the Giants made the signing of defensive end Dawuane Smoot official.

title: NY Giants news: Changing the offense, Jameis Winston, Isaiah Likely, more
summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants get set to host the New Orleans Saints. Let Jameis Winston cook? Why Giants should ditch run-heavy approach and let QB air it out | The Athletic The Giants may have stumbled into the world Winston is most comfortable in during the […]
full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories as the Giants get set to host the New Orleans Saints. Let Jameis Winston cook? Why Giants should ditch run-heavy approach and let QB air it out | The Athletic The Giants may have stumbled into the world Winston is most comfortable in during the second half of Sunday’s 27-27 tie with the Commanders. Partly due to the game flow — the Giants were trailing by two scores for most of the second half — and partly due to a need to shake things up after a woeful first half, the coaches opened up the passing game and went up-tempo with a no-huddle offense. The Giants’ best playmakers are wide receiver Malik Nabers and tight end Isaiah Likely. It makes more sense to run the offense through that duo rather than the underwhelming running backs corps of Cam Skattebo, Najee Harris and Tyrone Tracy Jr. Now, 33 combined targets like Nabers and Likely had Sunday may be excessive. But it’s not a coincidence that the offense took off when Winston started feeding that duo in the second half. John Harbaugh defends surprising Giants call to play for OT instead of a win | New York Post Kicking the extra point to pull within seven points seemed to make the most sense, but the analytic assessment is to go for the 2-point conversion to boost the chances to win the game in regulation. The thinking is the trailing team will need 15 points to win the game, so go for two after the first touchdown and if you do not get it, go for two after the second touchdown. “I think generally speaking, theoretically, you go for two,” Harbaugh said Monday. “Then you see if you have to go for two twice, give yourself a chance to win the game in regulation. But the way the game was going, I just decided I wanted to put it into overtime. I didn’t want to take the chance on the 2-point conversion. I thought overtime would give us the best chance. Plus, it’s a road division game, so the tie isn’t the worst thing for the road team. So, I just feel like all in all, I made that decision to go for one and put it in overtime if it came down to two scores.” Isaiah Likely: Halftime dialogue, Jameis Winston’s open ears fueled Giants’ OT push | USAToday.com Likely said the feedback loop with Winston centered on trust in leverage and winning individual plays. He added that Winston responded by placing the ball in their hands and expecting them to produce. “Great feedback at halftime. Player dialogue, coaches’ dialogue, and really just getting behind your brother,” said Likely. “You know, Jameis was open ears. He understood that the job in the second half was to get us back in the game and that’s exactly what he did…Jameis is one of those, when he’s clicking, he’s clicking. I feel like he showed that fire in his eyes coming into the huddle every time, knowing that when there’s plays to be made, he can make a play.” Top 10 best NFL free agent acquisitions through Week 5 | CBSSports.com 7. Giants TE Isaiah Likely. Contract: Three years, $40 million with $26 million guaranteed. Despite losing starting quarterback Jaxson Dart with a season-ending knee injury in Week 2, the New York Giants remain in first place in the NFC East division through five weeks with a 3-1-1 record. Free agency acquisition tight end Isaiah Likely is a big reason why New York has been able to maintain any semblance of a coherent passing game despite fill-in quarterback Jameis Winston ranking second-to-last in the league in completion percentage at 57.6%. Likely’s four receiving touchdowns are tied for the fourth-most in the NFL and rank as tied for the most among tight ends leaguewide. His 19 receiving first downs are the most among all tight ends through five weeks this season. With No. 1 wide receiver Malik Nabers still finding his footing in 2026 after returning from a torn ACL, Likely has been a godsend for the Giants’ passing game. Jameis on building chemistry in the pass game . @Jaboowins is enjoying the chemistry being built with @whyguard13 & @DaGorilla4 🙌🏽 pic.twitter.com/HSLMbfJSIF — Where’s Jameis (@WheresJameis) October 13, 2026 Can John Harbaugh’s Giants sustain winning while walking NFL tightrope? | New York Daily News Harbaugh noted that he and his coaching staff have been able to pivot week-to-week so far to find new ways of concealing weaknesses and highlighting strengths of their shorthanded and evolving roster. They are without Dart, edge rusher Brian Burns, wide receiver Calvin Austin and defensive tackle Roy Robertson-Harris already, among others, after all. “We as a coaching staff do a great job of kind of finding our identity in some of these different areas, and we will,” Harbaugh said. As Giants’ pass rush pressure improves, Jayden Daniels’ showing raises concerns | NJ.com Still, it’ll be fascinating to see how Carter and the Giants’ defense handle Daniels the next time they see him, in Week 10 at MetLife Stadium. Daniels on Sunday ran nine times for 103 yards, with touchdowns of 26 and 38 yards. Carter knows this is something the Giants must fix. “We’ve just got to be more disciplined in our rush lanes,” he said. “We talked about it all week. So honestly, if that happens in the game, it’s on us as a front. We really got to be better at caging him and stopping our rush [to not over pursue]. We’ve got to be better at that next time we see them for sure.” Radio call of Nabers touchdown last weekend "Big time play by a big time player!" 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/NYSmd5P7tv — New York Giants (@Giants) October 12, 2026 NFL Insider Explains Why Giants Really Traded for J.J. McCarthy | SI.com “They do wanna see whether or not someone drafted that high and that young is capable of being a backup or even a starter at some point,” Schultz said, adding that there could be more sightings of McCarthy on the field “in certain situations.” But not as a starter, at least not for the immediate future.“That would really surprise me,” Schultz said. “If Jameis were to play really badly in a couple of weeks in a row and they lost two in a row, I think it’s a different conversation. I don’t really expect that to happen. Not only did they sign Jameis, but they extended him, and they gave him real money in a two-year extension. And that was, I think, a manifestation of how they feel about him, knowing that if he did need to start and play, he could win them football games.” From Big Blue View The Giants may need to change how they think about offense NFL power rankings: Nick’s picks for how teams stack up before Week 6 This week’s opponent Saints look to turn things around entering Week 6 | NewOrleansSaints.com How Does the Saints’ Latest Loss Affect Season Outlook? | Yahoo! title: Eagles Injury Report: Jalen Hurts, Saquon Barkley, and DeVonta Smith among 24 players listed
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles issued their first official injury report of the week on Wednesday in advance of their Week 6 game against the Carolina Panthers. There are 24 players listed. 24! Not all of them are on the 53-man roster, which is really a 52-man roster since Lane Johnson will count against the team’s limit […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 5: Jalen Hurts #1 of the Philadelphia Eagles celebrates with Saquon Barkley #26 and Devonta Smith #6 after scoring a touchdown during the second quarter of an NFL football game against the Denver Broncos at Lincoln Financial Field on October 5, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles issued their first official injury report of the week on Wednesday in advance of their Week 6 game against the Carolina Panthers. There are 24 players listed. 24! Not all of them are on the 53-man roster, which is really a 52-man roster since Lane Johnson will count against the team’s limit all season, but that’s still insane. Let’s sort through it all. The Eagles listed six players under DID NOT PARTICIPATE: Saquon Barkley, DeVonta Smith, Drew Kendall, Jalyx Hunt, Michael Carter II, and Will Shipley. Earlier this week, there was a report that Barkley and Smith “have a shot” to return against the Panthers. Both of them missing Wednesday’s practice isn’t an encouraging start in that regard. With Barkley hurt, Tank Bigsby on injured reserve, and Shipley also banged up, the Eagles are tracking to be without their top three running backs on Sunday. They currently have two healthy backfield options on the roster: Dameon Pierce and Carson Steele. They also have Jaydon Blue on the practice squad … and they’re reportedly going to sign Ja’Quinden Jackson , though that move has yet to become official. Smitty is now listed with “hamstring/toe” injuries after previously just being listed with a hamstring injury. Seems like he’s in jeopardy of missing his third straight game. Kendall is “week-to-week,” according to a report from NJ.com’s Cayden Steele . Steele noted that Kendall was walking gingerly in the locker room with a big sleeve on his leg. With Kendall expected to miss a second straight game, the Eagles could once again go with Jake Majors at center. Unless they move Willie Lampkin to the pivot if Landon Dickerson comes back at left guard? Or go with Dickerson at center and Lampkin at guard, which seems less likely? Vic Fangio said “ it’ll be pretty miraculous ” for Hunt to play this week. But it sounds like Hunt will avoid going on injured reserve, which is good. Still, the Eagles are going to be without their leader in quarterback hits this season. MC2 got hurt in Week 5 and it looks like he’ll be out this week after previously filling in for Marcus Epps as a starting safety in nickel packages. The Eagles listed 11 players under LIMITED PARTICIPATION: Landon Dickerson, Tyler Steen, Dontayvion Wicks, Marquise Brown, Jonathan Greenard, Marcus Epps, Grant Calcaterra, Eli Stowers, Jakorian Bennett, A.J. Epenesa, and E.J. Jenkins. The Eagles opened 21-day practice windows for Dickerson, Calcaterra, Stowers, and Bennett earlier on Wednesday. Dickerson wouldn’t say if he’s ready to play on Sunday. It doesn’t seem like the Eagles should be rushing him back since, by Dickerson’s own admission, he played pretty poorly in Week 1. One must also wonder to what degree he might be physically diminished at this point in his injury-riddled career. The Eagles have until 4:00 PM Eastern on Saturday to activate Dickerson (or not) from injured reserve in order to play on Sunday. So, we’ll see. Landon Dickerson on whether he believes the team still views him as the long-term LG: “That’s a great question. Do they have a media day for Nick and Howie? You can ask them that.” — Zach Berman (@ZBerm) October 14, 2026 Steen got banged up in Week 5 but was able to return to the game. Guessing the Eagles are managing his practice workload to help get him to Sunday. Wicks suffered a hamstring injury in practice last week but played through it. Guessing he’ll do the same in Week 6. Brown participated in practice for the first time since missing the Eagles’ last three games. Seems like he might be able to suit up on Sunday. One would expect his role to be minor since he wasn’t playing much when healthy earlier this season. Greenard was able to practice for the first time since getting hurt in Week 4. With Hunt out and the Eagles’ pass rush off to a slow start, getting him back would be ideal. Epps might be able to play after missing multiple games. The Eagles could use him back with Carter II likely unable to play. The Eagles should be in no rush to activate Calcaterra when they already have three tight ends on the roster and Zach Ertz on the practice squad. But they seem to like him more than their fans do. Stowers practiced for the first time since the lead up to Week 1. There’s really no room for him on the roster as a depth tight end who doesn’t really help on special teams. They could and should be slow-playing any potential return here. The Eagles aren’t necessarily hurting for cornerback depth but they could eventually look to activate Bennett if they prefer him over Jonathan Jones and/or Mac McWilliams. Epenesa being limited with a back injury isn’t really ideal when the Eagles are already missing Hunt and Greenard is also banged up. Nolan Smith is the only Eagles edge rusher who is not listed on the injury report. Jenkins was added to the report on Friday last week as a full participant with a toe injury. The depth tight end was limited on Wednesday. The Eagles listed seven players under FULL PARTICIPATION: Jalen Hurts, Jalen Carter, Zack Baun, Andrew Mukuba, Jihaad Campbell, Arnold Ebiketie, and Fred Johnson. Speaking during his post-practice press conference on Wednesday, Hurts revealed that he got “nicked up” in Week 4. He wasn’t added to the report until Friday of last week, however, as a full participant with a calf injury. Hurts will play but it’s notable that his rushing production has really taken a dip. He tied a career-low in carries with just two in Week 5. Carter continues to be listed on the injury report with the hairline fracture in his wrist. But he was wearing a less restrictive wrap in Week 5, so, he seems to be getting healthier. Which is a big deal for this defense! Baun is now listed with a shoulder injury after previously being listed with a concussion over the past two weeks. Mukuba is also listed with a shoulder. Campbell is listed with knee/wrist injuries. He is expected to lose playing time as he takes part in an off-ball linebacker rotation with Jeremiah Trotter Jr . Ebiketie is listed with a shoulder injury. Again, Nolan Smith is the only edge rusher on the Eagles’ roster who is not on the injury report. Fred Johnson is listed with a knee injury. title: Eagles-Jaguars Film Review: Feeling much better about the defense
summary: This defense deserved a win. The Jaguars have a good offense, and they were always going to make some plays. But the Eagles repeatedly gave themselves a chance with outstanding individual performances, physical run defense, and some ridiculous goal-line stops. Once again, the other side of the ball let them down. Being at this game […]
full_text: LONDON, ENGLAND - OCTOBER 11: Bhayshul Tuten of the Jacksonville Jaguars is tackled by Riq Woolen of the Philadelphia Eagles during the 2026 NFL London Games match between Philadelphia Eagles and Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on October 11, 2026 in London, England. (Photo by Ryan Pierse/Getty Images) | Getty Images This defense deserved a win. The Jaguars have a good offense, and they were always going to make some plays. But the Eagles repeatedly gave themselves a chance with outstanding individual performances, physical run defense, and some ridiculous goal-line stops. Once again, the other side of the ball let them down. Being at this game was awesome. The goal-line stand in the first half happened right in front of where I was sitting, and it was easily my favorite moment of the afternoon. You could feel the intensity. There has been criticism of this defense for being a little soft this season, and some of that criticism has been fair. There was nothing soft about those reps. This group came to fight. It was so cool to see. This was not a flawless performance. But when your offense produces 10 yards over 15 plays across four consecutive second-half punts, you are asking an awful lot of the defense. They kept coming up with stops anyway. Let’s get into it. Defense Jalyx Hunt was outstanding against the run in the first half. He was a big loss when he went down. The Jaguars use their tight ends heavily in the run game, which makes the edge defenders’ ability to handle those blocks particularly important. Hunt does not just hold his ground here. He knocks the tight end backward and disrupts the play before the runner has a chance to get going. This was not a one-off, either. Hunt did this multiple times before his injury, and the Jaguars struggled to establish their run game. The Jaguars finished with 36 yards on nine outside zone attempts, which is impressive considering this is a big part of the Jags’ offense, and the Eagles have struggled with outside zone runs at times this year. Hunt’s ability to defeat tight end blocks was a big part of that. Eagles' Defense All22 Thread vs. Jags. 1) I thought Jalyx Hunt was outstanding in the first half against the run. The Jags use their tight ends a lot in the run game, but Hunt blows up this play by knocking the tight end back. He did this multiple times in the first half, and… pic.twitter.com/oEgGZfBmTz — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 13, 2026 Jalen Carter. My word. When he is healthy and moving like this, he is as good as nearly any defensive player in the league. The frustrating part is getting this version of him consistently, because health has been such an issue. Here, the quickness and violence were back, and the Jaguars had very few answers in the first half. His club move is such a weapon. He can knock a blocker off balance and get past him before the protection can recover. But what I particularly loved was the finish. Carter was not content to just sack Trevor Lawrence. He went after the football. Carter was wrecking the offense. 2) Jalen Carter, my word, was he good in the first half. When Carter is healthy, he is as good as nearly any defensive player in the league. His issue is just staying healthy. He wrecked the Jags' offense in the first half, with a number of quick pressures and 2 forced fumbles.… pic.twitter.com/PTY4N70Fo2 — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 13, 2026 Unfortunately, there were still some mistakes, and this was a really disappointing one. Both safeties came downhill, which left the Eagles without a deep defender to chase down Parker Washington. My assumption is that Michael Carter II should be playing as the single-high safety here, but I cannot be certain of the coverage. What we can say is that the defense ends up without the protection it needs behind the play. Andrew Mukuba’s aggression is also part of the issue. I have mentioned this repeatedly: he is very eager to come downhill, and play action is catching him out. Some of that comes from what the scheme asks him to do against the run. This scheme does ask safeties to fly downhill from depth vs. the run. But there has to be a balance, and I think Mukuba is too aggressive at times. 3) This play was really disappointing because it's not a play you associate with this defense. It's a weird coverage, because both safeties come downhill, so I'm assuming Michael Carter got it wrong and should be a single-high safety. Without him at deep safety, there's no deep… pic.twitter.com/0yGHHJ6GoZ — Jonny Page (@JonnyPage9) October 13, 2026 Despite that rep, I thought the secondary’s communication was much better overall. The Jaguars used plenty of motion and switch releases to test how the Eagles pass routes off, and we didn’t see the same frequency of coverage busts that have hurt this defense in recent weeks. This third-down stop by Quinyon Mitchell is a fantastic example of playing the situation. One of the biggest changes was the use of dime personnel on third-and-long. That means six defensive backs, with Jihaad Campbell coming off, Kenny Moore II entering at safety, and Carter II moving to the slot. I liked it. I generally like getting more defensive backs on the field in obvious passing situations, provided they can communicate and play together. There is no point adding coverage players if everyone ends up confused about their assignments. Here, the group looked comfortable, and I thought the package worked well until Carter II got injured. 4) I thought the Eagles' communication in the secondary was so much better this week than in previous weeks. title: Eagles open practice windows for 4 players to return from injured reserve
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced some roster news on Wednesday afternoon. Here’s an overview: Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. LANDON DICKERSON Dickerson became eligible to return from IR after the Eagles’ Week 5 game. The three-time Pro Bowler looked like a shell of himself in Week 1 as he played through […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JUNE 10: Philadelphia Eagles guard Landon Dickerson #69 looks on during the Philadelphia Eagles off season minicamp on June 10th, 2026 at the Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles officially announced some roster news on Wednesday afternoon. Here’s an overview: 21-day practice windows to return from injured reserve were opened for OG Landon Dickerson, TE Eli Stowers, TE Grant Calcaterra, and CB Jakorian Bennett. DB Dean Clark was signed to the practice squad. Let’s sort through this news on a player-by-player basis. LANDON DICKERSON Dickerson became eligible to return from IR after the Eagles’ Week 5 game. The three-time Pro Bowler looked like a shell of himself in Week 1 as he played through injury. He admitted after the game that he was “ a complete liability .” The hope is that Dickerson is truly healthy now. But it’s hard not to wonder if his previous injuries have left him physically diminished moving forward. The guess here is that the Eagles aren’t going to rush Dickerson back into the starting lineup. But perhaps I’m wrong about that. If/when he does return, one would figure he’ll take his place at his normal starting position at left guard. ELI STOWERS Stowers became eligible to return from IR after the Eagles’ Week 4 game. It’s curious how the rookie tight end ended up on IR in the first place since he told reporters he was set to play in Week 1 before being ruled questionable on the final injury report. He was then downgraded one day later with talk of the Eagles discovering he was more injured than initially realized. Had he not been placed on IR, there was thought he would be a healthy scratch in the Eagles’ season opener. Stowers was pretty invisible during the Eagles’ offseason practices and preseason games. He never took any first-team reps, meaning he hasn’t had much time to develop chemistry with Jalen Hurts. And it’s not like he’s known for blocking or helping out on special teams. So, it’ll be interesting to see what the Eagles do with Stowers. The team is currently carrying three tight ends on the roster: Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, and E.J. Jenkins. They also have Zach Ertz on the practice squad and the veteran is out of temporary elevations. The Eagles will have to sign Ertz to the roster if they want him available on game days moving forward. Stowers needs reps in order to get better, so, it’s good to see he’s back on the practice squad. But I don’t know how he fits on the roster. Guessing the Eagles aren’t rushing to activate him. GRANT CALCATERRA Oh, that’s right, Calcaterra is still on the team. He became eligible to return from IR after the Eagles’ Week 4 game. As previously noted, the Eagles already have plenty of bodies at tight end. Not sure how Calcaterra fits in the picture here. It is worth noting that just because the Eagles open a player’s 21-day practice window doesn’t mean they will definitely activate them to the roster. They can let the window close, leaving the player on IR. Why open the window at all, then? Well, there’s value in having the flexibility of having them ready in case injury issues arise. But, at this point in time, I don’t see the need for Calcaterra to take up a roster spot. JAKORIAN BENNETT Bennett became eligible to return from IR after the Eagles’ Week 4 game. The Eagles aren’t really hurting for corner depth. And it seems like they might trust veteran Jonathan Jones to be the top backup on the outside than Bennett anyway. But, again, the value in opening Bennett’s window is that he can be ready should the team find themselves in need of corner help over the next few weeks. DEAN CLARK Clark, 25, went unpicked in the 2025 NFL Draft before signing with the New York Jets. He played 180 defensive snaps and 172 special teams snaps last season. The Jets waived him in roster cuts prior to the start of the 2026 season. The majority of Clark’s snaps have come at safety but he has some nickel corner experience as well. With the Eagles already behind thin at safety and Michael Carter II getting hurt in Week 5, doesn’t hurt to add some more depth on the back end of the defense.
