title: Sean Mannion is still having a blast despite Eagles’ struggles
summary: The Eagles offense took steps in the right direction on Sunday in London, but with injuries and depth issues, the group still has room to grow. Offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to reporters this week about their second-half struggles, what he’s seen from the passing game, and explained that late-game catch by Makai Lemon. Here’s […]
full_text: Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles offense took steps in the right direction on Sunday in London, but with injuries and depth issues, the group still has room to grow. Offensive coordinator Sean Mannion spoke to reporters this week about their second-half struggles, what he’s seen from the passing game, and explained that late-game catch by Makai Lemon. Here’s what else the OC had to say: On Jalen Hurts in the run game “I think we’re always looking for ways to integrate [Jalen Hurts] into the run game. Some of it’s dependent on the opponent and the fronts they’re giving us, the looks you’re getting. But like I’ve said in here before, it’s a unique trait that he has that makes him dangerous. Some of them are designed, some of them are kind of the off-schedule plays. I think he’s had a good feel for that in terms of when to take off and run. He had some big plays early in the year, first few weeks, of using his legs in the pass game, kind of those off-schedule scrambles. So, there’s a place for both of them. I think he’s found a nice balance of that. Mannion went on to say that every week present a different challenge and they’re going to adjust accordingly, and this week against the Jaguars, they planned for a more pass-oriented offense. He noted that some of that was intentional, and some was just how the game played out. “We want to be an offense that is balanced and can attack you in the run game and the pass game. Then, within the game, within the week, the opponent that you’re facing, your personnel, there can be little tweaks along the way that lead to a different end result in terms of your run-pass balance.” The OC also said he didn’t think that the calf injury that popped up late last week affected Hurts, and overall felt the QB was ready to play and performed well. On the young OL players Mannion said that early in the game, everything is heightened being their first regular season NFL action, but as the game went on, he felt like C/G Jake Majors, C/G Willie Lampkin and T Markel Bell found their footing, communicated well, and played hard. “That’s one thing, and I say it every week, but this group really, really plays hard, especially Willie, Jake, Markel, those young guys. You can just see the ferocity they’re playing with out there. That’s what you appreciate about them. These are three young players that we have a ton of confidence in. They’re talented. They’re getting their first taste of real action. I think they’re going to keep getting better. We feel good about the depth of this group while we’re kind of weathering the storm through some of these injuries.” On second-half struggles The OC said that he felt like they did a better job last week against the Jaguars coming out of halftime, and they had some opportunities in the second-half, but need to be finishing drives. He pointed out that they did have some third down conversions, and were close on the deep throw to Dontayvion Wicks. “I think there were some chances there that we just didn’t quite capitalize on. Ultimately as a staff, I’m looking every week to put ourselves in the best position possible leaving halftime to extend those drives. I think we’re closer. I know the result hasn’t been what we want or what we hold ourselves to as an offense, but I felt like we were getting closer in the second half. We really just have to finish some of those drives.” On Makai Lemon’s late-game catch Mannion was asked if Lemon was supposed to go out of bounds on his catch ahead of the Eagles final field goal on Sunday. He explained that their focus there was just to advance the ball. “They were in a cover zero look. With that comes some leverage issues where you’re inside. The primary focus there was [to] advance the ball to do our best to help the kick and then get us into the best play possible to do so and avoid a negative play. So, that was the outcome we had there. Obviously, he was caught on the outbreak right by the sideline, kind of got pushed out, but our primary focus with the call and with the execution of it was to advance the ball. With the look, that’s what ended up happening. We’re in an outbreak and he ends up getting pushed out.” Ultimately, the OC felt like it was a bang-bang play on the sidelined, and they were primarily focused on how to help the field goal distance. He also revealed that Lemon was the first read on that play. On the pass game Mannion doesn’t think Jalen Hurts step back in completions this year is any one thing. He noted that across the board offensively, they want to improve, and that’s in the run and pass games. “I think [Jalen Hurts] is a naturally very accurate guy, so I’m confident that those numbers will continue to improve. His comfort level grows each and every week. Getting these live game reps week after week after week, he’s going to grow more and more comfortable. I think the good thing is he’s been making good decisions with the ball. Obviously, we had an uptick in our pass attempts last game and I thought he made good decisions with where the ball was supposed to go. I’m confident, because he is a naturally accurate passer, that those numbers will rise. On the run game “I feel confident this group’s going to be able to move the ball. We had some nice runs earlier on in the run game. We just need to keep sustaining that. Then honestly, some of it’s not necessarily a negative. You feel better about some of the other calls you have on the sheet and you get to those.” Mannion also talked about Carson Steele, noting that the RB did a phenomenal job in the preseason, and he’s wearing a lot of different hats for them on the practice field. “He’s a versatile player who can do a lot of nice things for us. We’re looking to use all of our guys in every way possible. So, [using Steele at fullback is] certainly something we’re considering.” Other notables Mannion said that working with head coach Nick Sirianni with game management decisions has been smooth, and they had a lot of opportunities during practices to work through a lot of different scenarios. Most of the game management scenarios are talked through during the week, and they map out decisions based on different parameters and move forward accordingly. The OC talked about how he loves coming to work everyday and getting a chance to collaborate with staff and players as a unit to achieve the best result possible. He noted his enthusiasm and his enjoyment of the process and the work hasn’t waned. “It’s been a blast. There are new challenges every day, whether it be managing injuries or whether it be managing a practice plan or traveling overseas, how does that adjust our offensive meeting schedule? But that honestly is the enjoyable part. That’s why you love getting into coaching is you get to work with other great coaches, get to work with a phenomenal group of players that work their butts off, they’re coachable, they want to win, they want to get better. It’s a new challenge every day in this role, but it’s everything I hoped it would be and it’s been a blast. I am really confident that if we keep attacking each day with the right mindset, with a high level of enthusiasm, with a will to just get better bit by bit, day by day, we are going to get the results that we’re after.”
author: Alexis Chassen

title: 5 Eagles thoughts after 5 games
summary: The Philadelphia Eagles have played five games. These are five thoughts on the team. 1) The Eagles’ vibes are bad but the season is not over. This Eagles season is off to a dreadful start. The offense feels out of sorts. Lane Johnson retired. Cam Jurgens has been traded. The defense has regressed mightily. The […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JUNE 10: Eagles owner Jeffrey Lurie and General manager Howie Roseman converse during the Philadelphia Eagles off season minicamp on June 10th, 2026 at the Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Philadelphia Eagles have played five games. These are five thoughts on the team. 1) The Eagles’ vibes are bad but the season is not over . This Eagles season is off to a dreadful start. The offense feels out of sorts. Lane Johnson retired. Cam Jurgens has been traded. The defense has regressed mightily. The coaching has felt bad to the point of malpractice. The vibes haven’t been bad since, well, since two years ago after a blowout loss to the Buccaneers. Two weeks after getting lit up by Kirk Cousins, the Eagles went to Tampa Bay and got boat raced in the brutal heat. People (including me!) wanted Nick Sirianni fired and the hope bottomed out on Jalen Hurts. And we all know what happened after that. Now, I would be shocked if the Eagles repeated 2024. The pieces just aren’t there the way they were then. But despite all the things that are bad about this team, and there is plenty to be frustrated about, I don’t want to throw in the towel on this season. Washington is a mess, the bottom is going to come out on Jameis Winston in New York, and the Dallas Cowboys have been the same 9-8 team since the Obama administration. The NFC East is stupid every year and the Eagles can still tighten up the operation and go on a run. 10 games probably wins the East and if you would rather blow it up midseason instead of piss off Cowboys fans with a third straight division title… I don’t know what to tell you. 2) Nick Sirianni is still not the guy. Just like everyone else, I have gone back and forth on Sirianni basically since he got hired. But I feel confident (for now) that he is just not fit to lead this team. His whole schtick was supposed to be that he’s a culture and preparation guy. But the Eagles have felt unprepared at the beginning of every season he’s been head coach and the culture has officially fallen off a cliff with the Lane Johnson exit. Every week it feels like the Eagles are battling their own offensive coaching. Big plays seem to happen outside of the offensive structure and when Hurts is calling audibles at the line. That has been a trend for years. Nick’s influence on the offense feels obvious from coordinator to coordinator. Unless he miraculously runs this team to an NFC title appearance, you gotta move on. 3) The Howie Roseman Conundrum . Howie Roseman is the best GM in the NFL. I don’t think there’s really any debating that. I think you can say the last two drafts have yet to prove themselves, but those are two question marks on an otherwise exceptional track record, especially since 2021. However… If and when the Eagles fire Sirianni, the Eagles have to contend with a dynamic that has followed Howie Roseman around since he became the GM over 15 years ago. Howie doesn’t share power very well, and people get fired when they try to usurp his power. Now, it’s great he believes in his abilities as a GM so much: He is very good at it. However, the Eagles clearly need a head coach who can build a sustainable offensive ecosystem. Having the entire operation being reliant on young offensive coordinators who can be hired away every year is not a great way to move. However, the archetype of the offensive architect head coach typically means a guy who wants a lot of say in roster construction. When the Eagles initially hired Sirianni, I said that Howie got a guy he could push around and would never push back. I still believe that. He did not play nice with Andy Reid, or Chip Kelly, or Doug Pederson. Now obviously this worked with Nick over the course of his tenure. There’s no arguing that. But if (when) the Eagles move on to a new head coach, is Howie’s looming presence going to keep certain personalities away from the team? 4) The youth movement is rarely pretty. The Eagles were really good for a few years, in large part due to some amazing veteran players on both sides of the ball serving as a great influence to talented youngsters. Brandon Graham, Fletcher Cox, Lane Johnson, Jason Kelce, and Darius Slay are all gone now. A new era has to begin. As I mentioned above, the jury is still out on the last two drafts, but so far it doesn’t look great. However, this year will really show one way or the other if the Eagles have anything in Jihaad Campbell, Makai Lemon, Andrew Mukuba, Markel Bell, Willie Lampkin, Eli Stowers, and Micah Morris. All have flashed some good and might just need more snaps to become more consistent. But these kinds of transition periods are rarely smooth even for the best teams. We saw it last year with the Chiefs. Ultimately getting these young guys snaps now could be really good for the team in the long term. 5) Howie knows the team is in transition. Howie is a smart guy. He knows he has to prepare for the next era. Even if the Eagles can make the playoffs this year, Howie is going to be aggressive in the 2027 offseason to reload the roster. The team has seven picks in what should be a very good 2027 draft, and seven picks in the 2028 draft, including two picks in the first round and two in the second. Howie is smart enough to remember what happened after the 2018 Super Bowl win where bad drafting and roster aging led to the team bottoming out in 2020. I think he’s doing his best to avoid that. We’ll see how it works out.

title: Eagles News: NFL insider senses “the concern is quite high” in Philadelphia
summary: Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I don’t think the Eagles are sitting back and saying “Hey, we’re almost 4-1! We’re going to be fine.” Which is good. You don’t want them to be delusional about how they’ve played thus far. You want them to feel the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 04: Head coach Nick Sirianni of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on from the sideline during the second quarter of the game against the Los Angeles Rams at Lincoln Financial Field on October 04, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to The Linc, the daily Philadelphia Eagles links roundup at Bleeding Green Nation! I don’t think the Eagles are sitting back and saying “Hey, we’re almost 4-1! We’re going to be fine.” Which is good. You don’t want them to be delusional about how they’ve played thus far. You want them to feel the need to get things fixed. But maybe some of the internal concern speaks to a lack of confidence in turning things around. We’ll see. Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … NFL Week 6 latest intel, buzz questions, news, fantasy tips: What we’re hearing – ESPN How concerned are the Eagles amid three straight losses? … Graziano: Pretty concerned. This is a team that just saw a nearly complete overhaul of its offensive line last week, and not all of it was intentional. Lane Johnson’s retirement leaves a significant hole on the line and in the locker room. The Eagles are also still awaiting Landon Dickerson’s return from injury, and they’re counting on significant contributions from the likes of Drew Kendall, Willie Lampkin and third-round rookie Markel Bell. This comes while still breaking in rookie wide receiver Makai Lemon, playing the past two games without top wideout DeVonta Smith and missing the top three running backs from their depth chart. The defense has looked better the past couple of weeks — but it wasn’t able to carry the Eagles through the early part of the season as they had hoped it would while the offense found itself under first-year coordinator Sean Mannion. That offense is dealing with a lot more than just growing pains right now, and after consecutive losses in which the Eagles’ win probability exceeded 96%, there’s reason to wonder where they’ll find the leadership to get them through a tough part of their season. … Fowler: Yeah, my sense is the concern is quite high. The Eagles sought to implement an offense that, in part, utilizes play-action passes over the middle to match a potent running game. But that’s not working as intended. The offense ranks in the bottom third in play-action usage. It ranks 31st in total offense. Jalen Hurts struggles at times throwing inside the numbers, which was apparent Sunday in London. The impending return of Saquon Barkley and Smith will help, but I’m not sure that will solve the problems that run deeper than one or two players. Eagles-Jaguars Film Review: This team isn’t going anywhere unless they fix the run game – BGN Ugh. Another week, another game where the Eagles’ offense found a way to make everything feel painfully difficult. There were some signs of life on the rewatch. I promise. But it was rough in places. Before getting into all of that, I was at the game, and it was freaking awesome. It was so loud, and I had an absolute blast. Watching the Eagles in person is special, even when the football itself leaves you wanting to scream. I loved being there. Eagles fans are the absolute best, and the atmosphere was unbelievable. The Eagles finished with 22 rushing yards on 18 attempts. That is not a typo. Before the final drive, their second-half offense had produced 10 yards on 15 plays across four punts. You cannot keep asking the defense to survive that. The offensive line is dealing with a lot of change, but some of the assignments and calls made an already difficult situation even harder. The passing game was a little more interesting. Empty formations gave Jalen Hurts some clearer answers against pressure, and there were a couple of successful under-center play-action throws. Hurts also left opportunities on the field, particularly over the middle, so this wasn’t another game where I thought the quarterback had almost no chance. There was enough here to see a way forward. The Eagles’ bubble is about to burst – SB Nation DeVonta Smith has dealt with the aforementioned hamstring injury, which has kept him out of two games. Makai Lemon is averaging just 7.2 yards per catch, and Hurts is averaging less than 190 yards passing. Through five weeks, the Eagles’ offense ranks 30th in EPA per play and 30th in passing success rate. They also can’t put points on the board, ranking 29th in scoring. Which leads us to the bubble. The bubble that will inevitably pop. Jalen Hurts’ contract is becoming worse by the day. He ranks 31st in EPA per play (min. 25 dropbacks), and carries a dead cap hit of $101 million in 2027. His contract’s total value is the seventh-highest among quarterbacks, and his play is much closer to reflecting that of the 27th best quarterback in the league. Panthers vs Eagles: Storylines to watch – Cat Scratch Reader Defense: Contain Jalen Hurts. The common denominator in both of the Panthers losses this season was facing a mobile quarterback. While week 1 was an all around bad defensive effort, the Panthers defense has done a relatively solid job in the other 3 games. However, when they faced the Browns, Deshaun Watson’s ability to extend plays and break contain was ultimately the downfall of the defense, who again weren’t “bad”, but those scrambles by Watson were back breaking when the defense was attempting to get off the field. Things won’t get any easier this week, as Hurts can definitely run and likely will since the rest of the offense for the Eagles has very much struggled to get much going. If there’s ever a game for the defense to clean up the issues with containing the quarterback and preventing scrambles, its this one. Having Devin Lloyd back will certainly help, but he can’t do it all and he very much needs the edge defenders to do their job. NFC Hierarchy/Obituary: Week 6 edition – PhillyVoice 11) Eagles (2-3): “The Eagles are two plays away from being 4-1” is a true statement, I suppose, and a bit of a rallying cry for optimistic fans. Of course… They aren’t 4-1, because they blew it in two games. Half the teams in the league can probably make similar claims if they had simply made one or two plays that they didn’t make. That line of thinking ignores what the product on the field actually looks like, and the offense is awful, partly because of injuries, but also the scheme stinks. They could just as easily be 1-4. (Some would say 0-5.) Nick Sirianni’s decisions draw debate, but the Eagles’ offense is the bigger problem – The Athletic The conversation about coaching decisions shouldn’t obscure the bigger problem with this team at the moment: the offense.The Eagles rank No. 29 in EPA/drive, No. 31 in yards, No. 29 in points. The second-half problems are more pronounced. The Eagles haven’t scored a touchdown after halftime in the previous three games. The Eagles are No. 32 in the NFL in average second-half yards. The gap between the Eagles and the No. 31 team is larger than the gap between the No. 31 team and the No. 12 team. “We’re looking at that hard each and every week as a staff, how to find our rhythm, find our footing in the second half,” Mannion said. “I thought we did a better job and there were some close calls. It was more about finishing those drives. … I think there were some chances there that we just didn’t quite capitalize on.” I don’t get wrapped up in the “identity” talk as much as others might because that can change based on the opponent, but I’m also not sure what the Eagles can hang their hats on at this point. They’re not running the ball effectively — it would help to get Saquon Barkley back, which is expected to happen this week — and they’re not a strong play-action team (No. 29 in the NFL in EPA/play in play-action). A big change this year was supposed to be how they’re playing under center, yet they’re No. 30 in EPA/play from under center. They’re running condensed sets more than any other team in the NFL, but that…

full_text: Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images | Getty Images The Steelers had nine players on their first injury report ahead of Sunday’s matchup against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. The most surprising name on the report is defensive tackle Keeanu Benton, who didn’t participate in practice Wednesday with an ankle injury, the team announced . Other non-participants included defensive back Jalen Ramsey (wrist), wide receivers Roman Wilson (finger) and Ben Skowronek (calf), and defensive tackle Cam Heyward (rest). Ramsey has played through his wrist injury in recent games, while Heyward normally takes a veteran rest day on Wednesday. Both Wilson and Skowronek are expected to miss the Buccaneers game at minimum. The Steelers’ limited players were running back Rico Dowdle (toe), safety DeShon Elliott (knee — injured reserve), cornerback Jamel Dean (ankle) and outside linebacker T.J. Watt (rest). Some lateral mobility from #Steelers S DeShon Elliott (hamstring/knee) and CB Jamel Dean (ankle): pic.twitter.com/XpGsdsvzjL — Brendan Howe (@bybrendanhowe) October 14, 2026 Dowdle, Elliott and Dean all missed the Steelers’ Week 5 matchup against the Colts, but have a chance to suit up against Tampa Bay. Elliott is in his return window from injured reserve, but has yet to be activated back to the 53-man roster. At the time of this writing, the Buccaneers have yet to release their Wednesday report.

title: Elandon Roberts has no hard feelings towards Steelers
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers brought back fan-favorite linebacker Elandon Roberts following their win over the Indianapolis Colts. Roberts was signed in the middle of the preseason, and put together quality performances against the New York Jets and Buffalo Bills to close exhibition play. Many expected him to be a lock to make the roster, but he […]
full_text: (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Pittsburgh Steelers brought back fan-favorite linebacker Elandon Roberts following their win over the Indianapolis Colts. Roberts was signed in the middle of the preseason, and put together quality performances against the New York Jets and Buffalo Bills to close exhibition play. Many expected him to be a lock to make the roster, but he was one of the bigger surprise cuts from around the league. He remained unsigned through the first five weeks of the season, and says that he doesn’t harbor any sort of ill will towards the Steelers for releasing him. “I wouldn’t have came back if I was uncomfortable,” Roberts said via Brooke Pryo r. “I know a lot of people feel a way. It’s a business at the end of the day. I kind of went through something personal that I would’ve had to step away from the team for anyway to take care of that. So that’s why I say everything happened for a reason, and I’m always trying to be the best version of myself.” Roberts joins a linebacking group that could use a bump. Pittsburgh ranks in the top 10 in terms of missed tackles. And while they also rank near the top of the league in stuffed runs, adding a tried-and-true run stuffer is never a bad idea. title: Mike Tomlin admits to taking play-calling away from Steelers coordinators
summary: Former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin revealed that he occasionally took over play-calling duties when things weren’t going well, explaining that it comes with the territory of being an NFL head coach. Speaking on the New Heights podcast with Jason Kelce and Travis Kelce, Tomlin discussed how head coaches sometimes reclaim play-calling responsibilities from […]
full_text: (Photo by Shelley Lipton/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) Former Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin revealed that he occasionally took over play-calling duties when things weren’t going well, explaining that it comes with the territory of being an NFL head coach. Speaking on the New Heights podcast with Jason Kelce and Travis Kelce, Tomlin discussed how head coaches sometimes reclaim play-calling responsibilities from their coordinators when their respective sides of the ball struggle. He pointed to Houston Texans head coach DeMeco Ryans as an example of a defensive-minded coach who has faced similar circumstances this season. “I’ve done it some over the years,” Tomlin said. “I’ll tell you this: Any coordinator that works on the side of the ball that’s the head coach’s area of expertise is subject to that if things aren’t going well. You get head jobs because of your expertise and your experience in certain areas of a game. And so if you’re not hanging your hat there, where are you hanging your hat?” Tomlin emphasized that a head coach’s specialty often comes under scrutiny when that unit struggles, making it difficult to leave all the responsibility with a coordinator. “If you’re a defensive specialist and your defense isn’t great, like DeMeco, that’s what you do,” Tomlin said. “It comes with the territory.” Tomlin’s comments offer insight into how he approached his responsibilities in Pittsburgh, where he guided the Steelers for nearly two decades before stepping down in January 2026. His willingness to take over play-calling at times also highlights the pressure head coaches face to make adjustments when their teams fail to meet expectations. The Steelers offense showed some serious big-play ability with touchdown plays of 80 and 50 yards in the contest, both coming from their emerging star at running back, Jaylen Warren. The breakout back was rewarded for his performance by being named the AFC Offensive Player of the Week. AFC Players of the Week! (Week 5) @Nunless2 | @gregrousseau pic.twitter.com/wsavBPaARN — NFL (@NFL) October 14, 2026 Warren posted 188 yards from scrimmage in Week 5, the highest mark of his career. Through five weeks, Warren is third in the NFL in scrimmage yards, only trailing superstar running backs Jahmyr Gibbs and Bijan Robinson. This is the first AFC Offensive Player of the Week honor in Warren’s career. The running back is the first Steeler to earn an AFC Offensive Player of the Week honor since Ben Roethlisberger did all the way back in Week 10 of the 202 NFL season. Warren is finally getting some attention for how well he has been playing over the course of the season. The running back is averaging 5.9 yards per carry through the team’s first five contests, and will likely continue to see a feature back workload even when fellow back Rico Dowdle returns from injury. Warren is the engine of the Steelers offense and has now earned an honor that any other Steelers offensive player hasn’t in six seasons. Let us know what you think in the comments . The offense is down two receivers, but Jaylen Warren has been excellent, and Germie Bernard has a huge opportunity. Aaron Rodgers will look to get the ball out quickly as usual, which helps out the offensive line, right? What about the Steelers offensive line so far in 2026? According to Football Insights , the highest offensive line positions in allowed pressure percentages are left tackle (21.7%), right guard (20%), and right tackle (21.7%). Now, the chart also assigns blame to the quarterback (15%) and others, which are tight ends or running backs, in blitz pickup (8.3%). Troy Fantanu has allowed 13 pressures (team-high), seven hurries (team-high), five QB hits, and a sack. Meanwhile, Mason McCormick has allowed ten pressures (second most), four hurries, three QB hits, and a team-high three sacks. Now, the Steelers’ offensive line had a great outing against the Colts, as Aaron Rodgers was the least-pressured quarterback in the league in Week 5. title: Pat Freiermuth says Steelers have the best tight end duo in the NFL
summary: The Pittsburgh Steelers are 3-2 after their win over the Indianapolis Colts last Sunday at Acrisure Stadium. The Steelers offense has come alive over their last three games despite several injuries to their receivers, and the production from their tight end room has been a huge part of the reason why. Veteran tight end Pat […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Barry Reeger-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Pittsburgh Steelers are 3-2 after their win over the Indianapolis Colts last Sunday at Acrisure Stadium. The Steelers offense has come alive over their last three games despite several injuries to their receivers, and the production from their tight end room has been a huge part of the reason why. Veteran tight end Pat Freiermuth caught five balls for 44 yards and a pair of touchdowns in the contest. Freiermuth has now caught four touchdown passes this season, putting him in a four-way tie with George Kittle, Isaiah Likely, and Mike Gesicki for the most touchdown receptions among tight ends this season. After his big game, Freiermuth was asked about how encouraging it was to see the tight end room step up with the injuries to Pittsburgh’s receivers. “Selfishly, I think you know, me and Darnell (Washington) are the best tight end duo in the NFL,” Freiermuth said. “Anytime we can go out there and utilize our skill sets to the best of our abilities, I think we have a pretty good chance to win the game on offense.” I asked Pat Freiermuth after the game how encouraging it is for the tight end room to step up while the team's thin at WR. His answer: "I think me and Darnell are the best tight end duo in the NFL". pic.twitter.com/2EgstLaOCW — Eddie P (@eddie_p_412) October 11, 2026 The Steelers tight end feels strongly about the room’s ability regardless of who is available, and it’s hard to argue with him. Fellow tight end Darnell Washington is fresh off receiving a $42 million contract extension this summer, and has continued to prove why he is worth the money with his impact blocking and the threat he provides as a red zone mismatch. The Steelers came into the game without Michael Pittman Jr., as the receiver had been placed on short-term injured reserve earlier in the week after aggravating a foot injury he had been dealing with for several weeks. The hits kept coming to the Steelers’ receiver room, as Roman Wilson and Ben Skowronek both left with injuries in the first half and did not return. The injuries have already been deemed serious enough to rule both receivers out for at least the team’s Week 6 game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, while Wilson is reportedly set to miss at least a few more games after that. Even with all of the injuries to their wide receivers, Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy believes they can lean more into their tight ends and running backs . With one of the better tight end rooms in all of football, there is still plenty of reason to have faith in the Steelers offense moving forward. Good things have happened when the ball is in the hands of a tight end in Pittsburgh’s offense this season, so why not see how far one of the better tight end duos in the league can take you? title: Seahawks injury update: Drake Thomas, Zach Charbonnet out vs. Broncos
summary: The curse of the short week has hit the Seattle Seahawks ahead of their Thursday night showdown with the Denver Broncos, as the team will be without one of their starting linebackers. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald ruled out linebacker Drake Thomas, running back Zach Charbonnet and linebacker Chazz Surratt on Wednesday. Thomas, who emerged […]
full_text: The curse of the short week has hit the Seattle Seahawks ahead of their Thursday night showdown with the Denver Broncos, as the team will be without one of their starting linebackers. Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald ruled out linebacker Drake Thomas, running back Zach Charbonnet and linebacker Chazz Surratt on Wednesday. Thomas, who emerged as Ernest Jones IV’s partner in crime in 2025, is recovering from an ankle injury he suffered late in the second quarter against the San Francisco 49ers last week. In place of the injured Thomas, Macdonald said the team will lean on the team’s 2024 fourth-round pick Tyrice Knight. The UTEP product has had several stints in the starting lineup throughout his three years with the Seahawks, but hasn’t found the field much and only recorded one tackle in 2026. Charbonnet continues his ACL rehab and will not make it back for the pivotal game against the Broncos. The Seahawks running back was so dearly missed last week, but fans will hope for a bounce-back week from Emmanuel Wilson and George Holani, who struggled against the 49ers. Velus Jones Jr. appears to be the other running back option after the Seahawks added him to their active roster on Wednesday . There may be positive news on Charbonnet soon, at least according to ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler, who reported that there is a “legitimate chance” that the Seahawks back returns in Week 7. Surratt mostly serves as a special teams player, so it wouldn’t be shocking to see the team elevate wide reciever Irv Charles from the practice squad to bolster that unit and give them more positional flexibility. A mostly healthy Seahawks team will head to Denver and look to get back on track this Thursday at 5:15 p.m.
author: Jack Freeman

title: Seahawks shift Irv Charles to practice squad
summary: With running back Zach Charbonnet (knee) expected to remain on the physically unable to perform list for the time being, the Seattle Seahawks added depth ahead of their Thursday night showdown against the Denver Broncos. The team announced they signed running back Velus Jones Jr. back to their 53-man roster just a day after he […]
full_text: With running back Zach Charbonnet (knee) expected to remain on the physically unable to perform list for the time being, the Seattle Seahawks added depth ahead of their Thursday night showdown against the Denver Broncos. The team announced they signed running back Velus Jones Jr. back to their 53-man roster just a day after he was released to make room for wide receiver and special teams gunner Irv Charles , who was activated from injured reserve on Tuesday. In a corresponding move, Charles was released and re-signed to the practice squad. As vested veterans, neither were subject to waivers meaning the special teams star is eligible to practice with the team on Wednesday. Charles, 29, was placed on injured reserve prior to the start of the regular season with a knee injury and has yet to make his Seahawks debut after being acquired from the New York Jets in the spring. Further indication on whether he’ll suit up against Denver will become available when the team announces their practice squad elevations on Thursday.

title: How the tale of Nehemiah Pritchett lays a path for Julian Neal on the Seahawks
summary: Games between the Seattle Seahawks and the San Francisco 49ers always seem to be weird and double-sided. In the same game in which layers of commentary and criticism surrounded the play of CB2, Josh Jobe, this year’s breakout corner, Nehemiah Pritchett pulled down another INT. Now, Jobe? The day after, it doesn’t sound like Jobe’s […]
full_text: Games between the Seattle Seahawks and the San Francisco 49ers always seem to be weird and double-sided. In the same game in which layers of commentary and criticism surrounded the play of CB2, Josh Jobe , this year’s breakout corner, Nehemiah Pritchett pulled down another INT. Now, Jobe? The day after, it doesn’t sound like Jobe’s job is in jeopardy . But the gap in good will is interesting, in that it illuminates the system of player maturation that’s in place for the defending world champion Seahawks. Pritchett has been balling, and everybody has seen it. He’s looked dominant at times. Best #NFL Defenders by Coverage EPA 1. Jourdan Lewis (-18.9) 2. Talanoa Hufanga (-17.7) 3. Trent McDuffie (-15.8) 4. Emmanuel Forbes (-15.1) t5. Nehemiah Pritchett (-14.5) t5. Foye Oluokun (-14.5) Data: @NextGenStats — Daniel Griffis (@DanDGriffis) October 13, 2026 Number 28 intercepted Brock Purdy , an early MVP candidate in a big game. He also forced a fumble on punt coverage. Pritchett is the guy who outlasted his draft classmate and more heralded (by some, including the NFL’s website ) Auburn teammate, D.J. James a couple of years ago. In his young career, he made some mistakes that I can remember (posted a 147.2 passer rating in his one start in 2024), early on… but he also made a few plays. Fantastic PBU by Nehemiah Pritchett 🙅‍♂️ pic.twitter.com/lquPWwfgOb — NFL (@NFL) November 9, 2025 Mike Macdonald when discussing the competition for cornerback roles back in July: “It’s not something where you can just walk in and just know what to do immediately,” Macdonald said of the rookies. “It takes a lot of work, guys are putting in extra work, great attitudes. They’re still rookies. They’re still probably not playing at the speed that we’re going to expect come training camp time, but that’s not for a lack of trying. They’ve got to trust that got to go through, not around on this thing. Just keep going through the process, it’ll clear up… It’ll clear up for them, and I expect them to have great training camps and compete for a large role.” Now that Pritchett won the role, Coach Mike had this to say: “He competed and won it. It’s a daily input. Also, execution. Your part fits in a hole in the defense, and Nehemiah has improved in that. He has covered well and is aggressive when he needs to, and he’s done a great job in press. He definitely has earned it.” Macdonald said after Sunday’s divisional loss that Pritchett , “stuck to the process and just kept making plays.” There certainly is a process. This regime really commits to seeking players with experience, and they have even prioritized that, at times, over draft stock. There are exceptions: high draft picks like Byron Murphy II and Jadarian Price come to mind… but even then, both were surrounded by commentary and questions about why they were only receiving limited snaps. It’s worked out, as Seattle has gotten a ton of production from veterans, i.e. DeMarcus Lawrence, Julian Love, Leonard Williams, Jarran Reed, Uchenna Nwosu, Eric Saubert, Cooper Kupp, Emanuel Wilson and Sam Darnold, just to name a few. This stretches back to Coach Macdonald’s time in Baltimore as well (think Roquon Smith, Jadeveon Clowney and Kyle Van Noy). Pritchett played behind vets such as Tre Brown and Artie Burns (among others) in his rookie season and didn’t look super confident in his limited playing time. He played mostly special teams in his sophomore year, last year. It’s been shown that the Hawks let guys simmer and learn, then get chances down the road, when they truly know the system well and can prove that they know where to be and when. Think of Jalen Sundell, Drake Thomas, Ty Okada, Nehemiah Pritchett, Christian Haynes, George Holani, A.J. Barner and Josh Jobe as guys who have come up through the systems to seize their shot. But also, Coach Mike isn’t afraid to fade a role if the player doesn’t necessarily meet expectations. Remember Tyrel Dodson and Jerome Baker? Riq Woolen? Some Olu Oluwatimi? Tyrice Knight, to some extent? Every situation is different, but there are honest appraisals. Nehemiah Pritchett and D.J. James were drafted in the fifth and sixth rounds of the NFL draft (respectively), but only one came out of the fire. That gives you hope for a prospect like Julian Neal, taken in the third round, and who could conceivably have a shorter path to prominence because of his draft pedigree. It’s also slightly reminiscent of Seattle taking two late-round guys in the same draft class, in Michael Dansby and Andre Fuller (ready squad). Will any of the three rookies make it out of future fires to fight for this franchise and play on defense? Neal is excited for his opportunity, if nothing else: And let’s remember that it’s not just about playing on defense. Pritchett became a mainstay on special teams, and in that way became a trusted player that got his shot on defense. He still plays there. After the Week 1 win in the PNW, in which this Pritchett guy that they nicknamed “Mighty” came up with his first pick, here’s defensive coordinator Aden Durde on what he thought of Nehemiah’s big game: “I really thought Nehemiah played confident. He challenged. He was getting some really good players. He didn’t just stand up; he went for it. He had a great third down stop and an interception. For the whole defense, it was a proud moment to see Nehemiah, kind of graduate from being the young player he was… go to be a gunner, and he’s excelling when he comes on the field. He’s done a great job.” There it is, there’s the pathway. Will it be the same path for Neal? J-Neal has been playing on special teams early in the year as well. He was called for holding on a punt against the Cardinals and did step in for a couple of snaps at the end of that blowout game. Maybe his journey will be shorter in length, due to being a third-rounder (vs. Pritchett coming to Seattle in the fifth)! Before his injury, Neal spoke with Seattle Sports , on his situation: “I don’t want anything to be given to me, and I’m not entitled to anything. So, I understand what’s going on. I’m just trying to make my stance on special teams right now and earn my way on the field–and whatever happens, just be ready.” Sounds like he does understand. He understands that he’ll have to forge a path to playing time, whenever he comes back. That’s the Seahawk way. If Seattle hopes to bottle up Mike Evans in a rematch down the road, the size of Neal could be an enticing foil. But this goes well beyond that. This is a long-term project, that an embedded coaching staff can approach with patience. They’ve proven it.

title: Seahawks All-22 review: The good and bad from another home loss to the 49ers
summary: The Seahawks’ 32–29 loss to the San Francisco 49ers was painful precisely because Seattle did enough to make a victory feel possible. Despite committing four turnovers and repeatedly putting themselves in difficult situations, the Seahawks remained in the game until the final moments. There were stretches when the defense delivered, Jaxon Smith-Njigba continued to look […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: Cooper Kupp #10 of the Seattle Seahawks reaches out to the first down marker to try to get a first down during the fourth quarter against the San Francisco 49ers at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Olivia Vanni/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Seahawks’ 32–29 loss to the San Francisco 49ers was painful precisely because Seattle did enough to make a victory feel possible. Despite committing four turnovers and repeatedly putting themselves in difficult situations, the Seahawks remained in the game until the final moments. There were stretches when the defense delivered, Jaxon Smith-Njigba continued to look like one of the NFL’s best receivers, and Seattle found ways to overcome its own mistakes. But every time the team appeared ready to take control, another self-inflicted wound made the comeback more difficult. The San Francisco 49ers turned Seattle’s four turnovers into 21 points, including a defensive touchdown just before halftime. That is the difference between competing with an undefeated divisional rival and actually beating one. The Seahawks showed enough talent to win this game, but their execution repeatedly failed them. The offensive line struggled to protect Sam Darnold and establish the running game, the quarterback made costly decisions, and the defense could not consistently contain San Francisco’s most dangerous offensive weapon when the game was on the line. This was not a game in which Seattle was outclassed. It was a game the Seahawks repeatedly made harder for themselves. That makes the loss even more frustrating, particularly with the NFC West race already becoming more complicated. The Good Jaxon Smith-Njigba is incredible Jaxon Smith-Njigba continues to be the foundation of Seattle’s passing attack. Through five games, he has recorded 37 receptions for 583 yards and seven touchdowns, leading the league in receiving yards at this point in the season. Against San Francisco, he caught five passes for 102 yards and a touchdown, accounting for approximately 52% of the Seahawks’ 195 passing yards. His production is remarkable, but the larger concern is just how heavily Seattle has come to depend on him. Brian Fleury uses 12 personnel to isolate JSN and Kupp against two DBs after the 49ers load the box. Kupp’s initial block gives JSN room to hit his second gear and generate YAC. A simple concept, a favorable matchup, and explosive results. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-14T02:45:53.173Z The play above shows the play in which JSN injured his ankle. Brian Fleury uses a two-tight-end package to isolate Smith-Njigba and Cooper Kupp against two defensive backs once Niners reacted loading the front. Kupp, one of the NFL’s best blocking receivers, only needs to establish the initial block to give JSN enough space to accelerate into his one-on-one matchup. Once Smith-Njigba hits that second gear, the defensive back has little chance of stopping him immediately, and the receiver generates substantial yards after the catch. The play also illustrates how Fleury can use personnel and alignment to create favorable matchups without needing a complicated route concept. San Francisco protects the sticks, leaving a void between the second and third levels. JSN’s route holds the deep safety, opening a window underneath. He settles in, secures the catch, breaks multiple tackles, and turns it into a big gain toward midfield. Great zone awareness and YAC. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-14T02:45:21.289Z San Francisco prioritizes defending the first-down marker, leaving a significant amount of space between the second and third levels of the defense. JSN’s route holds the deep safety, who must respect the possibility of being beaten vertically. Smith-Njigba recognizes the open space, settles into the window, catches the ball and breaks multiple tackles to bring it toward midfield. It is a simple concept executed exceptionally well, with the receiver understanding exactly where the defense has conceded space. What a release from JSN. Deommodore Lenoir can't disrupt the stem, and JSN wins leverage off the line. The separation is already there — Darnold just needs to pull the trigger on time. An earlier throw could've made this an even bigger gain. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-14T02:46:21.708Z What an incredible release. Deommodore Lenoir is still trying to find Smith-Njigba after the receiver defeats his initial attempt to establish contact. Lenoir cannot disrupt the release, leaving JSN with the leverage advantage. If Darnold had pulled the trigger sooner, the result could have been even more damaging for San Francisco. The separation is already there; the quarterback just needs to recognize it and deliver the football on time. Fleury uses Kupp’s route to occupy coverage and protect JSN’s release. JSN beats Fred Warner, scores through the ankle injury, and adds YAC. The design is excellent, but Seattle needs more from the supporting cast. No. 11 can’t carry the passing game forever. Or can… — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-14T02:47:10.533Z This is another example of Fleury finding ways to protect WR’s release. Kupp’s route occupies the coverage and helps to hide Smith-Njigba’s intentions, giving the receiver an opportunity to attack the defense. JSN gets another touchdown, this time after suffering the ankle injury, while also escaping Fred Warner and generating additional yards after the catch. It is an outstanding individual play and a reminder of how much Seattle’s offense can accomplish when its best players are put in positions to succeed. The concern is not JSN’s production. It is the lack of comparable involvement from the rest of the receiving corps. Seattle cannot expect him to carry this much of the passing game indefinitely, particularly when opponents can increasingly build their coverage plans around taking away No. 11. Byron Murphy II delivered a dominant performance Byron Murphy II was arguably Seattle’s best defensive player against San Francisco. He finished with six tackles, two sacks and seven quarterback pressures, tying his career high in pressures for a single game. His two sacks were particularly significant because the 49ers had not allowed a sack through their first four games of the season. Murphy now has three sacks through five games in 2026, following a seven-sack campaign in 2025. With Leonard Williams not at full strength, Seattle needed Murphy to take on a larger role against one of the league’s strongest rushing attacks. He responded with his most impactful performance of the season, consistently creating problems for the offensive line and making plays against both the run and the pass. The 49ers’ OL hadn’t allowed a sack all season. Murphy starts in the A-gap, reads McCaffrey, then attacks outside before working back inside once he recognizes pass. The patience, lateral quickness, and relentless effort keep the blocker guessing until Murphy gets home. — (@alexcastrofilho.bsky.social) 2026-10-14T02:49:20.838Z This was the first sack 49ers OL had surrendered all season. Murphy initially aligns in the A-gap, reading Christian McCaffrey and remaining prepared to make the tackle if the play develops as a run. Once he recognizes the pass, he attacks toward the outside gap before working back inside, keeping the offensive lineman off balance throughout the rep. The combination of patience, lateral quickness and relentless effort allows him to reach Purdy. Murphy does not win because of one move; he keeps working until the blocker runs out of answers. The life of San Francisco’s No. 75 was not getting any easier. Murphy appears to combine a swipe and rip move, using his hands to clear the guard’s contact before bringing his arm through to escape the block. title: Seahawks Week 6 power rankings: Close loss to 49ers drops Seattle nearly out of the top five
summary: Entering week 5, the Seattle Seahawks bounced back in their power rankings after defeating the Los Angeles Chargers. However, after losing to the San Francisco 49ers, will Seattle fall down those rankings once again? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (BR), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) […]
full_text: Entering week 5, the Seattle Seahawks bounced back in their power rankings after defeating the Los Angeles Chargers . However, after losing to the San Francisco 49ers, will Seattle fall down those rankings once again? Let’s take a look at five national media sites (NFL.com, CBS Sports, Bleacher Report (BR), Pro Football Talk (PFT), and ESPN) to see where they rank Seattle. Let’s start with the national sites that were most punishing of Seattle after their loss to the 49ers. B/R, which dropped the Seahawks down from 3rd to 6th, brought up the turnover issues that are plaguing the team. “ The Seattle Seahawks are turning the ball over at an alarming rate – nine giveaways over the last four weeks. ” Meanwhile, CBS also dropped Seattle down three spots, from 4th to 7th best . In this ranking, CBS mentions that Seattle has to get their running game going as it is the key to their offense working. ESPN did drop the Seahawks as well, however they remain in the top five, coming in at number 4th best in the league , one spot down from last week. ESPN noted that the Seahawks have an issue on defense, however that issue happens to be the offense. ESPN mentioned that Seattle has given up 44 points off turnovers, which is tied for most in the NFL. Both NFL.com and PFT did not penalize the Seahawks in their rankings despite the loss. PFT, who kept Seattle ranked at number five , stated that “they’re trying too hard to be something other than [what] they were in 2025.” Meanwhile, NFL.com who kept the Seahawks at third best in the NFL, also noted that the Seahawks (specifically Sam Darnold) need to clean up their play. However, NFL.com was also the only national site to maintain positivity over the team, stating that “ a narrow loss to the No. 1 team in my rankings doesn’t knock the ‘Hawks down the board. ” Overall, it is not surprising to see the Seahawks fall down the power rankings after their second loss in three weeks. However, despite the slight slide down, the national media seems to be high on the team despite their turnover and run game concerns. If Seattle can fix those then they will still be a threat for another title run. Entering week 5, the average power ranking between the five polled sites was 3.6. Entering Week 6, that average has fallen to an even 5.0. The Seahawks face the Denver Broncos next week on Thursday Night Football. Despite still having an average ranking in the top five, another loss (this time to the Broncos) could really have Seattle fall off of a cliff (at least in the power rankings sense).

title: Why Raheem Morris has quickly become a ‘great fit’ with 49ers as DC
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have had a bevy of strong defensive coordinators in the Kyle Shanahan era. It all started with Robert Saleh, one of the best defensive minds in the NFL, who has since been hired as a head coach twice after stints in San Francisco. The 49ers then had DeMeco Ryans, who quickly […]
full_text: The San Francisco 49ers have had a bevy of strong defensive coordinators in the Kyle Shanahan era. It all started with Robert Saleh, one of the best defensive minds in the NFL, who has since been hired as a head coach twice after stints in San Francisco. The 49ers then had DeMeco Ryans, who quickly established himself as a special defensive mind in his two-year stint as defensive coordinator. After two failed experiments with Steve Wilks and Nick Sorensen, and Saleh’s second stint last season, San Francisco had a vacancy at the coveted position again. A ton of names were floated around, but Kyle Shanahan and Co. focused on one: former Atlanta Falcons head coach Raheem Morris, who had been with Shanahan in Atlanta and Washington a decade ago. Morris had been an assistant in football since 1998 and a head coach twice, while having a ton of experience as a playcaller. Initially, despite all that, there were some who worried that the scheme difference could lead to some early growing pains. But through five games, Morris has been a fantastic addition, as several 49ers defenders are enjoying the best stints of their careers, while the unit as a whole has looked elite despite dealing with injuries. “It doesn’t surprise me with Raheem,” Kyle Shanahan said this week. “I’ve just been around him for too long. He’s one of the best people and best coaches I’ve ever been around. I tried to bring him here originally when I left Atlanta. They wouldn’t let him out. “So, it’s been a long time coming to get him here. He’s done an unbelievable job this year, especially with the injuries, but just overall everything he’s mixed up schematically. I love the confidence he’s given our DBs and the way they’ve been playing since training camp. He’s had a real huge effect on this team and we’re very lucky to have him.” The 49ers have been decimated on the defensive line. They ran it back with a secondary that was inconsistent last year. And they’re also relying on a good amount of young talent. Still, they rank third in EPA allowed per play, third in points allowed per game, and sixth in yards allowed per game. And that’s with the team facing the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Broncos, and Seattle Seahawks through the first five weeks. The 49ers’ defensive line personnel has been decimated. The team has been without Nick Bosa, Mykel Williams, Alfred Collins, Sam Okuayinonu, CJ West, and others for parts of the year. That’s prompted them to rely on a number of players who signed in training camp or later to play key snaps. And still, the group is producing. Osa Odighizuwa has been a very solid addition, leading the team with 15 pressures to go with a 12.8 pass-rush win rate on the interior so far. Keion White, a former New England Patriots second-round pick, has been a revelation. He’s second on the team in pressures (13) while recording eight defensive stops, good for fourth on the team. Gracen Halton has immediately stepped up as a rookie, and we’ve seen him get better each week. He had his best game yet against the Seahawks with three pressures and three defensive stops, along with a forced fumble. The same goes for both rookies Romello Height and Jaden Dugger, who had quality outings as well in Week 5. The veteran linebackers Fred Warner and Dre Greenlaw have looked very good, with Warner seeming like a Defensive Player of the Year candidate once again, despite coming off a major injury. And the secondary has exceeded all expectations. Renardo Green and Malik Mustapha are having the best years of their careers. The group as a whole has looked very good in coverage, and they’re playing with a high level of confidence as Shanahan noted. Morris’s blitz packages have also given opposing quarterbacks trouble. But the key part is that he’s keeping things simple for his defense, which has allowed the group to pick things up faster and play freely with more confidence. The 49ers are averaging 17 pressures a game, despite their personnel, while also swarming to the ball and looking good in coverage. That’s got me thinking about how good Morris is relative to his predecessors, which is a very high bar to meet. So far though, he’s passed every test with flying colors.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers rookie report: The long-term upside is there for this class
summary: The San Francisco 49ers have relied on rookies to play at a high level this season. So far, they have not disappointed. There will be inevitable growing pains. That’s par for the course when you’re talking about first-year players. But this draft class looks to have a few hits and potential long-term starters. Here is […]
full_text: (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers have relied on rookies to play at a high level this season. So far, they have not disappointed. There will be inevitable growing pains. That’s par for the course when you’re talking about first-year players. But this draft class looks to have a few hits and potential long-term starters. Here is our rookie report after five weeks. De’Zhaun Stribling We’re probably still another month and a half away from seeing Stribling, at the earliest. It’s a bummer, because you could see the impact he could make during the preseason. All is not lost, though. He’ll have the final month of the season to work himself back into the offense. Ideally, Stribling is up to speed and a regular contributor by the playoffs. Romello Height Height was drafted to be the designated pass rusher. So far, he’s rushed the passer on 62% of his snaps. We haven’t seen him kick inside often, as 88% of his snaps have come on the edge. Height has only three solo tackles on the season, with a modest pressure rate of 7.2%. He’s essentially a designated looper. Per Sumer Sports, 52% of Height’s pass rushes have been stunts. Raheem Morris has his rookie on the move on over half his pass-rushing snaps. He’s winning at a high clip, 13.3%. That’s a good sign, and it suggests Height’s production should follow shortly. Kaelon Black The 49ers rookie running back has been underwhelming to begin the year. It looked like he’d be a focal point of the offense in Week 1, but his snaps have dwindled since. He’s only playing about 11% of the time this year. Black has an explosive play rate of 2.6% and a -0.10 EPA per touch, with one impact play in his name. Black was seen as one of the better pass-blocking prospects in the draft, but he’s only been used 1.3% of the time in that role. Kyle Shanahan isn’t tipping his hand when Black is in the game. The split is pretty even: he runs the ball 47% of the time and runs a pass route 41% of the time. Black’s averaging 2.6 yards per carry in the red zone. That jumps to 3.9 yards per carry on non-red-zone carries. The good news is he’s bouncing off tackles, falling forward, and gaining yards after the contact. But he’s also getting stuffed behind the line of scrimmage and failing to force missed tackles. Black struggles to resist the urge to bounce runs that don’t need to or to stop his feet in the backfield. In 1-on-1 situations, he’s indecisive instead of being the aggressor. Gracen Halton Halton recorded his first sack of the season, but he’s 26th among all defensive tackles in the NFL in impact plays, with 13. He has one less impact play than Osa Odighizuwa, despite playing 91 fewer snaps. Halton has as many tackles for loss as DeForest Buckner and Zach Allen. Halton’s awareness is off the charts. He’s a much better run defender than anticipated. He’s the type of player who causes chaos, and his plays don’t always show up in the box score. Nothing about Halton’s first five games would tell you he should’ve fallen to Day 3 of the draft. Carver Willis Ephesians Prysock Incomplete. Jaden Dugger Dugger only has one missed tackle this year. He also got into the sack column for the first time last week. Dugger has been sneaky good as a pass rusher. He’s only rushed ten times, but he has three pressures and the sack we saw on the first drive of Week 5. It’s been impressive to watch Dugger hold his own against 300-pounders. Four of his seven targets have resulted in first downs, but he’s only surrendering 6.4 yards per reception on those. Week 5 showed that some of those were by design, essentially conceding underneath throws to take away the bigger threat. Dugger plays physically, stays in control, and rarely makes mistakes. His long-term upside is high, especially with Fred Warner at the position. Enrique Cruz Jr. Incomplete.

title: 5 questions with Andrew York of Hogs Haven: How is Adam Peters viewed three years in?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers face off with the Washington Commanders on Monday Night Football, and there is no shortage of storylines ahead of the primetime matchup. Remember Brandon Aiyuk? Yeah, he’s still neither a Commander or 49er. What about Javon Kinlaw’s time in Washington? Has Adam Peters turned Washington around? I asked Andrew York of […]
full_text: (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers face off with the Washington Commanders on Monday Night Football, and there is no shortage of storylines ahead of the primetime matchup. Remember Brandon Aiyuk? Yeah, he’s still neither a Commander or 49er. What about Javon Kinlaw’s time in Washington? Has Adam Peters turned Washington around? I asked Andrew York of Hogs Haven about those topics and more in our five questions with the opponents segment. 1. Thoughts on the Brandon Aiyuk saga? Mostly just glad we signed Stefon Diggs instead, but also a bit sad for Aiyuk, as he seems to be throwing his career away for no good reason. Washington has been a hub for drama in the past, so I don’t want a player who seems to thrive on drama like Aiyuk. I think most fans thought the same and sighed in relief when Diggs was signed, as it meant the end to the Aiyuk discussion. I do hope Aiyuk can get some professional help though, both in terms of some therapy and in terms of an agent who he’ll listen to, because it seems like he’s having a breakdown and he already did the hard work of getting a good second contract only to throw it away. It’s like watching a slow-motion car crash. Some people might be entertained by that, but I find it sad. 2. Assessment of Adam Peters so far Overall, he’s been good and he’s definitely improved the overall talent of the roster (which was abysmal when he was hired), but it definitely seems like he’s learning on the job and he’s made a few noticeable mistakes so far. His first draft (2024) was pretty bad outside of Jayden Daniels. He traded away players and accepted trade downs such that he had 6 picks in the top 100 of the 2024 draft, yet none of them outside of Jayden Daniels has looked like a full-time starter. Looking at his draft class, I think he focused too much on taking guys with high Relative Athletic Score (RAS) and not enough on traditional scouting. He certainly learned from it though, as his 2025 and 2026 draft classes look to be better with less draft capital. Speaking of less draft capital, he’s also made some big trades, primarily a trade for Marshon Lattimore in 2024 that looks like a waste of draft picks, but a much better trade for Laremy Tunsil in 2025 that looks great outside of his unfortunate injury this year. Some might question trading away draft picks with a rebuilding roster, but this team was in desperate need of blue-chip players and they at least got that with Tunsil. Peters’ biggest mistake this offseason was cutting Center Tyler Biadasz because he had a handshake agreement with Tyler Linderbaum. Linderbaum later backed out of the deal when he got a bigger offer from the Raiders, leaving Washington with backup IOL Nick Allegretti as the only viable Center on the roster. Street FA Lucas Patrick has since stepped into that role, but the hole at Center was noticeable in weeks 1 & 2. Adam Peters biggest strength so far has been his free agent signings. The hit rate among his free agents has been really good and allowed him to rebuild the roster quickly in his first year. However, in order to turn over so much of the roster and stay within the cap, he had to rely on many aging veterans on 1-year deals in 2024 and 2025, which led to an old, slow, and injury-prone roster as well as a significant amount of roster turnover every offseason. This past offseason, he finally signed more young free agents in their prime to multi-year deals, and pretty much all of them have been paying off, with standouts like CB Amik Robertson and EDGE Odafe Oweh looking like cornerstone players. So yeah, overall I think Adam Peters has been good, but he’s had a bit of a learning curve. 3. Could Terry McLaurin be available if the season goes south? Yes, I think so. Most of the beat reporters I listen to have indicated this is probably the last year on his current contract unless he agrees to a restructure next year. He’s still a good player, with soft hands, excellent route running, and enough speed to stretch the field, but I think he’s past his prime and starting to slow down a bit and become a bit more prone to injury. If the season goes south, I think it would make sense to focus on the future, especially with the coaching staff most likely being replaced. 4. Assessment of Javon Kinlaw Kinlaw has been a solid free agent signing. People seem to think that he’s a run stuffer due to his size, but he’s actually best at rushing the QB due to his suddenness and ability to accelerate. He’s already got 1 sack and 3 QB hits on the year, according to PFR. That said, he’s also been good against the run, with 11 combined tackles and 2 tackles for loss in 5 games so far. Overall, he’s been one of Washington’s better DL and a good DT to rotate at different positions due to his versatility (which is a good fit for this defense). 5. Thoughts on Peters bringing in former 49ers in different capacities For the most part, I think it’s been fine, as I don’t think he’s overpaid any of them and the ones with starter-level contracts (like Kinlaw or Deebo Samuel last year) have played up to the level of their contract. He also hasn’t gone too nuts about it, as I think the majority of 49ers players that he’s brought in (Nick Bellore, Ahkello Witherspoon, Drake Jackson) have been signed on very cheap contracts essentially to give them a shot, with not much downside to the team. Jake Moody was probably the worst signing, but even then we’ve moved on quickly and have a new young kicker in place now.
author: Jason Aponte

title: NFL insider on the 49ers’ WR trade market: ‘The issue is the amount of roster spots you’re allotting to the position’
summary: We spent Tuesday afternoon discussing potential trade targets for the San Francisco 49ers at wide receiver. Getting Mike Evans help feels like a priority. But the team has to balance that with what it would do when everyone is healthy. Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer answered the question in his weekly mailbag about the Niners potentially […]
full_text: (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images We spent Tuesday afternoon discussing potential trade targets for the San Francisco 49ers at wide receiver. Getting Mike Evans help feels like a priority. But the team has to balance that with what it would do when everyone is healthy. Sports Illustrated’s Albert Breer answered the question in his weekly mailbag about the Niners potentially adding a wide receiver. Here’s what he said: I would say keep an eye on veteran additions, like the ones they made with Brandin Cooks. Certainly, the hope would be that some of the younger players that they drafted over the last couple of years are able to step up and contribute. Jordan Watkins and Jacob Cowing have flashed over the course of the last couple of years and in training camp. Those would be two guys that I think you would hope would be able to step up and play some snaps. The key here is, to me, is what you’ve already got on the roster, and the fact that De’Zhaun Stribling is not out for the year. The fact that Deebo [Samuel] is not out for the year. The fact that Mike Evans is not out for the year. That to me would prevent you from really going all in on anybody. Especially when you consider 2027, you’re going to have Ricky Pearsall coming back. So, I know it’s not the sexy answer to say stand pat with what you’ve got, try to make your development work with guys like Cowing and Watkins. The issue is the amount of roster spots you’re allotting to the position, the logjam that you’ve got there, and the fact that I think when these guys are healthy, they’re a relatively good receiver group, who has Brock Purdy playing at an MVP level. And who has the Niners now 5-0. I wouldn’t be jamming the panic button. But again, if you can add a veteran body like they did Brandin Cooks, I’m good with that. Go ahead and do it. They’re a team, over the next couple of years, that’s going to need to get younger. At this point, they need draft picks. I don’t see a scenario where they’re gonna go out and spend two first-round picks off somebody else’s roster. To me, with the looming cap problems, with the looming questions about how you’re going to get younger, you hold on to the assets that you have, so you can go and get young, cost-controlled talent. There’s no mention of Demarcus Robinson, who might be Purdy’s second-most trustworthy option. It’s worth noting that Robinson and Deebo’s contracts expire after this season. If the 49ers get through the Commanders and Falcons, Robinson and Samuel will likely be back after the bye week. Over the past couple of weeks, there have been enough exposures to highlight Purdy’s lack of trust in Cowing and Watkins—especially Watkins. Washington’s defense is leaky. Atlanta’s is respectable, but it’s been propped up mostly by its run defense. The next couple of games feel like good chances to see whether Purdy can build trust with Cowing, Cooks, and Watkins. Then, heading into the bye, you can decide whether to add someone. Remember, one of the weeks, Christian Kirk should be available, too. If the 49ers do make a trade, it should be somebody who complements Evans. The Josh Downs example is perfect. He runs 70.3% of his routes from the slot, has only one drop on the season, and has proven he can win in the NFL. Plus, he’s in the final year of his contract. That is the ideal veteran.
