title: Week 6 NFL Power Rankings: Are the 49ers the unquestioned best team in the NFL?
summary: The San Francisco 49ers continued stacking up wins on Sunday, this time beating the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 in a thriller that went down to the final possession. Playing banged up offensively, the 49ers capitalized on Seattle’s mistakes in a seven-turnover game, as they improved to 5-0 and remained unbeaten atop the NFC West. While the […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - OCTOBER 11: Christian McCaffrey #23 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates with Dominick Puni #77 after his rushing touchdown against the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter at Lumen Field on October 11, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers continued stacking up wins on Sunday, this time beating the Seattle Seahawks 32-29 in a thriller that went down to the final possession. Playing banged up offensively, the 49ers capitalized on Seattle’s mistakes in a seven-turnover game, as they improved to 5-0 and remained unbeaten atop the NFC West. While the 49ers remained unbeaten, the Rams and Seahawks both lost, widening San Francisco’s lead in the NFC West heading into Week 6. With the changes in the NFL this past week, let’s take a look at the industry’s power rankings for Week 6. ESPN: No. 1 “Under new coordinator Raheem Morris, the Niners rank fifth in yards per play allowed (4.7) and have limited big plays as well as any team in the league,” ESPN’s Nick Wagoner wrote. “But they have struggled to get off the field consistently. The Niners rank 20th in third-down defense, giving up a first down on 40.8% of their opportunities. As a result, their defense has been on the field for 31 minutes, 12 seconds per game, which ranks 23rd in the NFL.” Rest of top five: Chiefs, Bills, Seahawks, and Jaguars. The 49ers’ biggest area for improvement is their third-down defense, which ranks 20th in the NFL. Still, despite all their injuries, the 49ers have found ways to keep winning. NFL.com: No. 1 San Francisco remained No. 1 on NFL.com’s power rankings of the week, and NFL.com’s Nick Shook also pointed out the defense, but in a more positive light. “There’s something special cooking within San Francisco’s defense, a unit that has every excuse to be average, at best, but continues to exceed expectations,” Shook wrote. “While the final score (32-29) doesn’t suggest it, Sunday’s win in Seattle was a defense-driven victory — and a big one for the team’s confidence as a true Super Bowl contender.” Rest of top five: Chiefs, Seahawks, Ravens, and Jaguars. There seems to be a consensus on the Chiefs, who are also undefeated and coming off their bye week. Meanwhile, most remain extremely high on the Seahawks, which only further validates the 49ers’ win on Sunday. The Athletic: No. 1 Just like the two above, the 49ers are the top team in The Athletic’s weekly power rankings, with their resume standing out through five games. “No team has a better resume than the 49ers, who overcame a rare so-so game from Brock Purdy in Seattle,” The Athletic’s Chad Graff and Josh Kendall said. “This time, it was San Francisco’s defense that led the way, limiting the Seahawks to just 4.2 yards per play. Oh, and Mike Evans and George Kittle certainly do not look like they are 33 years old.” It’s a good sign that the 49ers are winning in different ways, especially considering the gauntlet of a schedule they face to end the season. Rounding out the top five were the Chiefs, Bills, Vikings, and Jaguars. Despite being one of three undefeated teams, the Vikings haven’t received much love in the power rankings ahead of Week 6, but they did here. Sports Illustrated: No. 1 The 49ers jumped from No. 5 last week to No. 1 in Connor Orr’s latest power rankings. “The 49ers lead the league in wins…and players who are on injured reserve,” Orr wrote. “I heard a theory on Monday while making calls that stuck with me: the teams that are at the biggest advantage in the NFL are the ones with continuity at head coach, playcaller and quarterback over a multi-year period, especially during a season in which 10 head coaching jobs shifted this offseason. The steadiness of the Shanahan-Purdy partnership is shining.” Rounding out the top five were the Jaguars, Chiefs, Bills, and Seahawks. CBS Sports: No. 1 The 49ers remained atop Pete Prisco’s weekly power rankings for CBS Sports, and he believes this could be their year to win a Super Bowl. “San Francisco 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan hasn’t won a Super Bowl. That doesn’t mean he isn’t a great coach,” Prisco wrote. “If last season, in which he won 12 games with an injury-ravaged team, didn’t prove how good he is at leading the 49ers, this year is doing just that. The 49ers are 5-0 after going to Seattle and beating the Seahawks on Sunday, doing it with a defense leading the charge, rather than the Shanahan-led offense. “The 49ers limited the Seattle running attack, forced four turnovers, one of which was recovered in the end zone for a touchdown, and had five sacks, the most they’ve had in a game since 2024. They did it without star pass rusher Nick Bosa. First-year defensive coordinator Raheem Morris is using a much more aggressive scheme than past Shanahan coordinators, and it’s showing up in takeaways and sacks. The coverage is tighter. Combine that with Shanahan’s offensive wizardry and an MVP-type start for quarterback Brock Purdy, and it’s easy to understand why the 49ers sit atop my Power Rankings. Going to Seattle and beating the defending champs sends a loud message to the rest of the league. This team is really good. “As for Shanahan, his greatness as a coach might not truly be earned until he wins a Super Bowl. That’s just the way it is. He came close when his Jimmy Garoppolo-led 49ers had a lead against the Kansas City Chiefs in Super Bowl LIV after the 2019 season, only to see Patrick Mahomes rally to win it. They came close again four years later in Super Bowl LVIII, with Purdy and Co. pushing Mahomes and the Chiefs to overtime before losing. This team, provided it stays healthy, has a real shot at getting back there for Shanahan. For now, they are the league’s best team with a schedule that might not be as tough as expected before the season. Plus, they already have victories over division rivals in the Rams and Seahawks. This could be Shanahan’s year to win one.“ Rounding out the top five here are the Chiefs, Vikings, Jaguars, and Bills.
author: Rohan Chakravarthi

title: 49ers News: We’re on to Washington
summary: The Commanders are a fascinating team. The same guys that beat Seattle also just tied the New York Giants. At 1-3-1, they’ll be desperate to save their spiraling season. A win on national TV against the hottest team in the league would be exactly what the doctor ordered for them.  With Sonny Styles leading the […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - OCTOBER 20: San Francisco 49ers defenders Arik Armstead (91) (front) , DeForest Buckner (99) and Nick Bosa (97) slide on the wet turf to celebrate sacking Washington Redskins quarterback Case Keenum (8) to end the game at FedEx Field. (Photo by Jonathan Newton / The Washington Post via Getty Images) The Commanders are a fascinating team. The same guys that beat Seattle also just tied the New York Giants. At 1-3-1, they’ll be desperate to save their spiraling season. A win on national TV against the hottest team in the league would be exactly what the doctor ordered for them. With Sonny Styles leading the way, their front seven will be a problem. He’s been really really good… maybe one of the few linebackers that can keep up with George Kittle or Christian McCaffrey. Their secondary looks much more exploitable. On the other side of the ball, their interior offensive line seemed like their biggest vulnerability before the season started. They’ve stabilized by signing Lucas Patrick to play center and getting starting guard Sam Cosmi back from injury. The x-factor, which I’m sure will be talked about ad nauseam, is none other than Jayden Daniels. Niners LB Dre Greenlaw’s appeal of suspension rejected, will sit vs. Commanders “Rookie Jaden Dugger, who filled in for Greenlaw against the Seahawks, is likely to start in Greenlaw’s place Monday night.” NFL Week 5 film review: How Mike Evans, Kyler Murray, Jordan Love provided answers (paywall) “ The Seahawks’ two-deep shells discourage deep passing and can make the picture cloudy for quarterbacks. However, they play a fair amount of one-on-one outside when they rotate their safeties or when one of their safeties is “poaching.” Matthew Stafford has made a living finding those one-on-ones, and Puka Nacua and Davante Adams win in those situations. This week, Brock Purdy found those matchups, and Evans made the Seahawks pay. Here, the Seahawks lined up with two deep safeties, as they usually do. This could dissuade quarterbacks from looking deep because there could potentially be deep help on both sides of the formation. However, after the snap, the weak-side safety turned his hips and looked to the three-receiver side. They were playing a form of quarters that left the backside corner Josh Jobe one-on-one with Evans. Some quarterbacks might still see the safety’s presence on that half of the field and decide not to throw deep, but Purdy knew the safety couldn’t help Jobe on the outside with his technique.” 49ers report card, grades: The defensive line saved their best game in years for the Seahawks “Let’s talk about that intentional grounding play. On the left side, Luke Farrell is the in-line tight end; Brayden Willis is lined up next to him, but off the line of scrimmage. The wide receiver split out left is Jordan Watkins, who motions that he’s off the line, but lines up on the line of scrimmage. That covers Farrell up, making him ineligible. And those are the types of plays that are why we see Watkins only run nine routes. On one of those routes, Watkins was bullied and couldn’t shake free from press. Cooks made himself available on the touchdown, but was called for a penalty, had another declined, and looks disinterested as a blocker. There is a weird amount of hate for Jacob Cowing that I do not understand. The coaching staff is starting to figure out how and where to use Cowing. Against Seattle, Cowing ran 41% of his routes in the slot and leaned more on underneath routes where he could find soft spots in the zone. He will still run clear out routes, but in my opinion, Cowing could be Purdy’s best friend. Without Deebo, I see Jacob taking over that role….Any time a defensive lineman reads a screen, it’s a sign their IQ is through the roof. Guess what Mykel Williams did? Keion owes Mykel a steak dinner for the sack, since Williams forced Sam Darnold to move off his spot….Dugger was a difference-maker. He got caught peeking on a play-action pass and allowed a first down. Honestly, that may have been his lone mistake. His discipline was incredible. He stayed in windows where Darnold wanted to throw to JSN, instead of taking the bait on a shorter throw. Those are the plays that don’t go in the stat sheet. Dugger was in the stat sheet plenty. He ran through the right tackle’s block to stop a screen that could’ve resulted in a first down. Dugger set the edge, made multiple stops, and played with starter-level physicality.” 49ers game review: How Gracen Halton and defense’s recent draft picks saved the day in Seattle (paywall) “Mustapha channeled the best of his promising 2024 rookie season by also breaking up would-be completions to wideouts Cooper Kupp and Jaxon Smith-Njigba with shot-from-a-cannon blows before he sealed the win by belting Kupp out of bounds on a 9-yard reception on 4th-and-10 from midfield with just under a minute left. Three plays earlier, Mustapha’s shot on Smith-Njigba was vital. After Mustapha whacked him to break up a first-down pass, the reigning NFL Offensive Player of the Year rose slowly and went to the sideline for a snap with the game on the line. When he returned, Smith-Njigba dropped a deep third-down pass before Mustapha punctuated his violent performance with his fourth-down tackle. 49ers overreactions: Was Mike Evans missing piece to finally winning Super Bowl? “Now, we can’t confidently say that Corliss Waitman is the best punter in the NFL this season. But the point is . . . he has been very good for the 49ers this season. On Sunday, none of his five punts were returned. As a result, the Seahawks began those five drives at the 11, 18, 8, 9 and 4. And, yes, Gracen Halton’s touchdown was a direct result of that last Waitman punt right before the end of the first half. Waitman’s net punting average is 43.6 yards, and that is nearly a 7-yard improvement over Thomas Morstead from last season.”

title: Brian Daboll needs to change the Titans’ approach against Colts
summary: The 0-5 Tennessee Titans are averaging 11.5 points per game. That is historically bad. Paul Kuharsky was on Robby and Rexrode this morning and said that it is in the bottom 2% of 0-5 starts since the merger. This is a new all-time low for this franchise. It is time to change something on offense. […]
full_text: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - AUGUST 23: Offensive Coordinator Brian Daboll of the Tennessee Titans looks on prior to Week 2 of the preseason game against the Seattle Seahawks at Nissan Stadium on August 23, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The 0-5 Tennessee Titans are averaging 11.5 points per game. That is historically bad. Paul Kuharsky was on Robby and Rexrode this morning and said that it is in the bottom 2% of 0-5 starts since the merger. This is a new all-time low for this franchise. It is time to change something on offense. Brian Daboll is trying to keep the offense balanced. On the surface, that makes sense. The best offenses in the league are able to stay on schedule with the run game. It allows you to stay out of obvious passing downs, which makes things easier for the defense. The problem for the Titans is that their run game isn’t very good. They aren’t staying on schedule and are ending up in a lot of obvious passing downs. It is time to come up with a different plan of attack. Take the reins off of Cam Ward. Come out with some no-huddle and let him throw the ball around the yard. Look, I understand that is a scary idea. Ward hasn’t been good this season, but what is there to lose at this point? They are scoring 11.5 points per game! Mike Borgonzi spent a lot of money to get Wan’Dale Robinson here and the fourth overall pick on Carnell Tate. The idea there was to add some juice to the passing game. So, Daboll should do something to try to add some juice to the passing game. It’s dumb to say it can’t get worse. Ward could come out slinging and throw three picks, and the Titans could score zero points. That’s always possible, but the approach they are currently using isn’t working. Why not try something different?

title: 3-round Titans mock draft
summary: The Tennessee Titans are currently slated to possess the No. 1 overall selection in the 2027 NFL Draft. full_text: Tennessee Titans General Manager Mike Borgonzi addresses the media the day before training camp begins at Vanderbilt Health Football Center Tuesday, July 28, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The Tennessee Titans are currently slated to possess the No. 1 overall selection in the 2027 NFL Draft. After Week 5, they are winning the SOS tiebreaker versus the other 0-5 teams (Chargers, Dolphins). The Titans do look like legitimate contenders to earn the top pick, unfortunately. That has prompted this 3-round Titans mock draft. Titans GM Mike Borgonzi (or someone else?) will have difficult decisions to make if they actually end up owning the No. 1 overall pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. Round 1 (No. 1): Jeremiah Smith, WR, Ohio State Would the Titans draft a quarterback No. 1 overall to replace Cam Ward? Personally, we’re currently unimpressed by this upcoming QB class. Arch Manning and Dante Moore haven’t been good enough. The Titans may have to decide between choosing a QB to replace the current No. 1 overall quarterback, or a wide receiver who makes the rookie fourth overall pick a WR2. Jeremiah Smith is a generational prospect and the Titans shouldn’t overthink it, if given the opportunity. He looks like a legitimate Hall of Fame talent. Adding Smith to this offense would give Ward even fewer excuses in 2027. If the Titans have to draft a QB in 2028, inheriting Smith is a good problem for that rookie passer to have. Round 2 (No. 35): Clev Lubin, EDGE, Louisville Jeffery Simmons is the only Titans pass rusher currently capable of getting after the quarterback. The edge-rushing group is particularly bad. Jermaine Johnson II is on an expiring contract. Femi Oladejo doesn’t look like he’ll ever be more than a rotational player. Keldric Faulk is still growing and developing, but he’s more of a “BIG END” ala Arik Armstead in Robert Saleh’s system as opposed to a game-wrecking pass rusher. Louisville’s Clev Lubin is an exciting pass rusher. He proved capable of handling better competition by registering 8.5 sacks in 2025 after having 9.5 sacks at Coastal Carolina in 2024. Lubin already has another four sacks in 2026. Round 3 (No. 66): LJ Martin, RB, BYU Both Tony Pollard and Tyjae Spears are on expiring contracts. The Titans shouldn’t bring either player back in 2027. The offense’s inability to consistently run the football is hurting Cam Ward. If the Titans decide to give Ward one final opportunity in 2027, they’ll need a significant investment at running back. BYU’s LJ Martin is a good-sized back (6-2, 225) with a three-year period of excellent production. Martin is currently my fifth-ranked RB in this class.

title: Commanders Film Session: How Jayden Daniels powered Washington in his return
summary: Jayden Daniels’ return to the lineup against the New York Giants was nothing short of impressive. While his legs helped keep Washington’s offense afloat, accounting for 103 rushing yards and two touchdowns, his efficiency as a passer was just as dangerous. Daniels’ 199 passing yards may not jump off the stat sheet, but he completed […]
full_text: Jayden Daniels’ return to the lineup against the New York Giants was nothing short of impressive. While his legs helped keep Washington’s offense afloat, accounting for 103 rushing yards and two touchdowns, his efficiency as a passer was just as dangerous. Daniels’ 199 passing yards may not jump off the stat sheet , but he completed 68% of his passes, finishing with 17 completions . His decision-making, aggression and ball placement kept the offense moving and demonstrated how dangerous he can be when he’s operating at full strength. As Washington prepares for Monday night’s matchup against the San Francisco 49ers , who enter the game ranked sixth in the NFL in total defense by yards allowed per game, Daniels will need to maintain that dual-threat ability to give the Commanders a chance to secure their second win of the season. Mental processing and pocket patience On the first drive , Washington lines up in 12 personnel (one running back and two tight ends) against the Giants’ base 3-4 defense. After gaining 13 total yards on its first two plays, Washington faces second-and-8. Daniels does an excellent job processing the Giants’ coverage both before and after the snap. The Commanders run a switch-release concept with their tight ends against a Cover 4 structure, with two deep safeties. Ben Sinnott does an excellent job driving the cornerback upfield and away from Chig Okonkwo, who takes the inside release and runs a seam route. The Giants maintain their coverage structure after the snap, leaving the middle of the field open and giving Daniels an immediate answer. With the offensive line providing adequate protection, Daniels has enough time to stay with his primary read. He simply needs to deliver the ball beyond the linebacker and into Okonkwo’s path. His recognition of the coverage and ability to exploit the space allow Washington to capitalize on the defensive look. Leverage processing and elite placement Washington returns to 12 personnel on this next play , which comes at the start of the fourth quarter with the Commanders facing first-and-10. Daniels’ trust in Terry McLaurin is evident, but this completion stands out because he quickly processes defensive leverage and delivers the ball with precision. Washington runs a dagger concept involving Ben Sinnott, Treylon Burks, and McLaurin. McLaurin wins at the top of his route, gaining inside leverage against his defender as he breaks toward the middle of the field. Meanwhile, the Giants use edge rusher Kayvon Thibodeaux to account for the seam threat, dropping him into hook coverage. Daniels recognizes that Thibodeaux’s positioning leaves him unable to contest McLaurin’s dig route effectively. At the top of his dropback, Daniels delivers an on-time and accurate throw into a tight window and gets the ball out on schedule. It’s an excellent example of his ability to read leverage, trust his receiver and attack a defense before it can close the throwing lane. Reading progressions On the next example, Washington uses 11 personnel from an empty formation. Daniels begins his progressions toward the boundary, where McLaurin and Antonio Williams run corner and hook routes, respectively. The Giants’ deep-third and flat defenders effectively eliminate those initial options, forcing Daniels to work his progressions further. That’s where the route combination between Okonkwo and Burks becomes important. Their routes create a two-level read, putting linebacker Tremaine Edmunds in a position where his decision determines Daniels’ next move. Edmunds stays with Okonkwo, opening the middle of the field for Burks. Daniels recognizes the opening and delivers an accurate pass to Burks for a first down. It’s another example of his composure and processing ability. He doesn’t force the ball to his initial reads, instead allowing the coverage to dictate where he goes next. Daniels delivered an impressive performance against the Giants, making Washington’s final overtime sequence all the more frustrating. His ability to threaten the Giants’ defense as both a passer and a runner gave the Commanders chances to win, but the game ended in a tie. The encouraging takeaway for Washington is that a healthy Daniels gives the team a chance to compete every week. His performance against New York showed that he can win with his arm, punish defenses with his legs, and consistently make the decisions necessary to keep the offense on schedule. The challenge now is turning those flashes into a more complete offensive performance, especially with a tough matchup against San Francisco ahead. In the full Trap or Dive film session below, I break down Daniels’ performance against the Giants, including his work as a passer and runner, as well as the areas where Washington’s offense fell short under first-year offensive coordinator David Blough. Comment and let us know your thoughts on the state of the Commanders offense. Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

title: Commanders response to Giants tie will speak volumes about Dan Quinn
summary: The Commanders have been getting crushed for what happened at the end of what might be the fateful moment of the season.  The criticism is just.   The Commanders tied the New York Giants by a score of 27-27, as we all know. The result was unacceptable by any metric. Our gut tells us the […]
full_text: The Commanders have been getting crushed for what happened at the end of what might be the fateful moment of the season. The criticism is just. The Commanders tied the New York Giants by a score of 27-27 , as we all know. The result was unacceptable by any metric. Our gut tells us the same thing. We’re now at the acceptance phase of the grieving process; however, the past can’t be changed, head coach Dan Quinn isn’t getting fired (right now), and the sun still rose in the East. For as bad as Sunday was, with unbelievable mistakes made by several key individuals in the Commanders power structure, it’s over now. What happens next will be as telling as anything that happens with the Commanders this season. “I want to a make sure that’s a scar that has to be permanent, Quinn told on-site reporters in his Sunday evening press conference, “and making sure this is a situation, a scenario that would never present itself again.” We’ll see if that’s the case starting on Thursday, when the Commanders start their practice week leading up to Monday night’s game against the San Francisco 49ers. How the Commanders respond to this vicious body blow will define their entire season, which is already on the ropes. The response must be holistic. Quinn needs buy-in from the locker room. The players must come together and be better in all facets, not just running situational football drills in practice. It’s clear some defensive adjustments must be made to better suit the plays to the players, where execution is lacking, primarily when heavy pressure doesn’t get home. The Commanders, first, must get used to talking about Sunday’s ending, and they must be confident and resolute in their responses. It’s unavoidable. Jayden Daniels is going to be asked about it on Thursday. Offensive coordinator David Blough will be asked about it on Friday, and everyone from Quinn on down will need to discuss it in production meetings. The news cycle that won’t say die and the questions will be pervasive until the Commanders get off the mat. Coaches and players must be confident and resolute in their responses. They must not flinch, and they need to back that confidence up with better play. I covered the Chicago Bears during the 2024-25 seasons, before joining Hogs Haven . Back in 2024, you could point to the Hail Mary in Washington as the exact moment that season ended for the Bears. Chicago lost in the worst possible way, with a cornerback jawing at fans while Daniels took the snap on the game-winning play. The Bears response to that disaster might’ve been even worse than the play itself. Matt Eberflus deflected, dodged, and at times, cowered when addressing the moment. Eberflus didn’t get fired after that game, but got canned after a brutal loss in Detroit where players screamed at him in a tense postgame locker room. The Bears continued to lose after the Hail Mary. They were 4-2 entering that Washington game. They were 1-11 afterwards . I use that as a cautionary tale of how a singular disappointment can become an avalanche. The Commanders are in a dangerous spot. They have so much riding on the response to Sunday’s game, while having to travel across the country to play an undefeated NFC juggernaut in primetime, where you just know the Week 5 ending will be replayed and discussed during the game and its shoulder programming. Commanders leadership is being tested, from Quinn to the coordinators to the quarterback. What happens next will be telling, and an important piece of information for owner Josh Harris, who is certainly monitoring this situation closely while evaluating whether (or when) Quinn’s gotta go.

title: Who could replace Dan Quinn as Washington Commanders head coach?
summary: Dan Quinn’s fate is all but sealed. Barring an improbable Commanders playoff push that would need to see at least one postseason win, owner Josh Harris and general manager Adam Peters will be on the hunt for a new “leader of men” come January. The “brotherhood” has all but ended. The backwards hat, rah-rah bull-crap […]
full_text: Dan Quinn’s fate is all but sealed. Barring an improbable Commanders playoff push that would need to see at least one postseason win, owner Josh Harris and general manager Adam Peters will be on the hunt for a new “leader of men” come January. The “brotherhood” has all but ended. The backwards hat, rah-rah bull-crap is nearing a conclusion. The only question now becomes who will be his replacement and which Commanders decision maker will have the most say in the new hire. Below are my candidates for Dan Quinn’s replacement. There are more qualified coaches out there who are not on my list, and some who are on this list that are not top choices in my book. We can discuss this in the comment section. Offensive Coaches Klay Kubiak (49ers OC) : Sure, Kyle Shanahan calls the plays, but the word from the Bay Area is that Kubiak has a BIG hand in not only weekly game plans but offering game-day play input to Shanahan. I have heard that he’s the young coach that Adam Peters is absolutely smitten with. Klay has been with the 49ers since 2021. He started in a quality control role and quickly rose to his current position as offensive coordinator . 2026 is his second year in that role. He’s viewed as a young up-and-comer within NFL circles. Grant Udinski (Jaguars OC) : No list would be complete without Grant Udinski on it. The young protege of Liam Cohen in Jacksonville, Udinski has already received head coaching interest, and that’s sure to increase if the Jaguars remain on their current offensive trajectory. At just 30 years of age, he’s viewed as one of the bright young minds in the league. Grant cut his teeth as an assistant in Carolina and Minnesota before being hired by Kevin O’Connell as assistant quarterbacks coach in 2023. He added the title of assistant offensive coordinator the following season. He was poached by Liam Cohen to become his OC in Jacksonville, and during his first year helped Trevor Lawrence to his best season as a pro. Declan Doyle (Ravens OC) : Another young, rising NFL coaching star, Doyle made a name for himself as Ben Johnson’s right-hand man in Chicago in 2025. Because he wanted autonomy to call plays himself, he joined Jesse Minter in Baltimore where he’s the Ravens offensive architect. He currently has Baltimore’s offense at a top five unit in the NFL after five weeks. Mike McDaniel (Chargers OC) : If you want an offensive genius, McDaniel may be your guy. He cut his teeth under Kyle Shanahan in San Francisco and showed his chops as an innovative leader in Miami (albeit under poor ownership and with a limited roster). He was hired to be the Chargers offensive coordinator this past offseason and the results out in Los Angeles have not been pretty so far, but a lot of that has to do with injuries and a roster that was built for BIG Ten football. Nate Scheelhaase (Rams OC) : Scheelhaase is another young, innovative offensive mind who is learning the game under one of the best in Sean McVay. He may need another year of seasoning as an offensive coordinator but make no mistake – he’ll be on team’s radars this winter. Defensive Coaches Brian Flores (Vikings DC) : Flores is a well-respected defensive mind with head coaching experience. Minnesota’s defense was third in the NFL in EPA in 2025 and they currently rank third in 2026 through five games. A good thing if Flores were to come to Washington, is that he may elect to keep both Daronte Jones and David Blough as his coordinators. Anthony Campanile (Jaguars DC) : Campanile is viewed as a great leader and teacher. He’s a long-time position coach with stops at Miami and Green Bay before being hired to lead the Jaguars defense in 2025, and that defense would finish in the top 10 in the NFL in EPA. He received head coaching interest during the 2026 cycle and is certain to generate even more interest this next cycle. Chris Shula (Rams DC) : The grandson of the legendary Don Shula, Chris is forging his own path as a defensive guru in the NFL. He spent two years as a quality control coach with the Chargers before joining Sean McVay’s staff, where he now calls the defense that is currently ranked in the top five in EPA. Jim Leonhard (Bills DC) : It seems like dating back to his days as a defensive back at Wisconsin, Leonhard was destined to become a coach. He was a defensive coordinator and interim head coach at his alma mater before making the jump to the NFL with the Broncos in 2024. The Bills saw potential in him and he was hired away from Denver to be the new defensive coordinator under first-time head coach Joe Brady. He’s viewed as a great leader, and future head coach in the NFL. College Coaches Ryan Day (Ohio St. HC) : If Ohio State makes another national championship run, don’t be surprised if Day makes the jump to the NFL. He’s long had NFL coaching aspirations and, given the way he’s molded the Buckeyes and consistently put quality players into the NFL, he will garner a ton of interest. He’s viewed as a great leader and a coach players respect. Marcus Freeman (Notre Dame HC) : Much like Day, Freeman has NFL aspirations. There were rumors that he could make the jump to the NFL during the 2026 coaching cycle, but he chose to remain with the Irish. He has NFL ties from his brief time as a player, and insiders say he could put together a quality staff because of those relationships. Lincoln Riley (USC HC) : Riley is viewed as an innovative offensive mind who coaches to the strengths of his players. He has no current NFL experience, but there have been rumors in the past of his interest at the game’s highest level. Steve Sarkisian (Texas HC) : There have been rumors of Sark returning to the NFL for the past few years. He may not want to start again after Arch Manning leaves for the NFL, so this could be the year he tries his hand as an NFL head coach. He previously had stints with the Raiders (QB coach) and Falcons (OC). Former NFL head coaches who are currently unemployed Sean McDermott : McDermott, who went 98-50 as the Bills head coach , should have his pick of some openings in the 2027 cycle. I know there are some in the Commanders organization who really like him. Mike Tomlin: I’m reluctantly putting Tomlin on this list — not because I don’t respect him as a head coach (he was one of my favorite coaches in the league for many years), but because I feel he’s a bit old-school now for my liking. Still, he’s a great leader of men and CEO-type who can do well if put into the right situation.

full_text: The Daily Slop – 14 October 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Commanders links Articles The Athletic (paywall) That botched final play: What we know and still don’t know Daniels could have thrown the ball over Sinnott’s head — or even heaved it downfield, well beyond Okonkwo or Burks — and the clock would have stopped with time remaining. Instead, after he stumbled on his dropback and made the half-hearted fake to White, Daniels — how should we put this — freaked out . He ran to his left, then fell back to his right, just getting back to the line of scrimmage — where he then sat for about four seconds. “This is terrible situational awareness,” former fullback Michael Robinson said on NFL Network . “I don’t think Jayden Daniels knew whether he had timeouts or not. Look at the urgency. There was none. “He was about to lay on the ground. And to me, a picture is worth 1,000 words. Right here, the Washington Commanders did not know what to do in the situation.” Said Green Bay Packers pass rusher Micah Parsons of Daniels : “There’s no way I’m taking a sack with (12) seconds left and no timeouts. … This is your third year. … You’ve been to the NFC Championship Game. You’ve been in big moments before. And to me, even after a sack, you’re casually getting up.” To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Last Man Standig (paywall) New focus puts the onus on the QB The quarterback’s decision not to throw the ball away, followed by the offense’s lack of urgency as time expired, produced the lasting images of one of the more baffling endings in franchise history. Daniels’ role can’t be absolved, regardless of what happened earlier in the chain of command. Quarterbacks are the extension of a coach on the field. The greats have the instincts to know when the information no longer applies to the question presented. As the clock ticked down, the situation demanded an adjustment from Daniels. It never came. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE ESPN Seven things Solak thinks entering NFL Week 6 Daniels, independent of any call from the sideline, is the player holding the football. He knows the clock is running; he knows (or at least should know) he has no timeouts. He simply cannot be tackled in bounds. He has to throw the ball away. Quinn should not lose his job because Daniels short-circuited on a play he didn’t fully understand. But you can’t really come back from this. It’s Quinn’s third season as the head coach in Washington, and all the magic of Daniels’ rookie year and that deep 2024 playoff run is forgotten. If Washington can’t beat this version of the Giants — up by 14, in the rain, facing a backup quarterback and with a hand-delivered victory at the end of overtime — it’s hard to imagine it’ll beat enough teams to justify keeping the staff. Remember, Quinn made two coordinator changes last offseason. He’s all out of cards to play to keep his seat for another year if things don’t change very quickly. Bullock’s Film Room (subscription) Why did the Commanders defense struggle so much in the second half vs Giants? In the first half, they dominated, as they have done a few times this season. The Giants failed to get anything going on the ground and the passing game wasn’t much better. The Giants managed just three points in the first half, but things completely changed in the second half. The Giants scored on every possession in the second half, bar the kneel down on the final play before going to overtime. Going from conceding just a field goal in the first half, to giving up scores on four consecutive possessions in the second half is quite the change. So what changed? To break that down, we have to start by looking at what went well in the first half. The Giants came out looking to establish the run game, but the Commanders were very stout against the run early on, as they have been most of the season. To emphasize just how good the Commanders were against the run, after Daniels ran for his first touchdown, the TV broadcast put up a stat that Daniels had a 38-yard run for that touchdown, and at that point the Giants had 37 total rushing yards as a team. And that was midway through the third quarter. So the Giants had nothing going for them on the ground in the first half, which meant they were constantly in second and third and long situations. So what changed? In the second half, the Giants opted to almost abandon the run game and instead went to plays they would call “extensions of the run game”. title: The Commanders’ tie exposed two major problems on both sides of the ball
summary: The Washington Commanders’ final sequence of plays in overtime has earned its place in the league’s history books. But, amid the fallout from a historically bad 27-27 tie with the New York Giants, rookie coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones‘ inconsistent performances have largely been overshadowed. Jones’ defense has been particularly problematic in the second […]
full_text: The Washington Commanders’ final sequence of plays in overtime has earned its place in the league’s history books. But, amid the fallout from a historically bad 27-27 tie with the New York Giants, rookie coordinators David Blough and Daronte Jones ‘ inconsistent performances have largely been overshadowed. Jones’ defense has been particularly problematic in the second half of games. Over Washington’s last four contests, the unit has surrendered 21 points per game in the second half, up from 10 per game in the first. One of the biggest issues has been the defense’s inability to turn pressure into meaningful results. According to Telemetry Sports , the Commanders have generated just 57 pressures on 190 opponent pass attempts. Although those 190 attempts rank fourth-highest in the NFL, and Washington’s 57 total pressures rank 13th, its 30% pressure rate ranks 23rd in the league. The defense has also recorded just nine sacks, tied for 24th, while its 4.7% sack rate ranks 27th. Those shortcomings were on full display against the New York Giants. Jones’ defense failed to record a sack in the second half or overtime, allowing quarterback Jameis Winston and the Giants’ offense to produce 346 yards and 24 points during that stretch. Five games into Jones’ tenure, a legitimate question remains: Can he make the necessary adjustments at halftime to counter opposing offenses? Just as importantly, what is breaking down when the defense’s execution fails to match the intent of the play call? Against the Giants, Jones deployed Cover 0 on 17% of defensive snaps, a significant jump from the 4% rate he averaged over the first four weeks. He called the aggressive coverage 12 times in the second half, and Winston completed 6-of-10 passes against it for two touchdowns. The results raise questions about Jones’ willingness to continue relying on an approach that opposing offenses have begun to exploit. On the other side of the ball, Blough struggled to find answers against New York’s Cover 0 pressures. Washington didn’t consistently punish the Giants’ aggressive approach, but found some success late in the game after New York tied the score. A slant to Terry McLaurin and a screen to Dyami Brown finally provided answers against the blitz, but the adjustments came later than they were needed. Blough’s delayed response could have ultimately cost Washington the game, even with Jayden Daniels delivering a strong performance in his return. The tie against the Giants should serve as a wake-up call for both coordinators. Washington’s offensive and defensive struggles are no longer isolated issues; they are potential blueprints for future opponents to exploit. If Blough and Jones cannot identify solutions before the Commanders’ next opponents start replicating those successful game plans, the same problems could keep derailing the team. In the latest episode of the Trap or Dive Podcast , we broke down both coordinators’ struggles, examined what went wrong against the Giants, and discussed the urgency of their adjustments heading into yet another pivotal early-season matchup. Martenzie Johnson, Commanders reporter at the Washington Sun, joined the show to share his early-season takeaways. Podcast YouTube Comment and let us know your thoughts on Washington’s coordinators so far. Don’t forget to also subscribe to the Trap or Dive Podcast.

title: 15 NFL players, coaches on the hot seat entering Week 6: Quinn, McDaniel, others
summary: What now for Mike McDaniel? Should the Commanders or Eagles consider coaching changes? Could Jacoby Brissett or Brian Thomas Jr. get traded?
full_text:
Week 6 is about the point where seats start getting hot around the NFL. Five games isn't a huge sample for coaches and players, but it's enough time to see with some confidence that preseason expectations or hopes aren't going to be met. It's enough time for fans to be frustrated and make their feelings known in stadiums and on social media.

 
 Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show' 

 
 There's no joy in seeing anyone around the league lose their job or miss out on an opportunity, but it's also a reality that everybody who works for a team faces on an annual basis. Today, I'm going to run through some of the players and coaches on the proverbial hot seat after the first five weeks of the 2026 NFL season and break down what's going wrong and what might happen next.

 In no particular order, I'll hit on three head coaches, two coordinators and 10 players with questions about their futures with their current teams. And I'll begin with a coordinator for a winless team that entered the season with postseason aspirations.

 

 
 Jump to a player or coach: 
 McDaniel | Montgomery | Bland | Smack 
 Bowles | Quinn |  Sainristil | Sirianni 
 Sheppard | Hairston | Jeudy | Brissett 
 Smith | Thomas | Nix 

 
 

 

 Mike McDaniel, OC, Los Angeles Chargers 
 It seems natural to talk about what must be the most disappointing unit in football this season. And it's fair to note that, yet again, injuries have waylaid the Chargers on the offensive side of the ball. In last week's 23-17 loss to the Broncos , the Chargers were down their top two wide receivers ( Quentin Johnston and Ladd McConkey , the latter of whom was active but did not play a single snap) and their three best offensive linemen ( Joe Alt , Tyler Biadasz  and Rashawn Slater ). Justin Herbert 's lone touchdown pass went to Hayden Rucci , a tight end who was signed off Jacksonville's practice squad in mid-September.

 Even so, McDaniel's old employers in San Francisco have had plenty of injuries on offense and things are still humming along just fine for the 49ers. Frankly, even before the injuries really slowed this offense down, things didn't look the way they were supposed to in Los Angeles. The Chargers haven't been able to run the ball all season, ranking 28th in EPA per play on designed rushes.

 McDaniel has been insistent on running into heavy boxes with limited success; the Chargers have faced a numbers disadvantage in the run game 36.2% of the time per NFL Next Gen Stats, which is the fifth-worst rate in the league. It's fine to run into loaded boxes if you trust your linemen to pull it off, but the Chargers are averaging 2.5 yards per carry and minus-0.32 EPA per play on those attempts while picking up first downs at the fifth-lowest rate in the NFL.

 What has to be more concerning for coach Jim Harbaugh, though, is the regression of Herbert. Through five weeks, Herbert is last among qualifying passers in Total QBR (26.6). By several notable metrics, Herbert has completely collapsed as a passer:

 

 Herbert's sack rate is up, and he leads the league in interceptions with seven. And while a couple of those have been the customary snaps where a Chargers receiver is suddenly allergic to the football at the point of arrival and coughs it up to a defender, Herbert deserves plenty of blame for the problems the Chargers have had as games wear on. He has a 5.0 QBR in the fourth quarter, throwing four picks and taking a league-high five strip sacks. His fourth-down interception  against the Broncos last week was one of the worst throws you'll ever see Herbert make, a lowlight he seems adamant about challenging every week once the Chargers get behind late in games.

 There's usually not much benefit to making an in-season change at offensive coordinator, given that the positional coaches were likely brought in by that coordinator and would just be running the same scheme if they were promoted to the playcalling role. The most experienced assistant on McDaniel's staff is passing game specialist Adam Gase, which won't inspire much hope among Chargers fans.

 They do have Harbaugh, though, and there's a clear line that the offensive coordinator in Los Angeles can't cross. It's one thing to field a disappointing run game or fail to live up to expectations, but the offense can't break Herbert. If McDaniel can't turn things around, and Herbert continues to struggle badly, the Chargers might make a move sooner rather than later.

 

 
 

 David Montgomery , RB, Houston Texans 
 The latest in a series of offseason additions to try to fix a moribund Texans running game, Montgomery hasn't been able to transfer his successful three-year stretch in Detroit to Houston. Though the 2019 third-round pick scored three touchdowns in the Week 1 loss to the Bills , Montgomery has averaged just 2.7 yards per carry and posted a league-worst 23.1% success rate. You can help compensate for those issues with explosive runs, but Montgomery has just one gain of 10-plus yards across 52 carries this season.

 Montgomery left last week's win over the Titans in the first half with a groin injury , potentially opening up the door to a larger role for Woody Marks . The second-year pro had what qualifies as a great game on the ground for a Texans back, turning 15 carries into 62 yards while adding four catches for 23 yards as a receiver. The Texans have been hesitant to turn the lead role over to Marks, but Montgomery's struggles and the groin injury might leave them no choice.

 

 

 
 

 DaRon Bland , CB, Dallas Cowboys 
 Bland was a first-team All-Pro after he picked off nine passes in 2023, but the interceptions have dried up since then. He has just one INT across 24 games since the start of 2024. And when Bland isn't creating significant value with his takeaways, teams find it too easy to pick on him in coverage. He has allowed passer ratings north of 100  in coverage in each of the past three seasons, per Pro-Football-Reference.com, including a career-worst 126.2 mark this season.

 Jerry Jones and the Cowboys have had reasons to give Bland a long leash. Despite missing most of the 2024 season with a foot injury , the Cowboys gave their young corner a four-year, $90 million extension before the 2025 season. Bland missed more time last year before pronouncing himself to be all the way back this season ... but he has looked overmatched in coverage. Tez Johnson 's 64-yard catch against the Cowboys  in primetime last week came on a play where Bland was badly juked and fell to the ground like he was the child in one of those " dad crosses over baby " videos.

 The Cowboys didn't really have solutions to replace Bland on the outside at cornerback, but that has changed. Cobie Durant should be set to return from his hamstring injury in the coming weeks, while Joey Porter Jr . will be back in the lineup after missing the loss to the Buccaneers with an illness . When healthy, they should be the starters on the outside for Dallas. Bland could end up in the slot, but the Cowboys have been playing  Reddy Steward  there, and rookie safety Caleb Downs could move there once Jalen Thompson returns from his hamstring injury .

 Dallas restructured Bland's deal just before the season, which reduced his cap hit and made his contract more tradable. But it also creates more dead money if (or more realistically when) the Cowboys decide to move on from the 27-year-old cornerback. Bland is owed $13 million next year, and at the moment, it's only guaranteed for injury. The Cowboys don't want to be on the hook for that money, so it would hardly be a surprise if they took Bland out of the lineup altogether once Durant and Porter are back on the field to avoid triggering those guarantees, which would happen if Bland suffers a significant injury.

 

 
 

 Trey Smack , K, Green Bay Packers

summary: What is going on with the Eagles?! We have intel on Philly's three-game slide, three remaining unbeaten teams, QBs at risk of being benched, potential WR trades and more.
full_text:
Somehow, we have already made it to Week 6 of the  2026 NFL season . And insiders Jeremy Fowler and Dan Graziano have been making calls to sources around the league for the latest news and notable buzz.

 On the positive side, there is still a trio of undefeated teams. (The Chiefs had a Week 5 bye, so they are 4-0, while the 49ers and the Vikings are both 5-0.) Which of the three has earned the most confidence from people around the league? But on the other side of things, some teams are really struggling as we hit Week 6. The Eagles have lost three straight games and have fallen apart in the fourth quarter in the past two. Is the panic meter rising in Philadelphia? Could we see changes?

 Speaking of changes, are any quarterbacks in danger of getting benched? Could we see more wide receivers on the move before the trade deadline as some offenses try to find a spark? It's all here, as Jeremy and Dan answer big questions, hand out useful fantasy football nuggets and empty their reporting notebooks heading into Week 6.

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Eagles concern | Top undefeated 
 WR trades | Possible QB benchings 
 Fantasy football advice 
 More notes, intel 

 
 

 How concerned are the Eagles amid three straight losses? 
 Graziano: Pretty concerned. This is a team that just saw a nearly complete overhaul of its offensive line last week , and not all of it was intentional. Lane Johnson 's retirement leaves a significant hole on the line and in the locker room. The Eagles are also still awaiting Landon Dickerson 's return from injury , and they're counting on significant contributions from the likes of Drew Kendall , Willie Lampkin and third-round rookie Markel Bell . This comes while still breaking in rookie wide receiver Makai Lemon , playing the past two games without top wideout DeVonta Smith and missing the top three running backs from their depth chart.

 The defense has looked better the past couple of weeks -- but it wasn't able to carry the Eagles through the early part of the season as they had hoped it would while the offense found itself under first-year coordinator Sean Mannion. That offense is dealing with a lot more than just growing pains right now, and after consecutive losses in which the Eagles' win probability exceeded 96% , there's reason to wonder where they'll find the leadership to get them through a tough part of their season.

 Fowler: Yeah, my sense is the concern is quite high. The Eagles sought to implement an offense that, in part, utilizes play-action passes over the middle to match a potent running game. But that's not working as intended. The offense ranks in the bottom third in play-action usage. It ranks 31st in total offense. Jalen Hurts struggles at times throwing inside the numbers, which was apparent Sunday in London. The impending return of Saquon Barkley and Smith will help, but I'm not sure that will solve the problems that run deeper than one or two players.

 

 The hiring of Mannion signaled a shift in thinking, an implementation of more under-center and play-action work for Hurts. A transitional period was expected, if not inevitable. But the Eagles now have to rebuild the offensive line at the same time, which is a huge challenge. It can't be ignored that the Eagles needed a last-minute drive in Week 2 against still-winless Tennessee to avoid a 1-4 start, a reality no one in Philadelphia will tolerate very long.

 Graziano: That becomes the question, right? If they aren't going to tolerate it, then what are they going to do about it? We know general manager Howie Roseman is always on the lookout for trades to improve the roster, and the NFC East is certainly there for the taking . But the way the Eagles conduct themselves at this year's trade deadline will tell us a lot about how they view themselves. The Cam Jurgens trade wasn't a sign of a roster-wide sell-off; they were done with Jurgens, and the return was good . But if they lose a couple of more games in the next three to four weeks, things could get very interesting in Philly.

 Fowler: Very interesting. The schedule is manageable, even favorable. On deck is a two-game home slate against Carolina and Dallas, then at Washington, followed by the Giants at home and a perfectly placed Week 10 bye. After that comes Pittsburgh, Dallas, Arizona and Indianapolis.

 The good news is all of those games are winnable. But if the Eagles don't capitalize on that stretch, it feels as if there will be change at some level. Because while the defensive formula is sustainable, Philadelphia is going on two seasons of bad offense. So, Roseman might not be done making moves, and the offense seems like a potential spot to watch in that regard.

 

 
 Which of the three undefeated teams is getting the most confidence around the league? 
 Fowler: Kansas City was mentioned most when I asked league evaluators this week. The Chiefs' running game has been a revelation with Kenneth Walker III . Patrick Mahomes looks more comfortable by the week on his surgically repaired knee . Steve Spagnuolo's defense is as stingy as usual. The Chiefs are light at receiver, but a pass-catching trio of Travis Kelce , Rashee Rice and Xavier Worthy is plenty viable. (Rice is out with a hamstring issue but will be back.) Basically, the Chiefs are the team with the fewest concerns out of the group.

 San Francisco has been tremendous thus far -- you could argue no team is playing better -- but the looming question is whether the 49ers can stay healthy. That has been the question with them. And Minnesota rolls out a championship defense that has been enough to offset the team's 27th-ranked total offense -- so far. Whether Minnesota can win in January with this offensive attack is a real question unless it can prove otherwise in the coming weeks.

 Graziano: Agreed on all accounts. The Chiefs seem to be impressing people the most in terms of the sustainability of their success. But people are taking note of what Kyle Shanahan is doing in San Francisco amid its annual cascade of injuries . After last season -- when the 49ers lost Brock Purdy , Fred Warner , Nick Bosa and others for extended periods and still managed to win 12 games and make it to the second round of the playoffs -- Shanahan's message to his locker room was that San Francisco could overcome just about anything. The Niners are continuing to play with that mentality, and they're in pretty good shape at 5-0, with head-to-head victories over each of the other three teams in the NFC West.

 

 Fowler: San Francisco defensive coordinator Raheem Morris is pushing the right buttons. He has extensive knowledge of the NFC West from his time with the Rams and has a formula to combat the divisional gauntlet. The edge rusher position is still worrisome, as 2025 first-round pick Mykel Williams is working his way back and Bosa can't stay healthy . Perhaps GM John Lynch will look for a short-term fix at the trade deadline. But the 49ers' offense can score against anyone, and Purdy has proved that he stands with the best in the league's quarterback hierarchy.

 What do you make of Minnesota's offense, Dan? This is a timely bye week for coach Kevin O'Connell, a proven playcaller, to identify what works and accentuate the strengths of the passing game. O'Connell has smartly leaned into the running game while navigating the Kyler Murray transition, calling roughly 30 rushes per game. Aaron Jones Sr.  has been up to the task with 410 rushing yards, and Jordan Mason ( injured reserve, thumb ) should be back soon.

 Graziano: The Vikings are a fascinating case because they have largely been carried by Brian Flores' stifling defensive game plans. But they felt the offense showed improvement during the Week 4 victory over Miami and continued that progress in the Week 5 triumph in New Orleans. The Vikings felt Murray was distributing the ball better and using his legs more effectively than he had in previous outings. Murray missed most of the Week 1 game and the entire…

title: Super Bowl LXI odds: All 32 teams' odds to win the championship
summary: Every NFL team's win total, as well as odds to win the division, the conference and Super Bowl LXI.
full_text:
For the first time this season, the Los Angeles Rams are not the favorites to win Super Bowl LXI, as they have fallen to +700 after beginning the campaign at +500. The division-rival San Francisco 49ers are the new favorites at +680, having shortened after coming out of Week 5 tied with the Rams.

 L.A.'s latest loss came via an overtime thriller Monday night to the Buffalo Bills , who are tied for the third-best odds on the board with the Baltimore Ravens at +800.

 

 The next tier consists of the Kansas City Chiefs , who lengthened slightly from +900 to +950 during their bye week, and the Seattle Seahawks , who fell from +950 to 11-1 week-over-week after their close loss to San Francisco.

 The Jacksonville Jaguars continue to gain ground after beginning the season at 30-1, making it all the way to 12-1. The undefeated Minnesota Vikings have also been a notable improver, tied with three other teams at 20-1 after coming into the campaign at 50-1.

 The season's biggest disappointment is undoubtedly the Los Angeles Chargers , who began the season with sixth-best 17-1 odds and have fallen virtually out of contention to 200-1 after an 0-5 start.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings   and subject to change.

title: Revisiting 2026 preseason bold predictions for 32 NFL teams: Which are on track?
summary: In the preseason, we made bold predictions for every NFL team, from Jordan Love's MVP case to Isaiah Likely's catch total. Which ones are on track? Which seem unlikely?
full_text:
Part of making preseason predictions is seeing how those forecasts actually fare. It's easy to predict something, but we also need to check on our predictions and hold ourselves accountable.

 Before Week 1, I made one bold prediction for every NFL team as part of our lookahead to the 2026 season . These were big swings -- things I thought could happen but would be upsets if they did. And five weeks into the season, we've learned a lot.

 That makes this a great time to dive back into those preview predictions and find out how things are going. Which ones are on track? Which might still happen? And which were so far off that we might as well scrap them for a completely new one? In some cases, five weeks means everything has changed. In others, not so much.

 Let's take a look and see where we stand for all 32 teams.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 
 

 On target 
 

 Buffalo Bills 
 Original prediction: Wide receiver Keon Coleman will record 750 or more receiving yards and at least five touchdowns -- both career highs.
 

 Why it's on target: Coleman had been on a bit of a production tear on plays when DJ Moore was off the field until Monday night, when he managed only 7 receiving yards in a game that Moore missed. Still, Coleman's 224 receiving yards put him on pace for 761 yards over a full season. If Moore -- who did not play Monday due to a shoulder injury -- misses more time, that will help Coleman's cause. Not playing the Rams every week should, too.

 
 

 Jacksonville Jaguars 
 Original prediction: Cornerback Montaric Brown will record a worse-than-average yards allowed per coverage snap (1.1 per NFL Next Gen Stats).

 

 Why it's on target: Considering Brown is at 3.8 yards allowed per coverage snap, we're well on our way. The idea for this prediction was that Brown's strong 2025 campaign was fueled by on-ball results that tend not to be stable from year to year and that he would regress in 2026. So far, that looks right. Brown has missed all but six snaps in the past two games due to a hamstring injury.

 
 

 

 New York Giants 
 Original prediction: Tight end Isaiah Likely will lead the team in receptions.
 

 Why it's on target: Likely currently leads the Giants in receptions, with 33 catches to Malik Nabers ' 29. As Nabers continues to recover from the ACL injury he suffered last season, he might accrue more volume. But Likely is ahead right now and has proved to be a key part of this new Giants offense.

 
 

 Tennessee Titans 
 Original prediction: Cornerback Alontae Taylor will allow 1.4 yards per coverage snap or worse, per NFL Next Gen Stats.

 Why it's on target: Taylor is right on target at 1.4. Should that continue, this would be disappointing for the Titans after they signed Taylor in free agency following a 1.0 yards-per-coverage-snap season in 2025. But Taylor was at 1.6 in 2023 and 2024, which is a big reason I made this prediction. For context, the average for an outside cornerback is 1.1.

 

 

 Still a chance ... 
 

 Arizona Cardinals 
 Original prediction: The Cardinals will go 1-16.

 

 Why there's still a chance: I don't think this will hit anymore, especially since the Cardinals won their opener . But I won't quite throw this out yet because Arizona's remaining schedule is an absolute gauntlet. There could be winnable games against the Commanders, Jets and Saints down the road, but if the Cardinals can't win any of those, I could get the backdoor cover.

 
 

 Atlanta Falcons 
 Original prediction: Safety Xavier Watts will be a first- or second-team All-Pro.

 

 Why there's still a chance: Watts has one interception, one forced fumble and a half-sack as part of a Falcons defense that has been better than expected. He has allowed 0.8 yards per coverage snap -- higher than average for a safety, though I don't put a lot of stock in that number for safeties considering the variety and complexity of assignments at that position. This is a long shot, but you never know -- if Watts goes on an interception run, anything could happen.

 
 

 Baltimore Ravens 
 Original prediction: The Ravens' defense will rank in the top four in EPA per play.

 

 Why there's still a chance: Baltimore ranks 17th through five games. That's not ideal for making the top four, but it doesn't put the Ravens out of the running just yet, as we've seen their defenses turn it around in the second half of the season in recent years. Considering the talent the Ravens have and that they are playing under a new coach with a defensive background in Jesse Minter, I think it's at least feasible. Trey Hendrickson , who ranks sixth in pass rush win rate at edge, has missed the past two games due to a broken finger that required surgery . If Baltimore can get him back, that should help.

 
 

 Carolina Panthers 
 Original prediction: The Panthers will finish last in the NFC South.
 Why there's still a chance: Considering how well Carolina's offense has played, I sincerely doubt that I will be correct on this. But this is the NFC South, and you just never know. The Panthers are only 1½ games out of last place, and I have a strong opinion of cornerbacks Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson , so their absences could really sting.

 

 

 
 

 Cincinnati Bengals 
 Original prediction: Running back Chase Brown will record at least 15 total touchdowns.

 

 Why there's still a chance: With only one score thus far, this prediction is off to a pretty rough start. But a big part of why I backed Brown was the Bengals having the easiest schedule in the NFL. The beginning of that schedule wasn't easy, and it gets lighter from here, so there should be plenty more touchdowns to come.

 
 

 Cleveland Browns 
 Original prediction: Quarterback Taylen Green will start at least four games.

 

 Why there's still a chance: The odds have dropped. I had figured the Browns would already be on to Shedeur Sanders by this point. Even though Deshaun Watson hasn't been quite as bad as expected, I still think that the Browns will make the move to Sanders relatively soon and that an end-of-year stint for Green remains in play.

 
 

 Dallas Cowboys 
 Original prediction: Kicker Brandon Aubrey will record the most field goals over expected, per NFL Next Gen Stats.

 

 Why there's still a chance: Aubrey is off to a slower start than I would have guessed, with 1.3 field goals made over expectation. That ranks 13th, and he has missed a PAT, too. But there's still plenty of time for him to move to the top.

 
 

 Denver Broncos 
 Original prediction: Cornerback Riley Moss will command a $17 million-per-year contract after this season, either with the Broncos or someone else.

 

 Why there's still a chance: Moss missed Week 5 with a rib injury, but he has allowed 1.1 yards per coverage snap (average) this season, per NFL Next Gen Stats. He picked off Trevor Lawrence in Denver's Week 2 win over the Jaguars but was also burned badly by Konata Mumpfield on a double move for a 48-yard touchdown in the fourth quarter against the Rams in Week 3 . I still feel good about this one, though.

 
 

 Detroit Lions 
 Original prediction:  Edge rusher  Aidan Hutchinson will win Defensive Player of the Year.

 

 Why there's still a chance: Four sacks and a 66th percentile pass rush win rate at edge isn't a bad start, but he's going to have to pick it up to fulfill this prediction. He has the talent level to do it, but the fact that the rest of the Lions' defense is looking so weak is going to hurt Hutchinson's sack total, which in turn will hurt his DPOY chances.

 
 

 

 Green Bay Packers 
 Original prediction:  Quarterback  Jordan Love will finish in the top three in MVP voting.

 

 Why there's still a chance: I was prepared to throw this one out ... until Week 5, when Love posted a 94 QBR in the Packers' 31-7 dismantling of the…
