title: NFL survivor power rankings: Why this is the week to use Rams, Patriots, Colts
summary: ESPN NFL survivor pool strategy, predictions and ranking the top six options for Week 6
full_text:
Welcome to  ESPN NFL Survivor ! The rules are simple: Pick one NFL team each week to win its game. If that team wins (or ties), you advance to the next week. If that team loses, you are out. The catch is that each team can be chosen only once. ESPN's game requires just one team each week, so that will be the focus of this column, though I will touch on other major contests.

 For the third time in five weeks, the top-picked team in ESPN Survivor fell. This time, it was the Dallas Cowboys , who were picked by 35% of entries against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers . Since the loss came on Thursday, the concentrated selection on the Houston Texans and Cincinnati Bengals opened up other potential leverage opportunities.

 

 However, two of the top potential low-future value picks both tied or lost in the Washington Commanders and Atlanta Falcons . Luckily for those who play ESPN Survivor, Commanders backers advanced to Week 6, unlike in Circa Survivor or Splash Sports. Entering Week 6, only 9.7% of entries in ESPN Survivor remain.

 The biggest favorites in Week 6 are the Los Angeles Rams . While favorites of at least eight points are a paltry 5-5 outright, the four double-digit favorites this season are 4-0 outright.

 In contests that require one pick per week, the Rams are the optimal pick, especially in smaller groups that are unlikely to last all season. However, in large pools, and pools with multi-pick weeks, I prefer to  save the Rams for later.

 The Rams make a ton of sense as the biggest favorites of the week in their largest projected favorite role all season. However, Los Angeles is also projected to be favored in all but one or two of their remaining games, and as we get deeper into the season, having teams like the Rams available is valuable. That's especially true in Circa and Splash, which require multi-pick weeks, especially with the Rams projecting to be the biggest favorites on Circa's Thanksgiving slate.

 

 The San Francisco 49ers and Kansas City Chiefs are both laying over a touchdown, but they have the two lowest availabilities among all remaining teams (Chiefs 37%, 49ers 44%). Both are fine contrarian picks this week, though both have significant future value, especially the 49ers.

 The New England Patriots and Indianapolis Colts are the other strong choices this week. While they arguably have less win equity in Week 6, both have significantly less future value than the Rams, Chiefs and 49ers. However, both teams face the Dolphins in the next few weeks, so they will have other opportunities.

 Note: Odds by DraftKings and subject to change. Future value based on Mike Clay's cheat sheet .  

 1. Los Angeles Rams (vs Cardinals) 
 The Rams are the biggest favorites in the betting market by far in Week 6, and it's projected to be their largest favorite role all season. However, they are also projected to be one of the biggest favorites in each of the next three weeks (at Las Vegas Raiders , vs. Los Angeles Chargers , at Washington Commanders ), and they rank fifth in my future value model the rest of the season. Plus, on Circa, they play on both holiday slates, including a home game against the Green Bay Packers in the Thanksgiving slate. Ultimately, it comes down to what kind of Survivor player you are. Are you looking for the best pick in Week 6, or are you looking to map out your path for all 18 weeks?

 
 Chance to win: 88% (ESPN Analytics), 93% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Rams -12.5 (-900 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fifth 
 Availability: 95% 
 ESPN Selection: 33% 
 
 2. New England Patriots (vs. Jets) 
 

 In larger groups, or contests with multi-pick weeks, the Patriots would be my top pick. While they have two games left against the Miami Dolphins , the home game doesn't come until Week 18, while the road game in Week 8 also includes the Cincinnati Bengals hosting the Tennessee Titans and the Dallas Cowboys hosting the Arizona Cardinals , two other very strong pivots. Outside of those two games -- and I generally don't worry about Week 18 this early in the season -- this is the best chance all season to use New England. The Patriots are 16-1 over their last 17 home meetings against the Jets, with the only loss coming in Bill Belichick's final NFL game. Just make sure to monitor the injury reports, especially on the Jets offense.

 
 Chance to win: 79% (ESPN Analytics), 75% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Patriots -7.5 (-345 moneyline) 
 Future value: 13th 
 Availability: 96% 
 ESPN Selection: 21% 
 

 3. Indianapolis Colts (vs. Titans) 
 There are likely only two weeks all season where the Colts will be a strong favorite; this week, and Week 10 hosting the Dolphins. In a vacuum, the Dolphins matchup is better. However, with only 15% of ESPN entries on the Colts as of Tuesday evening, that Miami game looks like it will be the heavy chalk in Week 10. So if you are the kind of Survivor player who likes to fade the top pick each week, this is a great week to use the Colts in a great spot where they will be slightly lesser selected.

 
 Chance to win: 72% (ESPN Analytics), 77% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Colts -7 (-340 moneyline) 
 Future value: 17th 
 Availability: 99% 
 ESPN Selection: 15% 
 

 4. Kansas City Chiefs (vs. Chargers) 
 

 Both the betting market and Mike Clay's model view the Chiefs as the second-biggest favorites this week. And since the Chiefs are available by only 37% of entries in ESPN Survivor, they are projecting to be only 5% picked. The Chiefs host the Jets and Cardinals in Weeks 9 and 11, but outside of that, they probably won't be usable again until the final couple weeks. However, in each of those weeks, there are several other strong picks, making this week stand out as a strong week to burn the Chiefs.

 
 Chance to win: 74% (ESPN Analytics), 93% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Chiefs -8.5 (-500 moneyline) 
 Future value: Fourth 
 Availability: 37% 
 ESPN Selection: 5% 
 

 5. San Francisco 49ers (vs. Commanders) 
 

 The 49ers are now the Super Bowl favorites at DraftKings, and ESPN Analytics views them as the best team in the NFL. As a result, they rank highest in future value. Outside of Week 16 (at Chiefs), the 49ers will likely be favored in every game the rest of the season. Still, ESPN Analytics views this as the 49ers' easiest game the rest of the season, making this a fine week to burn them, especially since almost all the biggest favorites this week are some of the best teams in the NFL.

 
 Chance to win: 86% (ESPN Analytics), 86% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: 49ers -7.5 (-440 moneyline) 
 Future value: First 
 Availability: 44% 
 ESPN Selection: 8% 
 

 6. Buffalo Bills (at Raiders) 
 The Bills are a consideration for me in Splash only. While they are third in future value on ESPN, most of that value is in Week 11 hosting the Dolphins, where they will likely be one of the most popular selections all season. Their other easiest games are in Week 10 (at Jets), Week 17 (at Dolphins) and Week 18 (vs. Jets), none of which are double-pick weeks in the major Splash contests. So if you are looking to create a unique path and get off that Week 11 chalk, this is one of the best weeks to use Buffalo.

 
 Chance to win: 72% (ESPN Analytics), 57% (Mike Clay) 
 Spread: Bills -5.5 (-258 moneyline) 
 Future value: Third 
 Availability: 83% 
 ESPN Selection: 4% 
 

 The Road to 18-0 

 
 Week 1: Jaguars (vs Browns) - Win 
 Week 2: 49ers (vs Dolphins) - Win 
 Week 3: Chiefs (at Dolphins) - Win 
 Week 4: Vikings (vs Dolphins) - Win 
 Week 5: Texans (at Titans) - Win 
 Week 6: Rams (vs Cardinals)

title: Are Panthers positioned to add reinforcements before NFL trade deadline?
summary: Armed with draft capital and sitting at 2-2, Carolina has leverage unlike in years past. So what does it mean?
full_text:
CHARLOTTE, N.C. -- The Carolina Panthers come out of their bye week with their best four-game record in five seasons. And at 2-2, the Panthers stand alone at the top of NFC South division race with four weeks until the annual NFL trade deadline on Nov. 10 at 4 p.m. ET.

 With the Panthers sitting in an unprecedented position under the current front office, Carolina is in an interesting spot when it comes to consideration of midseason reinforcements. While several notable names -- including starting right tackle Taylor Moton (blood clot), starting defensive end Tershawn Wharton (neck) and top returner Trevor Etienne (ankle) -- are expected to make their 2026 debuts in short order, the Panthers could use improved depth at a few positions with injuries piling up. That's where the trade deadline could come into play, and Carolina is inarguably better positioned to add players than in years past, especially if the team finds a good fit on the market.

 

 Panthers general manager Dan Morgan has been methodical about parting with draft capital for incoming players during his tenure, which began in 2024. In fact, his first straight-up trade involving an outgoing pick for an incoming player -- without a player or pick swap -- happened less than two months ago, when Morgan traded a 2028 sixth-round pick to the Los Angeles Chargers in late-August for defensive lineman TeRah Edwards , who played in each of the Panthers' first four games before their Week 5 bye.

 The Edwards trade, while a minor deal, shows Morgan isn't going to be stubborn with his draft assets if it means he can upgrade a roster primed for a potential repeat division championship.

 Panthers coach Dave Canales said he and Morgan speak about potential roster moves "all the time."

 "I won't get into specific positions or anything like that, but Dan has done a great job of trying to look for opportunities that may present themselves to us to be able to challenge our roster in the right way," Canales said Tuesday. "We're always open, we're always looking. I'll pop into his office right after this meeting for about 15 or 20 minutes. And we may be watching [saying], 'Hey, let's take a look at this guy.' We may be watching a college player as he's starting to gather his evaluations, but always having those conversations, to be ready for what could be."

 While the Panthers have momentum coming off a Week 4 win against the Detroit Lions and quite a few talented players who are getting healthy, adding external talent could help push the team beyond the standard they set last season with an 8-9 playoff berth.

 Let's break down the ins and outs of the Panthers' outlook with less than four weeks before the trade deadline and ahead of their game Sunday at the Philadelphia Eagles ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ):

 
 

 Roster needs for Panthers entering Week 6 
 Carolina's injuries have established positional demands across the depth chart, even with several players eligible to return from injury prior to Nov. 10:

 Cornerback: Jaycee Horn (quad) and Mike Jackson (groin) are on injured reserve. They were replaced by rookie Will Lee III and special teams ace Akayleb Evans against the Lions in Week 4. And while Lee held his own, Evans was picked on relentlessly by Detroit quarterback Jared Goff to the tune of 12 completions for 208 yards and a touchdown on 16 throws.

 The Panthers could use an additional veteran presence with Horn and Jackson sidelined.

 Running back: The Panthers don't want to overload starting running back Chuba Hubbard , but he has already touched the ball 71 times in the first four weeks of the season. While that workload has been beneficial to the offense (390 total yards and five touchdowns), the Panthers have postseason aspirations and don't want to hinder Hubbard's late-season production on the way there.

 Etienne will return from an ankle injury this week, but he hasn't proven himself offensively in the NFL. And the early returns on AJ Dillon haven't been particularly glowing (46 yards on 19 total touches) as he has filled in for Jonathon Brooks , who is on injured reserve after undergoing core muscle surgery. A consistent pass-catching option out of the backfield would benefit the rotation. Maybe Etienne can become that option, and he'll have a decent runway to prove himself before the trade deadline.

 Defensive line: The Panthers plan to have Wharton back in the lineup shortly. However, while they've benefited from second-round pick Lee Hunter 's play, the Panthers' run defense has left a lot to be desired. Entering Week 5, Carolina ranks last in rushing yards allowed per carry (5.4) and 31st in rushing yards allowed per game (156.5).

 While those numbers are largely skewed by the Week 1 loss to the Chicago Bears , the unit has only held one rushing offense below 132 yards in four games. Wharton isn't known as a run defender and likely won't solve this issue. Nose tackle Cam Jackson (shoulder) was also placed on season-ending IR on Tuesday, so Morgan might need to look to add externally again.

 
 Panthers' draft capital for 2027 and 2028 
 The Panthers have eight draft picks coming their way in 2027, including an additional seventh-round pick (from the offseason trade of Andy Dalton to the Philadelphia Eagles) and a second fourth-round pick, which was upgraded from a fifth-round pick in a pick swap (with the Minnesota Vikings in the 2025 Adam Thielen trade).

 

 2027 draft inventory: 

 First round (1): Original pick 
 Second round (1): Original pick 
 Third round (1): Original pick 
 Fourth round (2): Original pick, additional pick from Minnesota 
 Fifth round (0): N/A (original pick traded to the Vikings) 
 Sixth round: Original pick 
 Seventh round (2): Original pick, additional pick from Philadelphia

 In 2028, the Panthers have six picks following the sixth-round swap for Edwards in August. All six are the Panthers' original picks.

 
 State of Panthers' salary cap 
 While the Panthers have an encouraging record, quality draft capital and clear needs at relatively attainable positions, their salary cap constraints could hold them back ahead of the deadline. According to the NFLPA, the Panthers have just $2.32 million in cap space (which ranks as second worst in the league behind the Los Angeles Rams with $1.78 million in space) as of Wednesday.

 The team has the ability to open up cap space with contract restructures, but that might not be the most sound strategy, even with the team looking to win now. While trading a future draft pick is one thing, pushing cap charges into the future, along with trading away that capital, might be hard to stomach for an organization that has largely balanced those scales under Morgan and executive vice president of football operations Brandt Tilis.

 The team could also look into releasing or waiving an underperforming player for salary cap space. That avenue would probably be the most likely strategy, as a cut player would also open up a spot for an acquired trade piece.

 
 Four games loom large for Carolina 
 The next four weeks will play a big factor into the Panthers' approach at the deadline. The team faces the Eagles (2-3) on Sunday and then has matchups against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (1-4) at home and the Green Bay Packers (3-2) on the road before hosting the Denver Broncos (3-2) in the final matchup before the deadline.  Given the Panthers' salary cap situation, though, their outlook on trades might be more about rentals toward the end of their rookie contracts or veterans with low-base salaries rather than the grandiose long-term splashes. title: Where is Jaylen Waddle? Broncos' big offseason acquisition is off to slow start
summary: With just 204 receiving yards through five games, Jaylen Waddle has been mostly contained and hasn't yet made the impact the Broncos hoped. What has gone wrong?
full_text:
ENGLEWOOD, Colo. -- After a failed third-down conversion Sunday in a game filled with failed third-down plays,  Denver Broncos  wide receiver Jaylen Waddle stormed into the bench area, ripped his helmet from his head as if it were in flames and slammed its crown into the bench.

 It summed up a frustrating day for the receiver, who finished with two receptions for 19 yards in a 23-17 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers . It marked the third time in five games in which he finished with fewer than 20 receiving yards, and the fourth in which he gained 35 or fewer.

 Waddle was by far the Broncos' most significant acquisition in an offseason in which they chose to mostly run it back with a roster that got them to the AFC Championship Game last season. Denver sent first- and third-round picks to the Miami Dolphins  to acquire him in March in addition to a fourth-round pick swap. But Waddle, who had 910 receiving yards and six TDs last season, has been rendered ornamental much of the time in an offense that coach Sean Payton said has a long list of problems. And as the 3-2 Broncos get set to host the defending Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks (3-2) on Thursday ( 8:15 p.m. ET, Empower Field at Mile High, Prime Video ), they're trying to figure out how to unleash Waddle.

 "I'm watching the film offensively and there are a ton of things we're not doing well right now," Payton said Monday. "So, that has to improve."

 

 Payton was giddy about Waddle's arrival this spring, calling the speed, acceleration, toughness and locker room demeanor of the receiver a "10, 10, 10, 10, 10." Throughout training camp, Waddle flashed his ability to turn any reception into a field-flipping play as a potent vertical threat.

 "[That] makes him so tough to play tight," said Broncos All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II , who played with Waddle in college at Alabama. "He can just run by you, or his routes are so clean if you play off, he's going to catch it and turn it into something big."

 But the Broncos' offense has been mired in an across-the-board struggle that has eaten into Waddle's production. While Waddle has 18 receptions for 204 receiving yards and a touchdown, much of that came in a Week 2 win over the Jacksonville Jaguars in which he caught eight passes for 138 receiving yards. His output has been meager otherwise -- a combined 10 receptions for 66 yards in the other four games. Waddle has been targeted an average of 6.2 times per game, a lower rate than he had in four of his five seasons with the Dolphins. That average falls to 5.3 when the Jaguars game is removed.

 But there might not be a redder flag in Waddle's lagging production than comparing it to that of backup running back RJ Harvey . Harvey, who has played only 42% of the team's offensive snaps this season and missed one game because of injury, leads the Broncos with 20 receptions.

 Waddle doesn't absolve himself of any of it. After a drop in a Week 4 loss to the San Francisco 49ers -- one of three he has had this season to equal his total from 2025 -- he said the play was just the kind of catch-and-run situation he usually flourishes in.

 "We're in prime position to score points and they call a play and I didn't execute," Waddle said. "... We've just got to make plays on a more consistent basis, that's what it comes down to. ... That's me, too, find a way anytime I get the opportunity to put us in a position for points."

 

 Waddle's slow start is part of a bigger malaise for Denver's offense. The Broncos are 31st in the league in plays of 20 or more yards (with 11). Waddle is 65th in the league at 11.3 yards per catch and 69th in receiving yards per route run at 1.63, far below his 2.27 yards per route run last season with the Dolphins or the 2.69 yards per route run in 2022. It's those types of figures that pushed Payton to retake playcalling duties from offensive coordinator Davis Webb after four games.

 But Waddle hasn't been the locksmith that he or the Broncos hoped. They envisioned him giving the other Broncos receivers, especially Courtland Sutton , more room to work while providing quarterback Bo Nix  with an explosive-play option both vertically and in catch-and-run situations. That hasn't materialized, as Sutton has 11 receptions for 104 receiving yards, his fewest through five games of any full season in his nine-year career.

 "You're like all right, we have to find more touches for ... X amount of receivers, even when [defenses] are in these deeper zones," Payton said. "We'll be able to do that, but we start with a mirror right away with ourselves."

 Nix has traced much of the passing game being stuck in neutral to the Broncos' inability to "stay out of third down," a drumbeat offensive tackle Mike McGlinchey summed up after the 49ers loss as "2-yard run, 2-yard run, dropback."

 Waddle might also be disproportionately suffering from what one AFC personnel executive called "a sped-up clock" in Nix's play in which the quarterback "seems to be in a hurry on every play." It's an issue Nix and Payton have acknowledged in recent weeks .

 Waddle is often the primary receiver on pass plays, so if Nix has moved too fast through his progressions before a receiver is at the top of the route, Nix will have already moved to the second or third read before that receiver is prepared to pay off his pattern.

 "A receiver can't throw himself the ball. Their impact is based on everything that needs to come together, route concept, timing, the quarterback's progression, footwork, all of it," a former longtime quarterbacks coach in the league said. "From what I've seen ... the drops and his footwork just seem off, so [Nix is] moving to the hot [receiver] or the outlet so often ... and that's not Waddle."

 

 All of this has resulted in an off-kilter offense that struggles to keep possessions going. The Broncos were 1-of-12 on third down Sunday and are 28th in frequency of drives that end in three-and-outs (a whopping 28.3% of possessions). This disjointed dynamic has also prevented them from taking advantage of something both Nix and Waddle should excel in together: crossing routes.

 Nix's highest QBR this season has come on crossing routes (96.6, much higher than his overall 41.5 QBR), yet Waddle has just two receptions on crosses, averaging 2.6 yards per crossing route run. Waddle has thrived on these routes in the past, averaging 3.0 yards per crossing route run last season and a stellar 4.5 in 2022. But when a team plays as many two-deep looks as the 49ers did in Week 4, the Broncos haven't punished those alignments enough with routes Nix and Waddle should nail.

 Nix has kept the faith, though, saying "it's close" and "it'll come." Waddle agrees.

 "We know we have the players in here, and the defense always gives us the ball back. It's about executing, me included, when we get the opportunities," he said.

title: What we've learned about the Detroit Lions after five weeks
summary: At 3-2, Detroit enters its bye having found some much-needed momentum in Arizona. Here is a closer look.
full_text:
DETROIT -- A smiling  Derrick Barnes was among the final Detroit Lions players to leave visitor's locker room at State Farm Stadium on Sunday.

 Fresh off a 45-21 win over the Arizona Cardinals , the linebacker admitted it "felt good" to enter Detroit's Week 6 bye on a high note -- especially after the team's defensive struggles early in the season.

 "I'm ready to get back to it. Out there, that's us. That's who we are," Barnes said. "Obviously, we have to continue to do it week in and week out but going out there and proving ourselves right today and then having the bye week. I said, 'I'm ready to get back to football already.' That's who we can be. It's a beautiful thing."

 

 Throughout the week, Barnes said he had received several text messages from Dan Campbell in which Detroit's head coach expressed his urgency to win and to go "whip ass" in Arizona.

 The Lions entered the Cardinals game allowing a league-worst 31.8 points per game, which was their highest mark allowed through four games of a season since 2022 when they allowed 35.3 points, per ESPN Research.

 But after giving up a touchdown on the Cardinals' opening drive, the defense adjusted. The Cards scored a late touchdown when the game had already been decided. 

 Campbell was fired up after the win, but also challenged his coaching staff to do a deep dive to find out "who are we really?"

 "I think we're five [games] in now and we've continued to evolve a little bit and we're mixing some things up," Campbell said on Monday. "But, at this point now we need to figure out what we really are and what we do well."

 At 3-2, Detroit enters its bye having found some much-needed momentum in Arizona. Here is a closer look at what we've learned about the Lions so far.

 

 

 What have we learned about the Lions on offense? 

 Under new offensive coordinator Drew Petzing, the Lions are averaging 32.8 points per game, which is tied with the Buffalo Bills for the most in the NFL. It's the second-most points they've scored through five games in franchise history, behind only last season (34.8 per game), but Campbell still feels they can get off to faster starts, involve wide receiver  Jameson Williams more consistently, create a stronger ground attack and become more dominant as a unit overall.

 Lions quarterback  Jared Goff has emerged as an early MVP candidate, throwing for 1,485 yards (second-most in the league) with 12 touchdowns and zero interceptions. Star running back  Jahmyr Gibbs  came out of Week 5 fourth in the league with 504 rushing yards and first in scrimmage touchdowns (nine) in his new role as the predominant back, but the standards are high in Detroit.

 "I think the sentiment is we have been good," Goff said after practice last week. "We've done some good things, and we've scored and had some good drives, but we haven't been great. And we're very, very capable of being great and above that. We want to be the best offense in the league, and we have to start playing like it."

 

 What have we learned about the Lions on defense? 

 Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard was under fire after his unit gave up at least 30 points in three of the first four games. But the unit put up a solid performance in Arizona entering the off week. The secondary has struggled the most, allowing a league-high 1,487 passing yards through the first five games. The defensive line, however, has produced the most sacks (20) through the first five games of any season in franchise history.

 Four players have at least three sacks, with edge  DJ Wonnum  leading the team with 5.0, followed by Aidan Hutchinson (4.0), DL Alim McNeill (3.5) and Barnes (3.0). Against Arizona, the defense committed to more man coverage which seemed to help, but also may not be the long-term the answer.

 "You have to go by what opponent it is," Campbell said.

 

 

 What do we still need to see from the Lions on offense? 

 Faster starts. Despite ending with 45 points, Detroit's offense went three-and-out on the first three drives in Arizona before scoring on its next seven.

 

 Detroit has scored one touchdown on 13 drives that have ended in the first quarter this season (7.7%) after scoring a touchdown on 24% of their first-quarter drives last season, which tied for ninth highest in the NFL, per ESPN Research.

 Goff would like to improve in that area.

 "It felt like (Petzing) could call whatever he wanted and we were going to make it work," Goff said after the Cardinals win. "I think today was a good example of, like I've said, where we can go and what we are capable of. I think I said it earlier last week (but) we've been good, right? Today we were great, and there are still some things to be better at certainly, but today we were like 'OK, that's what we were capable of.' It's good to know that's our standard now and we can hold guys accountable to what we just did today."

 

 What do we still need to see from the Lions on defense? 
 Improvement in the secondary. Moving forward, the Lions are anticipating the return of Pro Bowl defensive back  Brian Branch , who has been sidelined since December 2025 with a torn Achilles. They were also engaged in trade talks for Joey Porter Jr ., who ultimately ended up in Dallas, as part of their search to find another cornerback. ESPN insider Jeremy Fowler has suggested that Kansas City's Kristian Fulton and Pittsburgh's Jalen Ramsey could be potential targets.

 Branch, who started the season on the PUP list, had his 21-day practice window opened on Oct. 7. Campbell said he won't rush Branch back on the field, but he's very close to returning.

 "I told Dan, I'm starving since I got injured. Just been day by day. Just been working, just been grinding. Showing up at 7 a.m.," Branch said last week.

 Branch said he's "getting the rust off now in practice. I feel good."

 "I'm ready to go," Branch said.

 The Lions' depleted secondary also entered the season without Pro Bowl safety Kerby Joseph and is missing safety Thomas Harper and defensive back Avonte Maddox , who are on injured reserve.

title: Jaguars WR Parker Washington has the clutch gene: Will that earn him an extension?
summary: Did you see Washington's one-handed grab in London? How did he get so good at contested catches? And how did he quickly become a big part of the Jaguars' offense?
full_text:
LONDON -- Facing a fourth-and-5 from the  Philadelphia  27-yard line, the Jacksonville Jaguars got the look they wanted from the Eagles' defense. So, receiver  Parker Washington knew quarterback  Trevor Lawrence was going to throw him the football.

 Washington got a clean release off the line of scrimmage but then had to fight through contact with Eagles cornerback Riq Woolen , so he didn't see the ball in the air at first. As he got closer to the goal line, though, he finally picked it up.

 "As soon as I saw it, I was like, 'OK, there we go,'" he said.

 Washington reached out with his right hand, grabbed the ball and pulled it into his body while falling backward into the end zone. That gave the Jaguars the lead with little more than three minutes left in the fourth quarter, and they eventually won 19-17 on  Cam Little 's walk-off 57-yard field goal at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Sunday.

 

 There we go, indeed.

 That sequence isn't anything unusual for the 2023 sixth-round pick, who has been one of the league's most clutch receivers since Week 11 of 2025. Over that span, Washington has 17 catches for a league-high 381 yards on third and fourth downs; his 22.4 yards per catch there is the best in the NFL of any player with double-digit catches.

 The foundation for Washington's proficiency began long before he even started school, and it has helped him play as if he's 6-foot-4 despite being 5-foot-10 with 29-inch arms. As the Jaguars' 2026 leader in catches (25), receiving yards (352) and receiving TDs (four), he is well on his way to a contract extension that could pay him more than $30 million annually as one of the NFL's top-paid receivers.

 "We consider him an elite wide receiver," Lawrence said. "I don't know what everybody else thinks, but we feel like he's pretty freaking good."

 

 
 How Washington mastered contested catches 
 The aggressiveness to make every catch is innate, but Washington's expanded catch radius developed as a result of a game he played with his father, Christopher, beginning at 3 years old and continuing through college.

 "One thing me and my dad used to do, he would grab -- it would be anything, piece of balled-up paper, wrap tape around a piece of paper or something like that -- and he would [throw it to him and] say, 'Catch it with your eyes,'" Washington said. "And what I would do, I would literally catch it with my eyes and sometimes the paper would hit me with my face or whatever. So it was just a game, but it was fun.

 "But little did I know, we were really training."

 Washington's training eventually evolved into normal football drills, workouts and tape study as he got older. The summer before his freshman year at William B. Travis High School in Richmond, Texas, it also became an early-morning routine -- something that continues with the Jaguars.

 Washington is regularly one of the first people inside the Jaguars' facility every morning. He was getting there just before 5 a.m. during training camp, grabbing a quick FaceTime call with his trainer to prep for the day's workout. Washington even joked he needed the passcode to turn on the lights.

 In his final two seasons at Travis High, Washington caught 124 passes for 2,315 yards and 35 touchdowns, and he joined  Penn State  as a four-start prospect. Nittany Lions receivers coach Taylor Stubblefield said he was impressed with how quickly Washington picked up the offense. He finished second on the team in receptions (36), receiving yards (489) and receiving touchdowns (six) as a true freshman in 2020.

 

 Stubblefield said Washington's extended catch radius and ability to make contested catches showed up quickly. Washington flashed the latter ability repeatedly throughout his four-year college career, even when it was snowing in a 2021 loss to  Michigan State .

 "When the quarterback [ Sean Clifford ] threw it, you're like, 'OK, that's an overthrow,'" said Stubblefield of one play from that game. "And he somehow climbed not one ladder, but two ladders, to go up and high-point that ball."

 A detail that Stubblefield left out: Washington caught it with one hand. Then with less than a minute left, he made another clutch, contested grab for a touchdown.

 Stubblefield, who is now the receivers coach at  Air Force , said Washington makes those kinds of catches because he has a strong lower body -- "He's built like a running back," he said -- and elite body control.

 "Sometimes if somebody has bad body control or they're not judging the defense right, they are off balance, which then they might not have full explosion," Stubblefield said. "They're not in a position to be able to maximize that explosion, and Parker does a great job of that, which helps his catch rate be so large for somebody who doesn't necessarily have the measurables for it."

 
 Washington's ascension with the Jaguars 
 When the Jaguars drafted Washington with the No. 185 pick in 2023, they intended for him to learn behind Christian Kirk , who was coming off the best season of his career (84 catches for 1,108 yards and eight touchdowns) for a year or two. So, while Washington played sparingly early in his first season, Kirk, Zay Jones and Jamal Agnew  sat out a combined 19 games in 2023. That pressed Washington into a bigger role, and he responded with 16 catches for 132 yards and two touchdowns, including an acrobatic catch in the back of the end zone on "Monday Night Football"  against the  Cincinnati Bengals  in Week 13.

 The same routine of filling in for injured players continued in 2024, as Kirk, Gabe Davis and tight end Evan Engram all sat out time. It happened again in 2025, when injuries to receivers Brian Thomas Jr . and Travis Hunter essentially made Washington the team's No. 1 receiver. That's when he stuck to the starting lineup.

 Washington caught 58 passes for 847 yards and five touchdowns, and he topped 100 receiving yards in three of the Jaguars' final four games last season (including the playoffs). Among those catches was a slider against the New York Jets on a ball that Lawrence threw while rolling to his left.

 

 Since the start of the 2025 season, Washington has 80 catches for 1,199 yards and nine touchdowns. His last catch was the one-hander against the Eagles, further proof to Lawrence that -- other than throwing the ball into the stands -- there isn't a spot he can put a ball where Washington won't catch it.

 "I think if it's in his vicinity, he's shown that he can make just about any play," Lawrence said. "And I think that's a cool thing as a quarterback to have that trust in a guy to where ... you get a one-on-one with him and just put it near him, and he goes and makes an unbelievable play."

 Coach Liam Coen, who has been with Washington for only 23 games, acknowledged that he has seen Washington make so many difficult catches that it sometimes dulls the "wow" factor.

 "I mean, you're amazed because of the moment and because of how big of a time it was, but to look back and to continue to see this guy make plays for our team, especially in some of these critical moments, it just speaks to the dude and to make critical plays and critical moments, he's showing that he can step up and do that stuff," he said.

 
 What could Washington's contract extension look like? 
 The Jaguars have wanted to extend Washington, who is in the final year of his rookie contract (four years, $4 million), since the 2025 season ended. But the sides  could not come to an agreement on annual compensation before the season began.

 The team has not closed the door on in-season negotiations, and is not afraid to make those types of decisions -- wide receiver  Jakobi Meyers and offensive tackle  Cole Van Lanen both received extensions during the 2025 season. But with each passing week, impressive performance and contested catch, the price for a new deal certainly isn't going down.

 Arizona's Michael Wilson has had comparable production to Washington since the start of last…

title: Jacksonville Jaguars remain in the NFL hunt thanks to Foyesade Oluokun's bone-crunching efforts
summary: Runaway AFC South leaders the Jacksonville Jaguars continued their impressive start to the season, with Nigerian-American linebacker Foyesade Oluokun starring in a 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles.
full_text:
Runaway AFC South leaders the Jacksonville Jaguars continued their impressive start to the season, with Nigerian-American linebacker Foyesade Oluokun starring in a 19-17 win over the Philadelphia Eagles .

 Week 5 was a week in which many of the best performances from players with ties to Africa came from those who ultimately narrowly ended up on losing teams.

 

 Zimbabwe's Nate Landman (LA Rams) was up there with Oluokun for defensive impact in a 37-34 loss to the Buffalo Bills . Jaxon Smith-Njigba , who has proudly repped Sierra Leone on his helmet, was another prime example of an unlucky star performer, as the Seattle Seahawks went down 32-29 to the San Francisco 49ers .

 However, the Niners themselves benefitted from standout performances from two players with Nigerian ties -- Malik Mustapha and Osa Odighizuwa .

 African Player of the Week: Foyesade Oluokun (Jacksonville Jaguars) 
 The son of Nigerian parents, Oluokun has been instrumental in the Jaguars' success so far this season -- an understated but important part in one of the league's best defenses. In week 5, he starred with 10 tackles, including six solo and one for a loss, in the win over the Eagles.

 One could argue that Oluokun did not produce as many spectacular standout moments this week as the likes of Landman on defense and Smith-Njigba on offense and was fortunate to end up on the winning side when his main competitors for this week's award did not win their respective games.

 However, a counter to that would be that the often unseen steady contribution that Oluokun makes week-in-week-out is probably worthy of more accolades than he gets. In a sense, this Player of the Week prize could be seen as overdue recognition for a sturdy contribution over the course of five games -- four of which have seen the Jaguars come out on the winning side.

 

 African Moment of the Week: Jaxon Smith-Njigba (Seattle Seahawks) 
 Smith-Njigba -- of Sierra Leonean descent through his grandparents in a family with deep, complex West African ties -- weaved his way through four nearby Niners bodies to score a 16-yard catch-and-run touchdown off a Sam Darnold pass in the third quarter against the Niners, handing the defending Super Bowl champions the lead.

 The Seahawks may eventually have gone down in a narrow fight, but their star wide receiver was impactful as usual. He tallied 118 total yards, including 102 yards across five receptions.

 He did, it must be acknowledged, have a costly drop towards the end of the game. However, a bad moment towards the end of the game does not completely cancel out a memorable moment earlier - no matter how used to his brilliance we have become.

 With a record of 3-2 across the first five games, the defending champions can be forgiven for showing signs of growing pains, but as long as JSN is on board and on song, they cannot be written off.

 

 Honorable Mentions 
 The Niners' win over the Seahawks included major plays from Nigerian-American duo Osa Odighizuwa and Malik Mustapha, with the latter in particular having a game to remember with five solo tackles out of seven total, one fumble reception and one pass defended.

 The Nigerian missile was one of the key reasons why Smith-Njigba was unable to turn the game in the Seahawks' favor, making life tremendously difficult for the reigning Offensive Player of the Year in the decisive stages.

 One could make a case for Mustapha for Player of the Week based on high-intensity impactful moments alone, and the same could be said of the LA Rams' Landman - though he ended up on the losing side for the Rams against the Bills.

 Landman has become a master at the art of the punchout and forced two fumbles, making 13 tackles in a huge performance.

 The Tampa Bay Buccaneers ' win over the Dallas Cowboys saw big plays from Emeka Egbuka (of Nigerian descent) on offense and YaYa Diaby (of Guinean descent) on defense.

 Boye Mafe (Nigerian heritage) picked up a sack and a forced fumble for the Cincinnati Bengals in their 31-24 win over the Miami Dolphins .

 Sam Kamara , who has ties to Sierra Leone, picked up a first career sack - but in defeat as the Cleveland Browns went down 17-12 to the New York Jets .

 African-born Player Watch 
 Landman was the standout African-born player in Week 5, but Nigeria's Samson Ebukam notched up a sack in the Atlanta Falcons ' 30-23 loss to the Baltimore Ravens .

 Born in Onitsha, on the banks of the Niger River, Ebukam is on a tremendous run this season with 2.5 sacks in the last 3 games - half a sack against the Carolina Panthers followed by one apiece against the Baltimore Ravens and New Orleans Saints .

 The Falcons will, on Sunday, face a Chicago Bears side brimming with talented players with African ties. Kyle Monangai , who is of Cameroonian heritage, looks set to miss out through injury but Ebukam is likely to face Rome Odunze , who is of Nigerian descent through his father's side.

title: Chiefs still have faith in pass rush, despite going without a sack since Week 1
summary: Entering this week, the Chiefs ranked 27th in pass rush win rate and hadn't recorded a sack since Week 1.
full_text:
KANSAS CITY, Mo. -- Following their bye week, the Kansas City Chiefs returned to the training facility Tuesday, their first day in preparation for Sunday's game against the Los Angeles Chargers . Longtime defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo shared earlier this month that his first meeting with his players on Tuesday often includes him reminding them of where they must improve.

 "We like to have constructive criticism," Spagnuolo said then. "The good thing about this group is they're all pretty accountable. Even if I'm standing there and pointing something out, I see a lot of heads are shaking, [saying], 'Yeah, you're right.'"

 

 This week, one of the main areas for the Chiefs defense to address is the unit's lack of a single sack over the past month.

 The Chiefs, who are undefeated at 4-0, are hoping that statistical trend ends Sunday against a Chargers team that has struggled to properly protect quarterback Justin Herbert . One reason the Chargers are 0-5 is because Herbert has been sacked at least twice in every game. Without right tackle Joe Alt (neck), left tackle Rashawn Slater (right ankle), left guard Kayode Awosika (fibula) and backup guard Trevor Penning (concussion), Herbert was sacked five times last week in the Chargers' loss to the Denver Broncos .

 Entering this week, the Chiefs ranked 27th in pass rush win rate, generating pressure by beating the opponent's pass protection within 2.5 seconds just 45% of the time. The concern for the Chiefs after their most recent game, a comeback win over the Las Vegas Raiders , is that quarterback Kirk Cousins , who they pressured on just 34.6% of his pass drops, was the least mobile passer they have faced so far this season.

 "We've done a good job of keeping the quarterback busy back there, though, with pressure, which is important," coach Andy Reid said Monday. "Hands down, we want to have sacks. But the pressure on the quarterback ends up being an important thing, and I think our guys have been generating that."

 In the Chiefs' overtime win against the Indianapolis Colts , quarterback Daniel Jones was able to defeat pressure with quick completions, most of which occurred in the middle of the field. Miami Dolphins quarterback Malik Willis , who was sacked nine times in two games prior to facing the Chiefs, used his legs to escape pressure from pass rushers such as Chris Jones , George Karlaftis and rookie R Mason Thomas .

 Against the Raiders, Jones was quick to give his assessment of why Cousins wasn't sacked.

 "In order to win, you can't beat yourself," Jones said. "I think a lot of times we've made costly penalties that put us back."

 Late in the fourth quarter, Cousins was in the process of trying to get the Raiders to rally from an 11-point deficit. Just before the two-minute warning, Cousins was swarmed in the backfield by Karlaftis, Thomas and defensive end Ashton Gillotte . The problem, however, was that the sack was nullified by a holding penalty from nickel cornerback L'Jarius Sneed .

 

 Cousins was then able to finish the drive with a touchdown, the byproduct of him barely evading Thomas, who attempted a strip-sack. But Cousins was able to scramble out of the pocket and throw a 20-yard touchdown pass to tight end Brock Bowers . While the Raiders celebrated, Thomas displayed his disappointment by putting both of his hands on his helmet.

 "We're motivated and we're all trying to work all together," Karlaftis said after the game. "We weren't happy with the results of last year and our numbers aren't there yet, but we're trying to affect the quarterback and have an impact on the game.

 "Up front, we felt like we had some MOBPs -- missed opportunities [and] big plays. We'll get better as the season goes on."

 Last season, the Chiefs' ineffective pass rush was one of their biggest issues. The defense recorded just 35 sacks, the fifth fewest in the league. Entering Sunday's game against the Chargers, the Chiefs have just three sacks, which is tied with the Dolphins for the league's fewest.

 "I think our D-line did a good job of finding ways to make some pressures," linebacker Nick Bolton said after the game. "We've got to finish. We can take some of those points off the board."

 

 Through four games, opponents have used similar tactics to thwart the Chiefs' defensive line. Jones has been double teamed on most clear passing downs. Karlaftis, who is known for his strength and tenacity, leads the Chiefs with 10 quarterback hits despite not having a sack.

 Spagnuolo wants his pass rushers to be better on first- and second-down snaps, which should lead to more advantageous rushing situations on third down. The Raiders, though, were able to keep Cousins' jersey clean in the first half by utilizing play-action passes on those early downs. Cousins completed nine of his 13 play-action passes for 133 yards and a touchdown, according to NFL Next Gen Stats.

 "You create movement for the quarterback and get him open spaces for him to throw the ball," Jones said of the Raiders' play-action passes. "You bring the linebackers down and you've got to respect the run game. It opens up areas for the tight ends to get the ball. They did it a lot earlier in the game, and they were very successful with it. We had to adjust in the second half because they were operating under it so well."

 Of course, the Chiefs know much of their pass rush will be determined by how much their rookies, Thomas and defensive tackle Peter Woods , can contribute as the season progresses. This past offseason, the Chiefs wanted to provide better support to Jones and Karlaftis. Woods and Thomas then became the Chiefs' first pair of defensive linemen selected in the first and second rounds of the same draft since 2002.

 Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott , a second-year player, is also expected to return to the pass rush rotation later this season after recovering from a torn ACL in his right knee.

 Above all, Jones is not worried. He emphasized how close the Chiefs were to sacking Cousins. He also expects the Chiefs will have plenty of opportunities to redeem themselves by hitting, wrapping up and bringing the quarterback down the turf. Those opportunities, the Chiefs hope, start to occur Sunday against Herbert and the Chargers.

 "I think we don't waver from what we've been doing," Jones said. "We've done a lot of good and put a lot of good [plays] on film. A win is more important than a sack -- and sacks will come if we continue to do what we do."

title: How NFL pros such as Matthew Stafford gain perspective from coaching their kids
summary: ESPN spoke to 16 NFL players about what it's like to coach their children and what it means to spend that time with them.
full_text:
IT WAS THE middle of April, and Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford was drawing up a play on a whiteboard on the sideline of a youth flag football game.

 He was surrounded by a group that included his three oldest daughters -- Chandler (9), Sawyer (9) and Hunter (8) -- as he described how to read a quarterback's eyes and attack the run.

 Stafford's daughters, who expressed interest in playing the sport after watching a girls flag football camp at the Rams' facility last year, were supposed to be coached by a local high school student. But after a conflict came up with the student's schedule, Stafford said all eyes turned to him.

 "Everybody just kind of looked at me and was like, 'I mean ... it should be you,'" Stafford told ESPN.

 Stafford's team won the championship, but he said his focus was trying to teach the players -- six girls and four boys -- the fundamentals of flag football.

 "I tried to keep it as simple as I possibly could," Stafford said. "We kind of just lined up and played the same defense all the time and tried to keep it simple for them so they could go play and have fun."

 Stafford is one of many current NFL players who coach their kids in sports that include football, soccer, baseball, basketball and golf. ESPN spoke to 16 of those players about what it's like to coach their children and what it means to spend that time with them.

 New England Patriots right tackle Morgan Moses said he gets recognized at games when coaching his sons -- Isaiah (11), Jeremiah (10) and Legend (8) -- in youth football during the spring.

 "It's funny because a lot of the parents from the opposing team are like, 'They're running NFL plays!'" Moses said.

 

 Stafford, the reigning NFL MVP, said he didn't lean too hard on his NFL expertise.

 "I'm just a dad out there at that point," Stafford said. "I could scheme up some stuff, but can we execute it? Probably not.

 "I'd draw something up, we'd run the play, I'd look at my sheet and be like, 'That's not anything what I thought I was going to get,' but we score a touchdown on it."

 

 LOS ANGELES CHARGERS outside linebacker Bud Dupree  said he will never forget when his sons -- Jett (8) and Ace (6) -- told him that they wanted to play flag football. Jett was 4 when he joined a team rather than just playing around with his dad and brother.

 Dupree said it was important to him that he coached his sons because he has seen how much youth sports has changed from when he was a kid.

 "A lot of coaches are in it for the wrong reasons," Dupree said. "A lot of coaches are gambling on the games. They yelling at the kids that never played sports in their life.

 "So, I want to make sure that [when they're young what] they're doing is not necessarily focused on all wins. It's focused on maturing in the game, getting better at the actual sport and learning from the mistakes that they playing and understanding the actual game of football."

 Dupree created several teams called BD Elite. His sons play on the 8U team, but he also has 10U, 15U team and 18U teams.

 

 "I started it for my kids, but along the way, I just wanted to reach as many kids as I could, and I took upon that to make it stand, man," Dupree said. "Now, I'm trying to get kids in college, give them scholarships, taking on that. It's not only affecting my kids' life, but affecting other kids."

 Carolina Panthers long snapper JJ Jansen coaches sons Luke, 13, and Ben, 7, in baseball. Jansen called coaching his "greatest passion," saying, "[It] takes up a lot of my time because I want it to take up a lot of my time." For the past five years, Jansen said he has coached during the NFL season and spends time during the week thinking about how he can "positively impact" the kids on his team.

 "Everything from scripting practice, thinking through how they each should develop in their own way," Jansen said. "One of my absolute favorite things to do is scripting out practice and going through each player, thinking, 'What do they need? What are the skills they need to develop? What [are] the strategies they need to learn?' I spend way too much time on it, but I love it."

 When Jaguars quarterback Nick Mullens ' son, Luke, 7,  started his first season of coach-pitch baseball in Birmingham, Alabama, Mullens told the head coach of his son's team he was available to help if needed but didn't want too much authority.

 The offer was gladly accepted. The first part, anyway.

 "A week into practice, I was the second in command," Mullens said. "The first practice, I was timid, but three practices in, you're like, 'All right, listen up.' And the kids start listening to you a little bit, so I really enjoy that aspect of it. It's a lot of fun."

 Moses said his goal is simple: for the kids on his team to learn the fundamentals of football.

 "I told everybody I really don't care if we win or lose, I just want the kids to walk away knowing they learned great football strategy," Moses said. "So when they leave, and if they don't play on my team the following year, they have a set of fundamentals they can lean on."

 

 EVEN THOUGH MULLENS is entering his NFL ninth season (20 starts) and was coaching his son in Birmingham, Alabama, the town right next to Hoover, Alabama, where he grew up and attended high school, he didn't get recognized much by other parents or coaches. Which meant he was inevitably going to be asked, "What do you do for a living?" by those parents and coaches as the league is active in the NFL offseason.

 At first, he was reluctant to tell them he was a professional football player because he knew the conversation would then revolve around that, and he'd rather talk to the other parents and coaches about their professions. So, he'd sometimes ... embellish a bit about his career.

 Such as the time he told someone he worked for a logistics company. But that presented a different problem for him.

 "Then, they keep asking you questions. You've got to make stuff up as you go," he joked. "So I've been down that path, and it's like, 'Dude, you're better off just telling people what you do.'"

 Jansen has done most of his coaching with former Panthers tight end Greg Olsen, who gets more attention than Jansen.

 "I think my younger kids get a kick out of it," Jansen said. "My older kids, it's a little bit of, like -- it's not an eye roll. It's just sort of like, 'Oh, here we go again.'"

 

 Jaguars punter Logan Cooke said he gets recognized by parents at times when helping coach his 5-year-old Cooper play T-ball, but the fact that he's a Pro Bowl punter means absolutely nothing to the players.

 "I'm not Trevor Lawrence walking out there so there's always subtle comments about it, good luck this weekend, stuff like that," he said. "But the kids have no idea, and they wouldn't even care. They're so young."

 

 FORMER NEW ENGLAND Patriots quarterback Brian Hoyer  serves as the offensive coordinator for the freshman football team at Xaverian Brothers High School in Westwood, Massachusetts, where his son, Garrett, is the starting quarterback.

 Hoyer, who played in the NFL from 2009 to 2023, was helping coach the varsity team after former NFL quarterback -- and Xaverian alum -- Matt Hasselbeck convinced him to help out. Hasselbeck served as the team's quarterbacks coach while his son Henry was in high school. 

 But when a coaching change left the freshman team without an offensive coordinator, Hoyer was asked if he wanted to take over.

 "I could have never guessed what it was going to entail," Hoyer said. "That started with basically creating a whole new offensive playbook, but tailored to the freshman level.

 "Understanding what freshman football is -- it's been forever since I've been exposed to it. You have kids playing football for the first time. It's been an adventure."

title: WR Garrett Wilson deems Patriots matchup a 'big-ass game' for Jets
summary: New York knows its first divisional game means a lot for the standings.
full_text:
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. -- When it comes to recent AFC East history, the New York Jets are like the orange ghost named Clyde in the "Pac-Man" arcade game -- the most erratic of the four ghosts, the one always lagging in the pursuit of Pac-Man.

 The Jets have finished last seven times in the last 10 seasons, in large part because they've been dominated within their own division. Their 13-47 divisional record over that span, including a staggering 4-26 on the road, is easily the worst in the NFL and 19 games behind the next-closest AFC East opponent, the Miami Dolphins (32-28).

 It's no wonder their division-title drought is older than rookie sensation David Bailey . They last won the AFC East in 2002, the year before Bailey was born.

 Every year sparks new hope, this notion that the Jets -- finally free of the Tom Brady-Bill Belichick vice grip -- will rise up and put up a legitimate fight against the New England Patriots , Buffalo Bills and Dolphins (though Miami looks down and out this year).

 

 And it never happens.

 Well, here they go again, preparing for their first divisional game -- Sunday ( 1 p.m. ET, CBS ) against the Patriots (3-2) at Gillette Stadium.

 There's a good vibe around the Jets (2-3), coming off a win and an eight-sack performance against the  Cleveland Browns . Now there's an opportunity to make a statement that things are going to be different, that Clyde is re-programmed and no longer wandering aimlessly around the maze.

 In coach Aaron Glenn's first year, the Jets went 0-6 in the division.

 "There's a premium on this one because it is our first one [in the division]," wide receiver Garrett Wilson said Wednesday. "I don't know how to exactly put it, but it's a big-ass game."

 Since Wilson's arrival in 2022, their divisional record is 6-18, with the three most recent wins coming against a backup quarterback (Miami's Tyler Huntley , 2024, Week 18), a quarterback on the verge of being benched (New England's Jacoby Brissett , 2024, Week 3) and another backup (New England's Bailey Zappe , 2023, Week 18).

 True, they did defeat Buffalo's Josh Allen in the 2023 opener, but that victory will forever be tarnished by  Aaron Rodgers ' season-ending Achilles' injury.

 From 2020 to 2022, the Jets lost 15 straight in the division.

 

 As a rookie, Wilson heard about the Patriots' dominance, how they owned the rivalry with a 12-game winning streak at the time. Wilson noticed how it weighed on the Jets' organization. It ballooned to 15 games before the Jets finally ended the misery in the 2023 season finale. Now Wilson wants the current rookies to understand the importance of the AFC East games.

 "To put yourself in the hunt, it's how did you stack up with the teams you play twice a year?" he said. "And this is our first one."

 There's an old saying in football, that divisional games count more than non-divisional ones. Makes sense, especially when you consider the tiebreaking criteria. There's also symbolism, meaning: If you can't handle the playground bullies in your own neighborhood, how do you expect to do it crosstown?

 It's fitting that the Jets play their first divisional game in Foxborough because -- let's be honest -- it's where they get pushed around the most.

 Before their win over Zappe & Co. in the 2023 finale -- Belichick's final game as the Patriots' coach -- the Jets had gone 12 seasons without a victory at Gillette. It came in the 2010 AFC Divisional playoffs, probably their best moment as a franchise since Super Bowl III in 1969.

 Since then, they're 1-14 in Foxborough, including six losses by 14 or more points. So, yes, a win Sunday would be massive for Glenn, who is trying to establish credibility for the franchise.

 

 "We really don't focus on what happened in the past when it comes to us -- we just focus on what's happening right now -- but, yes, division games are definitely crucial," Glenn said. "Sometimes people say they count as two games, but the only thing that we're focused on is, this is the one game that we have to play, this is the one game we want to win, this is the one game that we're prepared for and look to win."

 The Patriots with Brady and Belichick had a stranglehold on the division for two decades. When they split up in 2020, it figured to create parity in the AFC East. The Jets, for one, have failed to capitalize on the opening -- four last-place finishes and a 6-30 division record. The Robert Saleh- Zach Wilson -Rodgers era was a bust, and now they're one-plus season into the Glenn regime.

 Meanwhile, the Patriots, after a brief post-Brady/Belichick swoon, reinvented themselves with coach Mike Vrabel and quarterback Drake Maye .

 "I think it means the world," nickelback Jarvis Brownlee Jr . said of Sunday's matchup. "I think it means everything to this team, this organization, that if we go over there to the defending division champs and get a dub, man, I think that'd be awesome."

title: Bring on the blitz! Changing the identity of the Giants' defense
summary: The Giants uptick in blitzing could be correlated to Brian Burns being out with injury.
full_text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- No Brian Burns ? Not a problem for the time being for the New York Giants . Defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson has found a workaround without the team's top rusher. He's now bringing the blitz at the levels of former D.C. Wink Martindale. 

 Wilson has called for more than four rushers on 56.6% of the opposition's dropbacks the past two weeks after Burns was lost for the season with a torn ACL in his right knee in Week 3. That is second only behind the blitz-happy Brian Flores and the Minnesota Vikings . This after the Giants blitzed 23.1% of the time over the first three weeks, 26 th most in the NFL during that span. 

 "Dennard does a great job," coach John Harbaugh said. "He's got pretty much every blitz known to man in the system."

 The Giants found something on Sunday against the Washington Commanders and quarterback Jayden Daniels that worked, leading to a surprising tie . Wilson kept going to the well. He sent a defensive back as a blitzer on 15 of Daniels' 37 dropbacks (41%), their second-highest DB blitz rate in the past 10 seasons.

 New York sacked Daniels three times when sending DB blitzes, two of which came from cornerback Dru Phillips .

 "It's definitely a fun thing to do," Phillips said. "But it was cool to get out there and blitz a little bit."

 

 Overall, Daniels was 2-of-7 passing for 23 yards with five sacks under pressure in the contest. The blitzing worked. It also worked the previous week against Arizona's Jacoby Brissett , especially on the goal-line stand in the final seconds when the Giants sent a blitz on three of the final four plays to secure a victory.

 Brissett and Daniels combined completed just 45.7% of their passes against the blitz in the two games.

 The Giants seem to suggest the sudden uptick in blitzing has something to do with playing without Burns, who had 16.5 sacks last season. His replacement, Kayvon Thibodeaux , isn't that level of a pass rusher. He has a pass rush win rate of 6.6%, which is 137 th out of 142 qualifying rushers.

 But it also has something to do with the opponent. The Giants played against veterans Dak Prescott and Matthew Stafford the first two weeks of the season. There was much more hesitation blitzing such accomplished passers.

 "It's a great week-to-week game-planning mindset. Whether it has to do with Brian Burns being out or not, could be, but it's also who you're playing, [the] quarterback and those kind of things, or what the game situation calls for," Harbaugh said. "I think in this game [vs. Washington] you saw probably more [cover] zero all-out pressure blitzes from two teams in the fourth quarter and the fifth quarter than you'll ever see again, probably. I mean, every play pretty much was zero blitz by both teams, it seemed like. So, that's probably going to drive the numbers up a little bit game situation wise.

 "But we feel like we would consider ourselves probably a blitzing team generally, but we also consider ourselves a cover defense, too. We think we play zone-match [coverage] well. We think we play man [coverage] well. We think we can do all those things. We want to keep it moving on people."

 This week's opponent could bring a different approach as the Giants take on the New Orleans Saints on Sunday (1 p.m. ET, Fox). Saints QB Tyler Shough has been just a touch above average against the blitz with a 0.1% completion percentage above expectation (CPOE) so far this season. He has five touchdown passes and two interceptions against the blitz.

 Wilson isn't about to simply commit to all-out blitzing just because Burns is out. Or with his current top edge rusher Abdul Carter dealing with a minor calf injury. The quarterback and opponent matters. 

 "Yeah, it'll be a mixture of both," he said. "I think that we've always had pressures in our system. You know, like I say, the first two games this season, we played quarterbacks that feast off of pressure, knowing where to go. I think it's always matchup dependent. It's how the guys are playing. It's rhythm of the game. It's feel of the game. It's the ability to adjust during the game. We always have pressures up. So, we'll use them when we have to and be smart and educated about it."

 Wilson's track record doesn't show a heavy lean on the blitz. His Titans defense blitzed just 22.8% of dropbacks over the previous two seasons, the 22 nd highest rate. He sent DB blitzes 9.3% of dropbacks, which was 25 th over that span.

 Perhaps that changes a bit with the Giants shorthanded on pass rushers. It might be the best way for them to survive.

 "Dennard has a way of cooking things up, but it's definitely not I would say a consistent thing. It's a week-by-week thing off of, I guess what we're seeing and how we feel," Phillips said. "So, you just go out there and if they send me I'm going to try my best to go get there and everything but the percentage is just it goes off the flow of the game."

title: Is Seahawks OC Brian Fleury a 'home run' hire? How the rookie playcaller is faring
summary: Fleury took over the reigns of the Seahawks' Super Bowl champion offense despite never having called plays. How's he doing through five weeks?
full_text:
SEATTLE -- Sam Darnold has a favorite adjective for first-year   Seattle Seahawks  offensive coordinator Brian Fleury: stoic.

 "Whether it's a good play or bad play," Darnold said over the summer, "his mentality never changes out there on the field."

 That was true even when a wrench was thrown into Fleury's playcalling debut -- his starting quarterback going down on the fifth play of the Seahawks' season opener with what was later determined to be a glute injury.

 After taking over for Darnold, backup Drew Lock led five straight scoreless possessions. With the Seahawks trailing by seven early in the fourth quarter, they faced a fourth-and-1 from the New England Patriots ' 45-yard line. Fleury put the ball in Lock's hands, dialing up a play-action throw that resulted in a tying touchdown to wide receiver Jaxon Smith-Njigba . With Darnold watching on his phone from a nearby hospital, Lock led another field goal drive on the ensuing possession, and Seattle's defense sealed a  13-10 win with a third interception of Patriots quarterback Drake Maye .

 Afterward, Lock credited Fleury for providing a calming voice amid the chaos.

 "I think as a quarterback, with someone in the headset, you want them [to have the same demeanor] all the time," Lock said. "It was awesome to feel that from him tonight and see that from him and know that's what we're going to get moving forward."

 

 It has become clear what kind of personality Seattle has spearheading the offense. There was never much question as to what the West Coast scheme itself would look like, as it's largely unchanged from the one Klint Kubiak ran before leaving to become the head coach for the  Las Vegas Raiders . But there is a question of whether Fleury can pick up where his predecessor left off and coordinate a championship-caliber offense in his first season in that role at any level.

 Heading into a Thursday night matchup with the Denver Broncos (3-2) at Empower Field at Mile High ( 8:15 p.m. ET, Prime Video ), Fleury's offense ranks eighth in scoring at 26.8 points per game. But it's also 25th in expected points added and 26th in ESPN's efficiency metric, indicative of flaws that Seattle's defense and special teams have helped cover.

 Those flaws? Too many turnovers and an insufficient run game. Darnold has not taken care of the ball, throwing five interceptions in three games since returning in Week 3. And neither has Seattle's backfield, which also hasn't generated much production on the ground with its top two options -- rookie first-round pick Jadarian Price (chest) and Zach Charbonnet (knee) -- currently sidelined by injuries.

 Can a rookie coordinator fix those issues before the Seahawks (3-2) lose any more ground to the  San Francisco 49ers  (5-0) in the NFC West standings ?

 "His approach of trying to find solutions and working through things that arise, I think he's done a great job of that," coach Mike Macdonald said. "... I think he's doing a good job.

 "But we've got to continue as an offensive staff -- and Brian's leading our offensive staff -- of generating really clear plans that we can execute, and as an offense, executing at really a higher level."

 
 Fleury's path to Seattle 
 Fleury's coaching career unofficially began before his playing career ended.

 As a senior at Seneca Valley High School in Germantown, Maryland, he quarterbacked the Screaming Eagles -- who were coached by his stepfather -- to a 13-0 record and a Class 4A state championship in 1997. He scored a 1420 on his SAT, walked on at Maryland and transferred to Towson after one season.

 "You just knew he was going to be a coach, you just knew it," Gordy Combs, Towson's head coach at the time, told ESPN. "How he acted in meetings and knowing what was going on and paying attention all the time."

 The idea of following in his stepfather's footsteps was always in the back of Fleury's mind. He began to realize that was his calling when he got a chance in the spring to compete for the starting job at Towson with two years of eligibility remaining, only for an injury to end that bid. A younger quarterback won the competition, and Fleury never got another shot.

 

 "Immediately, I was asked to go out there and coach him, stand in the huddle with him and mentor him," Fleury said. "Really that experience is what nudged me over the edge."

 Fleury accepted his role.

 "He had all his oars in the water," Combs said.

 After entry-level roles on Maryland's staff for two seasons, Fleury's coaching career took an interesting turn in 2005. He was hired as the secondary coach at Sacred Heart, where he would also serve as defensive coordinator and outside linebackers coach the next three seasons.

 The former quarterback wouldn't return to the offensive side of the ball for another 10 seasons. That was after stints with Towson (special teams coordinator, defensive backs coach), the Buffalo Bills (quality control), the Cleveland Browns (assistant linebackers coach, outside linebackers coach) and Miami Dolphins (football research analyst, director of football research).

 Fleury would have preferred a coaching gig after Cleveland, but his role in Miami had him working alongside the Dolphins' staff, arming them with insights he'd gather by studying the rest of the league. Without having to pour all of his time and energy into coaching a position group, he was free to absorb the data and begin developing his own philosophies.

 "So at the time, I was a little bit frustrated because I wasn't dealing with players directly," Fleury said, "but in hindsight, it probably was one of the most valuable three-year periods of my life, just from a development standpoint."

 The path to offensive coordinator included one more stop: a quality control gig with the 49ers under defensive coordinator Robert Saleh. He spent one season in that role before coach Kyle Shanahan moved him to the other side of the ball. He was a quality control coach on offense for two seasons before a promotion to tight ends coach in 2022. Though he didn't add the title of run game coordinator until 2025, he was helping Shanahan devise run plays before that.

 

 "You talk about a person who understands all three phases," Saleh, now the Tennessee Titans ' head coach, told ESPN. "He knows linebacker play, he knows the secondary. To get the growth he had with Kyle on the offensive side of the ball, I think that's where you find the greatest coaches, the ones who understand both sides of the ball. ... They can watch tape and understand what guys are trying to get accomplished from a schematic standpoint.

 "I think it was a home run hire for Mike and his staff."

 
 Fleury the playcaller 
 Training camp practices tend to bring out colorful language from Macdonald as he runs Seattle's defense.

 "You've got to know what the f--- you're doing!" he yelled one day this summer, chiding a young defensive back after a blown assignment.

 Fleury, on the other hand, had such a subtle presence that you wouldn't know he was running Seattle's offense if he didn't have a radio in one hand and a call sheet in the other.

 "I think Coach Fleury does a great job of being all about ball," tight end AJ Barner said. "He runs his meetings the right way. He expects great things out of his players. He comes to work each day with the same kind of attitude that's just straight business."

 Fleury, 46, has plenty in common with his predecessor Kubiak, including their low-key vibe.

 "There's times [that] there's going to be fiery moments and things like that, but I thought he was so calm and collected and all that stuff," wide receiver Cooper Kupp said, comparing his last two OCs. "Brian is giving Klint a run for the money in terms of that same demeanor. ... There's just a clear understanding, so there's no jittery energy, there's no false energy.

 "It's just, 'Hey, this is what I know to be true. This is how we're going to execute it. These are my expectations. We're going to go out…
